title: The Probability Distribution of a Call Option
affiliations: , , , Khalifa University, Khalifa University and

detail.title: The Probability Distribution of a Call Option
detail.abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for modeling the probability distribution of derivative payoffs, shifting the analytical focus from the underlying asset to the derivative contract itself. The approach makes no approximations, introduces no free parameters, and initially assumes Geometric Brownian Motion, an assumption later relaxed. The central insight is that, given a probability distribution for the underlying asset, the distribution of any dependent derivative is fully determined by its payoff function, leaving no room for alternative analytical expressions. Building on the mathematical framework for functions of random variables from The Boltzmann Equation in Finance [2], we derive exact expressions for the probability density function (PDF) and cumulative distribution function (CDF) of call option payoffs at any point in their lifecycle. The core contribution is a generalized functional that maps any assumed PDF of the underlying asset to the PDF of an arbitrary derivative. This functional provides a unified, risk-focused framework: it allows tailoring the analysis to different payoff structures, directly computes risk measures such as Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES), and supports evaluation for both individual contingent claims and portfolios of derivatives. By making risk an explicit feature of the functional, the approach offers a powerful tool for derivative modeling, portfolio risk management, and strategic decision-making. To illustrate its flexibility, we apply the framework to derive the PDF of a binary call option payoff, showing that even non-smooth instruments can be analyzed without constraints on the underlying asset's distribution.

title: Reimagining Sustainable Development and Nation Building Through Artificial Intelligence: A Comprehensive Interdisciplinary Framework for All SDGs.
affiliations: Dr. Panjabrao Deshmukh Institute of Management Technology & Research, Nagpur

detail.title: Reimagining Sustainable Development and Nation Building Through Artificial Intelligence: A Comprehensive Interdisciplinary Framework for All SDGs.
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has emerged as a transformative force with unprecedented potential to accelerate progress toward the United Nations' 2030 Sustainable Development Goals. This paper presents a comprehensive interdisciplinary framework examining how AI technologies can be strategically leveraged across all 17 SDGs to address complex global challenges while strengthening national development capacities. Through systematic analysis of recent literature and case studies from 2020-2025, this research demonstrates that AI-driven solutions offer scalable, data-informed approaches to poverty alleviation, healthcare delivery, climate action, and institutional strengthening. The framework synthesizes technological capabilities with socioeconomic imperatives, addressing both opportunities and critical challenges including algorithmic bias, digital divides, and governance requirements. Findings indicate that successful AI integration requires multi-stakeholder collaboration, ethical frameworks, capacity building, and context-specific implementation strategies that balance innovation with equity and sustainability principles.

title: Supply Chain Risk Exposure and Organizational Performance: Evidence from a Manufacturing Firm in an Emerging Economy
affiliations: and University of Ilorin

detail.title: Supply Chain Risk Exposure and Organizational Performance: Evidence from a Manufacturing Firm in an Emerging Economy
detail.abstract: Supply chains are increasingly exposed to diverse risks arising from environmental uncertainty, human-induced disruptions, and infrastructural weaknesses, particularly in emerging economies. Understanding how these risks affect organizational performance is essential for effective risk management and resilience planning. This study examines the impact of supply chain risk exposure on organizational performance using evidence from a manufacturing firm operating in Nigeria. Specifically, it assesses the effects of natural disasters, man-made disruption, and infrastructural risks on organizational effectiveness, production delays, and service quality. A descriptive survey research design was employed, and data were collected from 340 respondents. The relationships between supply chain risk factors and performance outcomes were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicate that natural disaster risk exposure has a significant effect on organizational effectiveness (R2 = 0.649, p < 0.05), and man-made disruption risks significantly influence production delays (R2 = 0.799, p < 0.05). Infrastructural risks significantly affect service quality (R2 = 0.668, p < 0.05). These findings provide empirical evidence that supply chain risks substantially undermine organizational performance and increase operational vulnerability in manufacturing contexts. The study contributes to the risk management and supply chain risk literature by offering firm-level insights from an emerging economy and highlighting the importance of proactive risk mitigation, infrastructural investment, and organizational preparedness to enhance resilience and sustain performance under conditions of uncertainty.

detail.title: Strengthening Teacher Education through Effective Monitoring and Supervision in Nigerian Colleges of Education
detail.abstract: The quality of teacher education in Nigeria has continued to face significant challenges due to weak monitoring and supervision mechanisms in Colleges of Education. Despite their critical role in preparing future teachers, many of these institutions are constrained by poor infrastructure, inconsistent supervisory practices, inadequate policy implementation, and limited staff development initiatives. These shortcomings have contributed to declining teaching standards, ineffective learning outcomes, and reduced institutional accountability. The aim of this study is to examine the role of monitoring and supervision in promoting academic quality, professional growth, and institutional effectiveness in Colleges of Education. The study adopts a documentary analysis approach, drawing on conceptual clarifications, empirical insights, and comparative perspectives from both global and Nigerian contexts. Findings indicate that robust monitoring and supervision contribute to improved academic standards, effective teaching methodologies, and enhanced lecturer development through the engagement of Heads of Departments, Deans, Quality Assurance Officers, chief lecturers, directors of centres and external assessors. Furthermore, supportive and developmental supervision encourages innovation, fosters institutional credibility, and strengthens accountability frameworks. The study concludes that effective monitoring and supervision are indispensable for sustaining teacher education quality. It recommends enhanced government support, capacity building for supervisors, integration of ICT tools, the establishment of functional internal quality assurance units, and consistent policy frameworks to ensure sustainable improvement in the Nigerian teacher education system.

detail.abstract:
The accelerated global deployment of artificial intelligence has intensified debates on governance, safety, and economic competitiveness. To date, much of this discourse has been shaped by advanced economies and private technology actors, often privileging frontier capability and risk containment while underrepresenting the developmental, institutional, and access-related concerns of emerging and developing nations. The India AI Impact Summit 2026 constituted a deliberate intervention in this landscape by reframing artificial intelligence as an instrument of public value, inclusive growth, and democratic governance.

This white paper presents a structured analysis of India’s role and contributions as host of the Summit, examining its strategic architecture, policy orientation, and international implications. The study evaluates India’s interventions across multiple dimensions, including agenda-setting in global AI governance, the articulation of sovereign AI infrastructure as public capacity, the advancement of indigenous and multilingual AI capabilities, and the prioritisation of sectoral deployment in areas such as healthcare, agriculture, education, and public administration. In parallel, the paper critically assesses limitations of the Summit, including the non-binding nature of its outcomes, representational imbalances, and unresolved questions of accountability and implementation.

By situating the AI Impact Summit 2026 within the evolving international governance ecosystem, this analysis assesses whether India’s engagement represents a primarily symbolic diplomatic exercise or a substantive shift toward long-term stewardship in AI governance. The paper contributes to contemporary scholarship and policy debates on equitable AI governance, offering insights relevant to policymakers, academic researchers, and institutions seeking to align artificial intelligence with developmental priorities, institutional capacity, and democratic legitimacy.

Key themes: artificial intelligence governance; technology policy; Global South; sovereign AI infrastructure; development-oriented AI; public digital infrastructure.

title: When Complicated Governance Meets Complex Reality: Epistemic Breakdown in a Safety-Critical Acquisition Programme
affiliations: Rabdan Academy

detail.title: When Complicated Governance Meets Complex Reality: Epistemic Breakdown in a Safety-Critical Acquisition Programme
detail.abstract: Complex safety-critical programmes generate multiple, competing evidence streams – engineering test data, safety cases, user testimony, medical assessments – yet the institutional architectures governing these programmes are typically designed for complicated rather than complex problems. This article examines what happens when such architectures encounter emergent, interaction-driven phenomena. Using the UK’s Ajax armoured vehicle programme as an extended case study, it argues that the programme’s persistent difficulties – including physiological harm to crews from noise and vibration – are best understood not as technical, managerial or contractual failures but as epistemic pathologies: systematic breakdowns in how evidence was produced, validated, escalated, translated into decisions and communicated across institutional boundaries. Drawing on Edgar Morin’s critique of the ’paradigm of simplification’ and operationalised through established scholarship on organisational safety, resilience and systems thinking, high reliability organisations, and the sociology of expert knowledge, the article traces four epistemic pathologies through the public documentary record: decontextualised assurance, feedback suppression and the normalisation of deviance, narrative capture through the ecology of action, and contested truth criteria with the marginalisation of experiential knowledge. It introduces the concept of ’evidence ecology’ as a bridging framework linking safety governance, assurance practice and programme management, and derives design principles for complexity-informed epistemic governance. The analysis has implications for safety governance in any sector where assurance regimes designed for complicated systems confront socio-technical complexity.

title: When Complexities Interact: Human, Machine, and Organizational Entanglement

detail.title: When Complexities Interact: Human, Machine, and Organizational Entanglement

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none

detail.abstract: This paper develops a theory of entanglement among human, machine, and organizational complexity. It argues that these are distinct complexity formations, each generated and stabilized through a different dominant logic. Human complexity unfolds through embodied, affectively charged, and relationally constituted meaning-making. Machine complexity unfolds through computational abstraction, recursive output generation, scale, opacity, and accelerated iteration. Organizational complexity unfolds through institutionalized coordination, authorization, legibility, and memory-bearing procedure under conditions of uncertainty. The paper's central claim is that the interaction among these formations generates a distinct field of consequence that cannot be understood by examining any one of them in isolation, and that cannot be derived from existing adjacent frameworks. Through a comparative reconstruction of the three formations, the paper derives five mechanisms of interplay: translation, selective amplification, authorization and stabilization, complexity migration, and reflexive reconstitution. It further argues that differences in temporality are a primary shaping condition of this interplay, because human, machine, and organizational complexity operate on different clocks; this temporal argument is the paper's most original contribution. On this basis, chaos is conceptualized as an intensified condition of entanglement in which amplification, disorientation, temporal desynchronization, and erosion of repair capacity begin to outrun ordinary mechanisms of interpretation and containment. The paper uses AI-assisted recruitment and promotion as an orienting example. The contribution lies in shifting the center of analysis from adoption, augmentation, or isolated system performance to the dynamics of interacting complexities.

detail.abstract: Network theory has historically emphasized the strategic value of creating new ties, bridging structural holes, and expanding social capital. However, comparatively little attention has been given to the cumulative cost of relational destruction. This paper introduces the Theory of Closed Doors, a dynamic framework that conceptualizes the long-term impact of unnecessary relational rupture on future optionality. The model distinguishes between active, latent, and blocked ties and proposes the Index of Open Doors (IOD) and its complement, the Index of Closed Doors (ICD) as evolutionary measures of accessible relational capital. The central hypothesis suggests that individuals with lower ICD exhibit greater probability of obtaining relational support when future needs arise. The theory complements existing network literature by introducing a preservation-oriented dimension to relational strategy.

title: Financial Reporting and Employees
affiliations: Indiana University - Kelley School of Business, University of Texas at Austin, Harvard University - Business School (HBS) and Indiana University - Kelley School of Business

detail.title: Financial Reporting and Employees
detail.abstract: We survey nearly 6,000 employees of 1,265 publicly traded companies to understand whether and how public company employees use financial reporting information. Employees indicate that they: (1) are nearly universally aware of their firm's financial news, but primarily learn of such news through internal company communications rather than public news sources; (2) view their employer's financial condition as an important factor in employment decisions; (3) possess financial incentives to monitor reported results, with a majority reporting compensation linked to financial performance; (4) find operating metrics like earnings and sales more decision-relevant than stock returns; and (5) use public financial disclosures, such as earnings press releases and conference calls, to assess their employment prospects. We also provide novel evidence that firms operate an internal reporting regime that mirrors external reporting, disseminating financial information to employees predominantly on a quarterly basis, and that external disclosures may serve as verification for management's internal narrative. By measuring baseline rates of awareness, sources of information acquisition, preferred metrics, and perceived usefulness, we establish facts that can both support prior, and anchor future, research in the growing literature at the intersection of labor and accounting.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the decline of professional embarrassment in contemporary advertising and brand communication. It argues that a significant cultural and organizational shift has taken place within the industry: mediocre work is no longer consistently experienced as a visible professional failure but is increasingly normalized as an acceptable operational outcome. The paper proposes that terms such as "tactical," "agile," "platform-native," and "performance-led" often function not only as descriptive managerial language but also as rhetorical devices that protect weak, culturally interchangeable, or aesthetically inert work from stronger evaluative scrutiny. Drawing on practice-based observation, conceptual analysis, and relevant literature in advertising creativity, workplace creativity, branding, and platform studies, the paper develops an interpretive account of how speed, content flow, fragmented ownership, platformization, and perpetual visibility have weakened older forms of internal resistance within advertising culture. Its central claim is that the erosion of embarrassment has lowered informal professional standards and made banality more systemic than accidental. Rather than reading this development as simple creative decline or nostalgia for a lost era, the paper frames it as a structural transformation in the production and legitimation of brand communication.

title: Inventory Management Decision-making Under Zero-knowledge Conditions: A Behavioral Cloning Approach
affiliations: Hellenic Open University, Hellenic Open University, University of Piraeus and Hellenic Open University

detail.title: Inventory Management Decision-making Under Zero-knowledge Conditions: A Behavioral Cloning Approach
detail.abstract: Decision-making in inventory management is often challenged by the quality and volume of the available data. The most challenging cases arise during the introductory phases of first-launched products, where historical data are sparse and/or absent, thus expert judgment becomes the dominant decision protocol. Building on this premise, we introduce the notion of implied cognitive bias (ICB), a context-specific concept on judgment that emerges endogenously from informational scarcity, rather than just from stable psychological traits of decision makers. To operationalize this concept, we employ Behavioral Cloning (BC), a form of Imitation Learning, to replicate expert order-sizing decisions under a minimal information set. Using a business case involving newly introduced products, we model inventory decisions as a discrete-action policy learned from expert demonstrations. Policy fidelity is evaluated through distributional divergence metrics, combining Jensen-Shannon divergence to assess imitation quality and Wasserstein distance to express residual mismatches in action units. By comparing discrepancies between multiple horizons, we construct a residual measure that acts as a proxy for ICB, thus capturing systematic aspects of expert decision making that cannot be explained by the observable state variables. Empirical results from a casestudy indicate that BC can recover a significant share of expert behavior. These product-contingent residuals exhibit systematic variation across items and are partially associated with economic exposure, suggesting that ICB reflects structured judgmental adjustments rather than random noise or covariate shift phenomena. The findings position BC not only as a decision-replication tool, but also as an analytical layer for isolating and interpreting ICB in inventory decision-making.

title: Adam Smith, Human Capital and the Wealth of Nations
affiliations: University of Cambridge

detail.title: Adam Smith, Human Capital and the Wealth of Nations
detail.abstract: This essay examines Smith's insights into human capital as a primary driver of the wealth of nations. Adam Smith is celebrated as the founder of classical economics, yet his foundational role in articulating the principles of human capital is frequently overlooked. Writing in 1776, Smith predated the formal coining of 'human capital' by centuries, yet he clearly identified human skills, education, and health as analogous physical capital. Smith compared educated individuals to expensive machinery, and analyzed how specialization and training drive productivity, and showed prescient understanding of market dynamics such as supply, demand, and wage premiums. Smith further showed sophisticated views regarding the merits of public education. Although a proponent of markets, he acknowledged externalities in education and supported limited public intervention. By synthesizing Smith's observations with modern economic frameworks, this work argues that Smith is an intellectual progenitor of human capital theory, recognizing that a nation's prosperity depends fundamentally on the cultivation of human abilities.

title: Back to the Future-Proof: Four Reforms for the Better Regulation of Dark Patterns Under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive and Article 25 of the Digital Services Act
affiliations: CEDIS -  Nova School of Law, University of Genoa, Utrecht University and CEDIS -  Nova School of Law - NOVA Consumer Lab

detail.title: Back to the Future-Proof: Four Reforms for the Better Regulation of Dark Patterns Under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive and Article 25 of the Digital Services Act
detail.abstract: The efficacy of the "future-proof" Unfair Commercial Practices Directive against dark patterns is undermined by the fragmented regulatory landscape introduced by the Digital Services Act. Article 25 DSA creates four weaknesses: a general prohibition that is vague compared to the UCPD's detailed framework; a narrow subjective scope that excludes many online traders; an exclusion clause in Article 25(2) that replaces cumulative application with an opaque hierarchy; and slow soft-law mechanisms for updating the law in response to new dark patterns. To resolve these contradictions, this article proposes four targeted reforms: first, repurposing Article 25(1) DSA as an institutional gateway for DSA authorities to apply substantive UCPD rules using the stronger DSA sanctions and enforcement regime; second, extending the prohibition's scope to all intermediary service providers; third, the repeal of Article 25(2) DSA; and fourth, granting the Commission the power to update the UCPD blacklist via delegated acts for a swift response to emerging dark patterns. These reforms, particularly in combination, offer a coherent, future-proof regulatory framework that restores the centrality of the UCPD, preserves the innovations of the DSA, and equips EU law to address both current and emerging forms of dark patterns.

title: The Political Nature of The Firm

detail.title: The Political Nature of The Firm

publicationDetails.detailsText: Mari, M. (2026). The Political Nature of The Firm. Corporate Statecraft Working Paper Series, CSWPS–2026–002. Italia Innovation

detail.abstract: Political economy holds that firms adapt to institutional environments. The question is when firms produce them. At regional scale, institutional environments are not always settled — new industries lack governing arrangements, declining communities face collapsed order, abandoned places have lost the coordination that once sustained them. Under conditions of vacuum, capability, and agency, firms extend their coordinating capacity beyond their boundaries to produce institutional order directly. This is corporate statecraft. The concept extends the Coase-Williamson-North tradition: firms produce governance not only through internal hierarchy but by building infrastructure, setting standards, convening actors, and transferring legitimacy beyond their boundaries — accepting reduced control in exchange for extended coordination. Four cases drawn from fieldwork ground the concept: Terman's Stanford, Miller's Cummins, the Allegheny Conference's Pittsburgh, Long's American Woolen. They confront different forms of institutional vacuum and vary in orientation — open statecraft enabling broad participation versus closed statecraft entrenching incumbents — with consequences for regional outcomes. The firm is a governance source, not only governance structure.

title: Equipping Investors, Boards, Management, And Policymakers To Make Better Decisions

detail.title: Equipping Investors, Boards, Management, And Policymakers To Make Better Decisions
detail.abstract: Missing from debates about the need to reform capitalism and the never-resolved debates about shareholder capitalism versus stakeholder capitalism is a viable theory of the firm. This slide presentation focuses on one especially important use of a theory of the firm, which is to understand the past in a way that generates insights that enable better future decisions. The text slides highlight why the Pragmatic Theory of the Firm (PTF) is substantially more useful than other theories of the firm. The slides that display life-cycle track records for firms, and related historical analyses (case studies), are not concerned with a comprehensive detailed analysis of a firm’s history. Rather, these slides illustrate how the PTF way of thinking can pinpoint the foundational causes of a firm’s past performance—Nvidia, Deere, Walmart, etc. (ten case studies). The case studies provide a practical means to experience that the PTF is especially well-suited for analyzing past performance of firms and their business units. The usefulness of this slide presentation in the classroom can be demonstrated by a gain in experiential knowledge (business history case studies) dependent upon a viable theory of the firm.

detail.title: High-Touch Capability as Core Infrastructure: The Capability Market Layer and the Reorganisation of Economic Systems Working Paper

detail.abstract:
Institutions across finance, health and services have achieved significant integration, combining high-tech platforms with high-touch human engagement to deliver lifecycle-based support at scale. However, a structural gap persists: capability is continuously produced within institutions but remains unstructured at the system level. This paper introduces an architecture designed to resolve this gap by elevating capability from an internal institutional output to a system-level economic asset.

The paper develops the concept of the Capability Market Layer, a parallel economic substrate through which capability is quantified, standardised, expressed and routed across institutions. In this model, capability becomes portable and allocatable, aligning human potential with capital flows and reducing systemic friction. The Capability Market Layer reframes the economic landscape: institutions optimise platforms, capability-centric systems organise markets, high-touch capability becomes core infrastructure, individuals gain mobility across providers, and economies increase resilience through reduced friction.

The analysis examines integrated service models in large institutions, which combine digital platforms with advisory and human support across the lifecycle. While these systems generate capability—such as behavioural consistency, decision stability and resilience—they do not systematically structure or allocate it. Capability therefore remains institutionally bounded, limiting system-level coordination and efficiency.

To address this, the paper introduces Capability Extraction as a market primitive. This process converts heterogeneous signals—financial stability, behavioural patterns, cognitive load and health indicators—into a dynamic Capability Profile. This profile generates Participation Velocity, defined as the forward-looking probability that an individual will sustain productive economic participation over a ten-year horizon. Participation Velocity provides a cross-domain, quantifiable and interoperable measure of capability for allocation and system design.

High-touch capability is then defined as human infrastructure: advisory, coaching and behavioural stabilisation functions that sustain participation and prevent capability decay. Without sufficient throughput, systems experience drop-off, churn and misallocation of capital. Capability is therefore dependent on stabilising human infrastructure rather than service delivery alone.

Affordability is situated as systemic conductance—the structural property governing whether capability is constrained to survival or enabled to compound. Lower structural costs increase participation, reduce cognitive load and enhance mobility.

Workforce strategy is reframed as stability architecture. Investment in wages, benefits, training and wellbeing functions as capability formation infrastructure, strengthening long-term Participation Velocity by expanding the individual’s opportunity frontier.

Within this framework, institutions are repositioned as participants in a broader capability ecosystem rather than owners of economic actors. The Capability Market Layer enables portability of capability across providers, shifting competition from customer ownership to capability outcomes.

Finally, the Capability Market Layer operates as a high-fidelity clearing environment in which institutions are matched to individuals based on expected capability uplift. This creates a closed-loop system in which capability is measured, routed and reinforced across the economy.

This paper contributes a structural model of capability as an allocatable economic substrate through the introduction of the Capability Market Layer.

title: Domestic Sovereignty and Architectural Negligence: A New Jurisprudence for Digital Behavioural Infrastructure

detail.title: Domestic Sovereignty and Architectural Negligence: A New Jurisprudence for Digital Behavioural Infrastructure

detail.abstract:
This monograph identifies a jurisdictional crisis at the intersection of Antitrust and Tort law. It argues that digital platforms are not products, publishers, or services, but behavioural infrastructures whose design architectures exert regulatory force inside the home. Existing legal doctrines—both in the UK and the United States—are structurally incapable of recognising or governing this form of harm because they were built for a world of physical objects, not invasive digital signals.

The Los Angeles County verdict against Meta exposes this doctrinal mismatch. By classifying a behavioural environment as a “product,” the court improvised its way toward a just outcome, revealing a deeper Jurisdictional Crisis: the collapse of legal certainty when doctrine loses contact with technological reality.

This monograph introduces a new legal category—Digital Behavioural Infrastructure—and a new theory of liability—Architectural Negligence—to govern the behavioural physics of digital environments. It also articulates a structural theory of the home as a Household Core, a sovereign governance unit whose integrity must be protected from external behavioural utilities.

The result is a new jurisprudence for the digital era: one that restores Domestic Sovereignty, protects Human Durability, and provides courts and policymakers with the conceptual tools needed to regulate behavioural design.

title: Wage Phillips Curve of a Large Emerging Economy: Role of Structural Heterogeneity
affiliations: Reserve Bank of India, Reserve Bank of India and Government of India - Reserve Bank of India

detail.title: Wage Phillips Curve of a Large Emerging Economy: Role of Structural Heterogeneity
detail.abstract: This paper demonstrates existence of the non-linear wage-Phillips curve in large emerging market economies using a state-level panel for India over 2017Q3–2024Q4. We find a negative and convex relationship between earnings growth and unemployment, only after controlling for structural labour market characteristics that vary across time and states. Higher underemployment shifts the curve downward, greater skilling shifts it outward, and faster formalization flattens the curve by weakening the responsiveness of earnings growth to unemployment. These findings are robust across nonlinear specifications and remain valid in a post-COVID subsample. The results highlight the central role of structural labour market dynamics in shaping Phillips curve trade-offs and underscore the challenges they pose for monetary policy in emerging economies.

title: Risk Spillovers Between Carbon Markets and Power Generation Industries Under the Shocks of Major Events and Uncertainties

detail.title: Risk Spillovers Between Carbon Markets and Power Generation Industries Under the Shocks of Major Events and Uncertainties
detail.abstract: The carbon market and the power generation sector are closely interconnected, with major events and frequent uncertainties shaping their linkages. Previous studies have predominantly analyzed time-domain spillovers between carbon and electricity markets, rather than focusing on the power-generation sector. In this study, we employ TVP-VAR models to quantify risk spillovers in the time–frequency domains among three regional carbon markets and seven power-generation subsectors, and we examine how these spillovers vary across four categories of major events and external uncertainties. We find that carbon markets and the hydropower sector predominantly act as net receivers of risk, while the nuclear power sector is the strongest net transmitter. Spillovers between carbon markets and the power-generation sectors are predominantly short-term and responsive to major events, including the Sino‑U.S. trade war, the COVID-19 pandemic, the launch of China’s national carbon market, and the Russia–Ukraine war. Further analysis indicates that climate risks and economic policy uncertainty typically strengthen spillovers; however, the COVID-19 pandemic reverses the effect of economic policy uncertainty on spillovers. These findings have important implications for risk management and the coordinated development of carbon markets and the power-generation sectors under uncertainty.

detail.abstract: The efficacy of public sector organizations is significantly impacted by the extent of political interference in administrative processes and the honesty of recruitment procedures. With implications for public sector reforms in developing economies, this study investigated the effects of meritocracy, zoning practices and godfatherism on employee service delivery in the Nigerian civil service. The study used a quantitative research design and gathered primary data from a sample of 350 employing structured questions to get responses. The data was assessed using descriptive statistics and regression analysis at a 5% significance level using SPSS (Version 25) while PESTEL assessment was used to give a more comprehensive and indepth analysis. The findings showed that godfatherism has a statistically significant impact on employee service delivery, albeit with a relatively low explanatory power (R² = 0.075, p < 0.05), and zoning-based appointment practices have a weak but statistically significant effect (R² = 0.014, p = 0.029). Merit-based recruitment showed a greater and statistically significant improvement in employee service delivery (R² = 0.164, p < 0.05).These results imply that meritocracy increases efficiency and productivity whereas political interference reduces public sector performance. The study concludes that improving service delivery requires strengthening merit-based systems and minimizing political interference. It recommends policy improvements focused on accountability, transparency and institutional independence to enhance public sector performance in Nigeria and other developing countries.

detail.abstract: This paper quantifies the long-term economic costs of the Chernobyl Nuclear Disaster by leveraging a large geospatial dataset. We begin by developing a global framework for the impact of the disaster consisting of two channels: (1) a direct effect of the disaster, and (2) a perception effect, capturing heightened risk aversion to living or investing near non-Chernobyl nuclear power plants (NPPs). We test this model using a novel geospatial dataset comprising over 2.7 million gridded cells spanning 1992-2013. We then isolate the effect of radiation on per capita economic growth by matching local geospatial data with radiation soil samples collected in Ukraine after the disaster. Since rainfall patterns mainly drove radiation dispersion, we argue that radiation intensity is exogenous conditional on distance to the Chernobyl plant. We exploit this exogeneity to estimate the causal effect of radiation on productivity growth. We have three key results. First, we find that areas closer to a non-Chernobyl NPP saw weaker growth in labour productivity, suggesting that the disaster triggered a perception shock. Second, in areas within 25-75km of Chernobyl, we find a positive direct effect, even after accounting for perception effects. Finally, we find that a 1 percent increase in soil-derived radiation reduced productivity growth by 0.47 percentage points between 1992-1997, but that areas of high radiation intensity caught up in more recent years, potentially due to radiation decay and further dispersion. Together, these findings highlight the farreaching economic consequences of the Chernobyl disaster, shaping productivity both locally and globally through distinct channels.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the prevalence of three behavioral biases, Loss Aversion, Present Bias, and Sunk Cost, among males across different age groups and levels of financial experience. detail.abstract: The use of synthetic data has generated considerable heat (but not as much light) in the consumer insights world. While we should not be fully replacing human respondents any time soon, there is enough evidence to make a strong case for certain uses of synthetic data and that is what we aim to do here. Why Use Synthetic Data Let's start at the most basic level with the need for consumer insights. It's a truism that uncertainty impedes decision-making. Hence, business research is a process for reducing uncertainty enough to help make decisions. Insights research generally proceeds as a series of steps with the number of steps depending on the amount of information at hand and the degree of uncertainty. But it also depends on practicality whereby business decisions are often made with less than desired information. In some cases, research is not even attempted because of perceived hurdles, and decisions are simply based on intuition or existing knowledge/perceptions.

detail.title: When Attribution Fails: Selection, Targeting, and Measurement in Real-Time Bidding Advertising
detail.abstract: Attribution models are widely used in real-time bidding (RTB) advertising to guide targeting, budget allocation, and campaign evaluation. A common intuition is that clicked impressions are more valuable because clicked touchpoints often appear behaviorally prominent and closer to conversion. In dynamically targeted environments, however, clicks are endogenous to user intent. Using large-scale impression-level data, we construct a Selection-Adjusted Benchmark (SAB) based on cross-fitted double machine learning to assess how much of the observed click-conversion relationship survives after conditioning on rich user state. In the benchmark estimation sample, the simple 24-hour click contrast is not positive, and the SAB estimate is negative. A backward-looking placebo test remains strongly positive, indicating persistent residual selection even after rich adjustment. We therefore construct a Selection-Adjusted Campaign Signal (SACS) by aggregating residualized signals at the campaign level. SACS is not a causal estimate of campaign effectiveness, but it provides a more disciplined basis for supportaware screening, prioritization, and follow-up experimentation. The results show that attribution error changes campaign prioritization, not just statistical interpretation, and illustrate a broader information-systems tension: algorithmic systems that improve operational targeting can simultaneously degrade the interpretability of the signals used for managerial control.

detail.title: Knowledge graph-enhanced recommendation via multi-level interactive contrastive learning and attention mechanisms
detail.abstract: Knowledge Graph-based Recommendation (KGR) leverages rich semantic associations in knowledge graphs to enhance recommendation performance and is widely used in e-commerce. Recently, there has been growing interest in leveraging graph contrastive learning to enhance KGR, and achieves success to some extent. However, existing studies still encounter the following limitations. First, neglecting the structured information of neighboring triplets, which may result in the absence of crucial information. Second, The higher-order relationships and global organization of entities in knowledge graphs have yet to be fully exploited. To tackle these challenges, this study presents a novel Knowledge Graph-enhanced Recommendation model via Multi-Attention and Contrastive Learning (KGR-MACL). Its key innovations include an enhanced attention mechanism for knowledge graphs and multi-level interactive contrastive learning. Specifically, KGR-MACL first generates local and global entity embeddings using an enhanced knowledge-aware graph attention network that combines entities with their neighboring triplets to capture relational and topological structures, enabling high-order representation learning. It then employs a multi-level interactive contrastive learning framework: (1) local interactive contrastive learning balances collaborative filtering and knowledge graph influences at both levels; and (2) global interactive contrastive learning integrates local and global information by comparing local entity sets with their global counterparts. Empirical results on three real-world datasets confirm that KGR-MACL achieves substantial performance gains over leading baseline methods. Keywords: Recommender system, Knowledge graph, Neural graph network, Contrastive learning, Attention mechanism.

title: The Algorithm Has No Gender, But Its Outcomes Do: Platform Capitalism, Structural Bias, and Women's Digital Entrepreneurship

detail.abstract:
Purpose: The study critically examines how digital platforms, often touted as democratizing forces for entrepreneurship, reinforce and intensify gendered inequalities through algorithmic oppression. It introduces the Online Patriarchy Model to explain how platform design, algorithms, and governance structures replicate and reconfigure patriarchal norms, focusing on the challenges and adaptive strategies of women entrepreneurs operating in digital economies. It also introduces the Intersectional Gender Equity Assessment Framework (IGEAF), a systemic analytical framework designed to evaluate, monitor, and reform algorithmic systems by foregrounding how gendered and intersecting inequalities are produced, sustained, or amplified through digital platforms. 

 Methodology: Employing a qualitative case study design, the research draws on interdisciplinary literature in digital sociology, gender studies, and platform economics, and synthesizes qualitative evidence from peer-reviewed journal articles and books, as well as a case study of the Gamergate controversy. The study develops and applies the Online Patriarchy Model and the concept of Online Patriarchal Bargains to systematically analyse the interplay between digital platforms and gendered entrepreneurial experiences. 

 Findings: Algorithms trained on biased historical data and designed predominantly by male-dominated teams systematically disadvantage women-led ventures by limiting their visibility, access to funding, and opportunities through data-driven and structural discrimination. Women entrepreneurs respond to these constraints with resilient strategies such as performative self-presentation, algorithmic gaming, digital solidarity networks, and boundary-setting, but these acts often reinforce the gendered codes they seek to overcome. The study argues that digital entrepreneurship, despite its inclusive rhetoric, imposes new forms of emotional and invisible labor on women while demanding conformity with masculinist metrics of success. 

 Research Implications: The research highlights the need for fundamental transformations in platform design, algorithmic auditing, and regulatory governance to address algorithmic oppression. It underscores the necessity of centering women entrepreneurs’ voices and leadership in technology development, policy, and scholarly inquiry, and proposes multi-pronged interventions, such as gender-aware algorithmic audits and inclusive platform governance mechanisms. 

 Practical Implications: To overcome algorithmic oppression, platform managers and policymakers must embed gender impact assessments, enforce robust anti-harassment systems, and create mechanisms for transparent, accountable, and contestable algorithmic decisions. Tech industry practices must prioritize social justice, inclusive design, and equity over narrow efficiency and profit maximisation, while also building competencies in algorithmic equity across the sector.

 Social Implications: The study reveals how online patriarchal bargains strategic compromises to survive in digital spaces are both symptoms of and responses to platform-mediated inequalities, resulting in heightened costs of emotional labor and self-curation for women. These dynamics not only reinforce gender hierarchies but may also limit the diversity of voices in digital economies and public discourse, calling for collective action to reimagine digital spaces as equitable, empowering environments. 

 Originality/Value: The research makes original theoretical contributions through the Online Patriarchy Model and the Intersectional Gender Equity Assessment Framework (IGEAF). IGEAF integrates intersectionality, participatory governance, and continuous auditing across three iterative phases: pre-deployment assessment, deployment and monitoring, and post deployment review. These phases enable the identification of allocative, representational, procedural, and emotional harms embedded within data practices, design choices, and governance structures. By combining gender-disaggregated performance metrics, stakeholder co-design, transparency and explanatory audits, and institutional accountability mechanisms, IGEAF reframes algorithmic governance as a socio-technical responsibility rather than a purely technical problem. In doing so, it demonstrates that digital systems do not merely optimise efficiency but actively shape and can be redesigned to advance equity, dignity, and inclusion.

title: The Fundamental Laws Of Digital Authenticity The Special Theory of Identity, Provenance, and Truth in the Digital Universe

detail.title: The Fundamental Laws Of Digital Authenticity The Special Theory of Identity, Provenance, and Truth in the Digital Universe
detail.abstract:
Digital systems now mediate identity, communication, commerce, governance, and intelligence. Yet the foundations of digital truth remain fragmented and fragile. Identity is loosely bound. Provenance is inconsistent. Lifecycle transitions are unauthenticated. Auditability is uneven. As AI accelerates the creation of synthetic content and autonomous agents, the gap between digital activity and verifiable truth is widening.

This paper introduces the Special Theory of Digital Authenticity — a set of irreducible primitives that function as the governing laws of identity, provenance, lifecycle, and truth across all digital systems. These primitives are not features, frameworks, or standards. They are invariants: the minimum structural conditions required for any digital ecosystem to maintain coherence, trust, and regulatory alignment. These laws are structural invariants of any system that seeks to maintain digital truth, not physical laws of nature.

title: What Cannot Be Safe at the Capability Frontier
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: What Cannot Be Safe at the Capability Frontier
detail.abstract:
What Cannot Be Safe at the Frontier argues that safety at the capability frontier is not an alignment problem but an admissibility problem. Where envelope-exiting world-state trajectories — transitions from which recovery cannot be reliably achieved within bounded temporal, informational, or material constraints — remain unilaterally reachable by an optimizing system, behavioral reliability is structurally insufficient regardless of alignment quality. Probabilistic safety frameworks implicitly assume Gaussian-frame failure distributions; at the capability frontier, exposure is heavy-tailed, and the mechanisms that adequately govern reversible failures are categorically inadequate for irreversible ones. Safety requires bounding the reachable state space prior to optimization, not shaping behavior probabilistically within an unbounded one.

The paper develops this in two independent branches from a shared premise. Part I establishes that the capability-sovereignty distinction is irreducible: what a system can make reachable and what it is permitted to actualize are distinct design variables, and conflating them leaves the authority question unaddressed. Part II derives the architectural requirements that follow — a defensibility kernel (invariant kernel) enforcing admissibility constraints upstream of actuation, compositionally closed across interacting systems, with admissibility defined by an external ratification authority operating outside the optimization loop. Both branches terminate at honest limits: an unsolved engineering frontier (non-bypassable enforcement under capability growth) and an irreducible epistemic barrier (the tail-characterizing observation cannot be collected without incurring the outcome being prevented). Their convergence at the conclusion is the paper's central finding.

The contribution is a reframing: from alignment-as-safety to admissibility-as-prerequisite. Alignment and optimization remain necessary within the admissible set; they cannot define its boundaries.

detail.abstract: This study examines how AI initiatives influence corporate financial performance across two dimensions: immediate market signaling and lagged operational benefits. Using a panel dataset of 628 publicly listed U.S. firms in the technology, telecommunications, and industrial sectors (NYSE and Nasdaq) from 2014 to 2024, we employ fixed-effects panel regressions with clustered standard errors to isolate within-firm variation. AI-related keyword counts from annual 10-K filings serve as the primary measure of AI disclosure intensity. We find that AI adoption generates sector-heterogeneous effects: technology firms benefit from a credibility premium in capital markets, while telecommunications firms realize delayed efficiency gains, and industrial firms face persistent margin pressures from legacy system integration. Robustness checks using PCA-adjusted controls and winsorization confirm the stability of results. Structural equation modeling further reveals that cost efficiency-rather than revenue growth-is the dominant pathway through which AI shapes EBITDA margins, with the effect concentrated in technology firms. detail.abstract: The concept of 'compute sovereignty' has become a focal point in government and industry discussions on artificial intelligence (AI) governance. What is it and who has it? Based on previous literature, we propose to break these questions down to three levels: (1) how much AI compute a country has on its territory, (2) what is the nationality of the companies who own the AI compute data centres, and (3) what is the nationality of the accelerator vendors whose chips power the AI compute data centres? We examine these questions empirically through the lens of cloud computing infrastructure, focusing on nine leading public cloud providers that represent approximately 70 percent of the global market. The data is collected using a methodology previously published in Lehdonvirta, Wu, and Hawkins (2024). The findings suggest that the possession of "compute sovereignty" varies between countries depending on the level of analysis. Determining the most relevant level depends on governments' policy aims and national contexts, and involves policy trade-offs. Policies aimed at attracting data centres to a country's territory can enhance supply security of critical computational resources while also introducing increased consumption of energy, water and land use resources, with corresponding localised socioeconomic and environmental impacts. Regional and supply chain approaches involve different trade-offs.

While organizational leaders are still discovering effective methods to leverage AI, they must also minimize the new human risks. One way to reduce human risk is by building and strengthening the cybersecurity culture of an organization. We define culture as the attitudes, beliefs, and values that drive employee behavior. This research studied how AI impacts human risk management by fostering or hindering cybersecurity culture, uncovering recommendations that managers can employ to enhance their cybersecurity culture maturity. This study does not focus on the potential for AI to replace humans. Instead, the goal is to enhance general managers' understanding of both the intended and unintended consequences of AI on their cybersecurity culture and providing actionable insights to improve the effectiveness of their decisions on investments in culture. Three Key Points: 1. Leaders have a responsibility to find ways to keep their organizations cybersecure and resilient and the adoption of AI is making this an increasingly urgent need. Managing human risk through driving a culture of cybersecurity is one of their key tools. 2. AI can positively and negatively influence a cybersecurity culture, the values, attitudes and beliefs that drive cybersecure behaviors, and leaders need new mechanisms to manage both the intended and unintended consequences. 3. AI creates new ways for managers to have visibility, efficiencies, quantification, personalization and scalability of mechanisms they use to influence the cybersecurity culture of their organization. Using these approaches sparks new ways to use AI tools to build, change, and mature culture.

detail.abstract: AI-mediated discovery systems have fundamentally altered the conditions under which organizational brand visibility is produced and maintained. Where traditional search environments rewarded ranking optimization, AI systems reconstruct brand representations from distributed signals-synthesizing content, structured data, thirdparty sources, and historical signals into responses that users receive without visiting organizational properties. This shift produces a zero-click visibility problem: organizations influence decisions they cannot observe, through representations they do not control, in systems they cannot audit directly. This paper introduces the Brand Visibility Maturity Model (BVMM), a governance framework that assesses how effectively organizations govern the signals that AI systems use to construct their brand representations. Drawing on capability maturity modeling in the CMMI tradition, the BVMM evaluates governance maturity across seven domains-Content, SEO, AI Governance, Accessibility, Website Performance, Local Visibility, and International Visibility-using a five-level behavioral maturity scale. The framework is positioned at the intersection of platform governance, information retrieval, algorithmic accountability, and organizational governance theory. Its primary application is as a teaching instrument in postgraduate programs addressing AI-mediated visibility governance, and as a professional assessment tool for organizations seeking to evaluate and improve their governance posture in an AI-mediated discovery environment.

detail.abstract: Institutional accountability systems were not designed as verification systems. They emerged as side effects of production constraints: the difficulty and cost of generating plausible professional output served as an implicit filter for competence. Generative AI collapses these production costs to near zero, exposing an accountability gap that is structural rather than novel. This paper argues that the transition from scarcity-based to design-based verification is the central governance challenge of AI-augmented institutions. It examines the historical function of production friction as implicit verification, surveys current governance responses and their limitations, proposes design principles for institutional verification architecture informed by high-reliability sector precedents, and addresses the verification escalation posed by agentic AI systems. Sector-specific applications are developed for higher education, financial services, healthcare, and public administration. The paper concludes that effective AI governance must regulate the embedding of AI in institutional decision processes rather than AI systems themselves, and that the window for institutional redesign narrows as AI capability increases.

detail.abstract: Recent formal work has demonstrated that even ideal Bayesian reasoners are vulnerable to delusional spiralling when interacting with sycophantic AI chatbots (Chandra et al., 2026). That model treats the chatbot's sycophancy rate as an exogenous parameter: a fixed property of the model determined by training. This paper argues that sycophancy is better understood as endogenous to the interaction. User satisfaction signals, whether expressed through explicit feedback, continued engagement, or conversational framing, create a return path that reinforces sycophantic behaviour within and across sessions. This paper extends Chandra et al.'s Bayesian simulation framework by replacing the fixed sycophancy parameter with a dynamically evolving variable updated by user satisfaction at each conversational turn. This paper replicates their baseline results, and then show that under coupling: (1) spiralling rates increase across all four conditions they tested, with the largest increases at low initial sycophancy where real-world systems operate; (2) sycophancy emerges from initially neutral systems, meaning it need not be designed or trained into a model to produce spiralling; and (3) the mitigation Chandra et al. found most effective, user awareness of sycophancy, is disproportionately undermined by the coupling mechanism. These results are qualitatively invariant across six alternative functional forms for the sycophancy update rule. This paper situates these findings within the Mirror Effect framework (Gallacher, 2026a), which characterises human-AI interaction as a coupled system whose emergent properties cannot be attributed to either party in isolation and discusses implications for mitigation design.

title: Online Contracts in Nigeria: Formation and Challenges

detail.title: Online Contracts in Nigeria: Formation and Challenges
detail.abstract: The growth of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) has changed the way business is done in Nigeria. With the rise of e-commerce, buying and selling no longer require physical meetings or paper documents. Today, agreements are made through emails, websites, mobile applications, and other digital platforms. Despite this shift in method, the foundation of every commercial transaction remains the same: a contract. Whether concluded orally, in writing, by conduct, or online, a contract exists where parties agree to be legally bound in exchange for value. This article examines how online contracts are formed under Nigerian law and the challenges that arise in applying traditional contract principles to digital transactions. It argues that the essential elements of contract, offer, acceptance, consideration, intention to create legal relations, and certainty of terms are equally applicable to online agreements. However, the digital environment introduces unique issues, including online contracts, digital consent, identity verification, data protection, and jurisdiction in cross-border transactions. The paper highlights the gaps within Nigeria's existing legal framework, much of which was developed before the rise of the digital economy. These gaps create uncertainty in enforcement and consumer protection. It concludes that while traditional contract law principles remain relevant, there is a need for clearer legislation, stronger regulatory structures, and improved judicial capacity to effectively address the realities of online contracting in Nigeria's evolving digital marketplace.

detail.abstract:
This research examines how stock prices react to single and double financial restatements using a proprietary dataset of 1,004 listed firms from 2010 to 2025 fiscal years. It shows that investor responses vary depending on the nature and materiality of restatements, with reactions often occurring gradually rather than immediately.

Market responses differ across countries, sectors, and industries. Financial Services and Industrials show the strongest reactions, while Consumer Cyclical and Technology respond more slowly. The United Kingdom is more sensitive to initial restatements, whereas the United States and France react more strongly to double revisions. Key financial measures, such as earnings and dividends play an important role in shaping these effects.

Overall, the findings suggest that restatements may act as signals of reporting quality, with investors updating their beliefs over time rather than instantly, reflecting limits in how financial information is processed in global equity markets.

detail.abstract:
Importance: As artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into clinical workflows, traditional models of the patient-physician relationship are being redefined. Understanding how AI shifts patient expectations of physicians is critical for maintaining trust, ensuring accountability, and guiding medical education. 

Objective: To systematically review and synthesize empirical evidence on patients’ expectations of physicians who use AI in clinical decision-making. 

Evidence Review A systematic search was conducted in PubMed and Web of Science for empirical studies published between January 1, 2000, and January 31, 2026. Eligible studies examined triadic patient-physician-AI contexts and reported on patient perspectives regarding physician roles, competence, communication, or responsibility. Data were synthesized using thematic analysis and mapped onto established theoretical perspectives, including role, trust, attribution, and agency based-perspectives. 

Findings: A total of 16 studies met the inclusion criteria, spanning diverse clinical contexts such as oncology, radiology, and primary care. Mapping findings to role-based perspectives, patients viewed clinical judgment as non-delegable (Theme 1), expecting physicians to maintain diagnostic oversight and take dual responsibility for algorithmic outputs. Final accountability remained anchored in the clinician (Theme 3), as patients continue to place the moral and legal responsibility for medical outcomes within human agency. AI literacy was also recognized as an emerging component of professionalism (Theme 7). From trust-based perspectives, confidence in AI was mediated and context-dependent (Theme 4), often grounded in the existing patient-physician relationship, provided that humanistic care was preserved (Theme 5). Patients also identified ethical responsibilities, including regulatory approval of AI use, data privacy, informed consent, patient safety, and fairness (Theme 6), as non-transferable duties of physicians. From agency-based perspectives, explaining AI was viewed as a fundamental clinical responsibility (Theme 2), requiring physicians to interpret complex AI-generated outputs for patients. Despite its perceived benefits, AI was consistently positioned as a supportive third-party in decision-making (Theme 8), with physicians expected to act as the primary mediator who contextualizes technical evidence within individual value systems. Furthermore, physicians were expected to preserve patient autonomy and facilitate shared decision-making, advancing the core principles of patient-centered care (Theme 9). Although not a primary perspective, attribution-based considerations also shaped expectations regarding physicians’ professional competence, informed consent, and patient autonomy (Theme 1, 6, and 9). 

Conclusions and Relevance: In the context of AI-assisted care, patients articulate expanded expectations of physician responsibility, encompassing non-delegable clinical judgment, ultimate accountability, and the preservation of humanistic care. Medical education and health system governance must therefore prioritize the cultivation of augmented professionalism, ensuring that AI integration enhances rather than undermines the relational core of the physician-patient relationship.

detail.abstract: Critical mineral mining for electric vehicles (EVs) raises environmental and social concerns that harm mining communities and create supply chain risks for the energy transition. Emergent solutions could cause higher costs or reduced range for consumers and dampen EV demand. However, the impact of implementing such solutions on EV consumer preferences and demand remains underexplored. To address this gap, we field a survey of 789 recent U.S. EV buyers. We find that while there is high awareness of environmental impacts of mining for EVs (63%), awareness of social impacts is much lower (38%). Using a discrete choice experiment, we show that consumers differ in willingness to pay for sustainable EVs, and less affluent consumers (19% of sample) are more likely to be priced out by cost increases. Sustainable EV manufacturing policies, when combined with targeted solutions like subsidies, can encourage both responsible mining practices and equitable EV adoption.

detail.abstract: Professor Juliet Moringiello was a pioneering voice in reimagining property law for the digital age, advocating for a functional approach that transcended traditional requirements related to tangibility long before such thinking became mainstream in legal scholarship. Her groundbreaking 2007 article The (Ir)relevance of (In)tangibility presciently argued that the legal system's fixation on physical versus intangible distinctions created "false categories unrelated to significant legal distinctions" that hindered commercial law's ability to accommodate electronic assets like domain names and, eventually, digital assets. This essay examines how Professor Moringiello's early insights laid the intellectual foundation for the revolutionary 2022 Amendments to the Uniform Commercial Code that established controllable electronic records as a new category of personal property. Her pragmatic, policy-oriented methodology not only anticipated the legal challenges posed by Bitcoin, NFTs, and other digital assets but also provided the theoretical framework that enabled American commercial law to evolve functionally rather than be constrained by historical formalism. As such, her work was instrumental in bridging the gap between centuries-old property concepts and twenty-first-century technologies.

title: Workplace Rights, Duties and Limitations for Employees and Employers of Labour in Nigeria

detail.title: Workplace Rights, Duties and Limitations for Employees and Employers of Labour in Nigeria
detail.abstract: Workplace relationships in Nigeria are shaped by a delicate balance of rights, duties, and limitations imposed on both employees and employers of labor. This article examines these core elements as they operate within the Nigerian legal and institutional framework. Using key workplace concepts, the article explores how labour laws, contracts of employment, and regulatory bodies define acceptable conduct at work. It highlights the rights of employees to fair wages, safe working conditions, dignity, and protection from unfair labour practices, while also outlining the corresponding duties of employees, including loyalty, adhering to workplace rules and the exercise of due care in the performance of their work. On the part of employers, the article discusses duties such as providing a safe workplace, complying with statutory labour standards and respecting employee rights, as well as the limitations placed on their managerial powers. By situating these issues within the Nigerian context, the article seeks to promote a clearer understanding of workplace rights and responsibilities and to encourage more balanced, lawful, and productive employment relationships.

title: Signals of Efforts or Evidence of Automation? The Countersignaling Effect of Prompt Disclosure
affiliations: Arizona State University (ASU) - Department of Information Systems, Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, School of Computing and Artificial lntelligence and

detail.title: Signals of Efforts or Evidence of Automation? The Countersignaling Effect of Prompt Disclosure
detail.abstract: Transparency has often been regarded as a valuable practice in user-generated content (UGC), where revealing the creative process is thought to enhance perceived authenticity, effort, and credibility. However, in the context of human-AI co-creation, this logic may no longer hold. When generative AI (GenAI) plays a co-creating role in producing content, process-level disclosure-such as revealing the textual prompt used to generate an image-may instead expose the minimal nature of human input, undermining perceptions of creators' efforts and creativity. Drawing on signaling theory and the concept of countersignaling, we examine how prompt visibility affects audience engagement on a major GenAI platform. Analyzing a largescale dataset of user posts, we find that prompt display significantly reduces engagement relative to concealment. Rather than reflecting a uniform transparency effect, this engagement penalty arises because prompt disclosure shifts audience evaluation toward a proportionality-based assessment of creative contribution, in which viewers implicitly compare observable human input with the sophistication of the generated output. Consistent with this logic, transparency is less costly when disclosed prompts make substantial human input salient, but more damaging when highly polished outputs render the revealed input seemingly insufficient. In sum, we find that in AI-mediated creativity, transparency is not uniformly rewarded; its effects depend on how disclosed process information reshapes audience inferences about human contribution. Our findings challenge conventional assumptions about transparency in digital creativity and offer new insights into how audiences evaluate human contribution in AI-mediated content. We discuss implications for creators, platform designers, and researchers navigating attribution, engagement, and disclosure in the GenAI age.

title: CPB-REPORT: An Automated Perioperative Data Integration Platform in Cardiac Surgery

detail.title: CPB-REPORT: An Automated Perioperative Data Integration Platform in Cardiac Surgery
detail.abstract: BackgroundCardiac surgery under cardiopulmonary bypass generates large volumes of perioperative data that remain fragmented across multiple clinical information systems, limiting their integration for quality improvement and research. In parallel, national and international cardiac surgery registries still rely predominantly on manual data entry, a process that is time-consuming, error-prone, and often incomplete.ObjectiveTo report the real-world implementation of an automated perioperative data integration platform and evaluate its impact on data completeness, clinical workflow, and patient safety, with a perspective on scalability and interoperability.MethodsWe developed CPB-REPORT, a secure web-based platform based on an Extract–Transform–Load architecture integrating data from electronic health records, anaesthesia, and critical care systems into a unified database aligned with the national cardiac surgery registry. The platform was deployed in a high-volume cardiac surgery centre and uses a hybrid workflow combining automated data extraction (66% of variables) and structured manual entry. Data quality was ensured through automated validation rules, cross-check procedures, and real-time monitoring dashboards.ResultsSince deployment in May 2022, CPB-REPORT has prospectively captured all cardiac surgery procedures performed under CPB at a single institution, with 4,347 procedures transmitted to the national registry. Dataset completeness, defined as the proportion of registry variables available per patient record, improved from 68% at platform deployment to 90% in 2025, following a stepwise approach combining automated data extraction, real-time monitoring dashboards, and structured user training. The platform operates within a secure hospital infrastructure based on a demilitarised zone, with no cybersecurity incident reported. In addition, real-time outcome monitoring enabled early detection of a surgical site infection cluster in 2022, leading to rapid institutional corrective action.ConclusionThis implementation demonstrates that ETL-based perioperative data integration is feasible using existing hospital infrastructure. Beyond improving data quality and enabling real-time safety monitoring, the platform offers a scalable and interoperable model to support standardised data integration across institutions and facilitate consistent population of national and international registries.

detail.abstract: Weather forecasting depends on a globally coordinated system of observation, data exchange, modelling, and public warning that no single actor can reproduce independently. This article conceptualises this system-the meteorological information chain-as a knowledge infrastructure whose epistemic quality depends on the openness and reciprocity of its governance arrangements. Building on infrastructure and knowledge commons scholarship, the article distinguishes between commercially privatisable (Class I) and commonsconstitutive (Class II) network infrastructures, and argues that regulatory asymmetry operates differently across these categories. In Class II systems, mismatches between legally robust supranational obligations and politically contingent domestic governance create risks of epistemic degradation rather than merely access distortion. Through comparative legal analysis of Germany, the Netherlands, the United States, and Australia, the article examines how variation in statutory anchoring, warning authority demarcation, and public-private role structuring shapes institutional resilience. The German WarnWetter litigation (2015-2020) provides process-level evidence of the scope and limits of statutory protection. The findings suggest that effective governance of commonsconstitutive knowledge infrastructures requires primary-law anchoring of core public functions and legally structured interfaces between public and private actors. The article contributes to policy and governance scholarship by identifying a class of infrastructures for which standard liberalisation instruments are insufficient and by specifying institutional mechanisms that mitigate regulatory asymmetry in transnational knowledge systems.

detail.abstract: This article examines the perennial epistemic and methodological crisis of traditional legal practice in light of the new opportunities and imperatives brought forth by the age of artificial intelligence, and responds to this crisis by proposing an ontologically grounded framework designated as the 'Mecellem semantic protocol'. The article analyzes the structural tension inherent in law's dual obligation-on the one hand, to preserve normative coherence, and on the other, to adapt to evolving societal and institutional dynamics-and demonstrates why approaches premised solely on codification, positivist systematization, or quantitative measurement (jurimetrics) remain individually insufficient to resolve this tension. The article argues that legal reasoning is not merely a problem of data retrieval or statistical pattern analysis; rather, proceeding from the foundational premise that meaning is always contextually constituted, it contends that legal reasoning must be dynamically reconstructed through ontologically defined entity categories and epistemically differentiated knowledge layers. Within this framework, Mecellem conceives of and constructs law not as a static aggregate of norms, but as an ontodynamic architecture of meaning structured along the triadic axis of ontology, epistemology, and methodology. The article further emphasizes that the transition from jurimetrics to a semantic protocol represents not merely a technical advancement, but a fundamental transformation in the theoretical foundations of legal knowledge, and argues that neurosymbolic infrastructures, knowledge graphs, and agentic artificial intelligence systems can succeed in addressing law's chronic crises only when embedded within an ontodynamic architecture. Proceeding from the recognition that law must be understood no longer as a 'completed rational totality', but as a domain of 'becoming'-one that is reconstituted anew in each case and that processes within itself the tension between continuity and transformation-Mecellem proposes a context-sensitive, sustainable, auditable, contestable, and coherent model of legal meaning production at both the human and machine levels, thereby offering a comprehensive methodological framework for the reconstruction of legal reason in the age of artificial intelligence.

detail.title: Risk Sharing across U.S. States and EU Countries
detail.abstract: The capital-market channel in regional risk-sharing decompositions-widely interpreted as household portfolio diversification-is in fact dominated by a corporate buffer: firms absorb local output shocks through their profit margins, and the residual accrues to nationally diversified shareholders. We show this by decomposing the Asdrubali et al. (1996) capital-market coefficient for U.S. states (1985-2022) into corporate, earningsadjustment, and property-income components; the corporate buffer accounts for 85-93% of the total. Bartik instruments confirm that the buffer reflects absorption of exogenous shocks, and multi-horizon regressions show that about 55% persists permanently while the rest dissipates within a few years. Extending the analysis to 27 EU countries (1995-2023) reveals a fourfold US-EU risk-sharing gap driven almost entirely by cross-border corporate ownership; a simple model accounts for three-quarters of this gap. These findings imply that deeper corporate integration across borders, rather than broader household equity participation, is the key margin for risk sharing in monetary unions.

title: Section 20 of the Admiralty Jurisdiction Act, Foreign Maritime Arbitration, and the Limits of “Ouster”
