detail.title: Section 20 of the Admiralty Jurisdiction Act, Foreign Maritime Arbitration, and the Limits of “Ouster”
detail.abstract:
The decision of the Federal High Court in PS Offshore Nigeria Ltd v. Miden Systems Nigeria Ltd & Anor raises a fundamental and unsettling question at the intersection of admiralty law and international arbitration in Nigeria: 

Does Section 20 of the Admiralty Jurisdiction Act (“AJA”) invalidate foreign seated arbitration agreements and render foreign arbitral awards unenforceable in Nigeria where the underlying dispute is a maritime claim with Nigerian connecting factors? 

The Court answered this question in the affirmative. It held that a Singapore-seated arbitration clause contained in a BIMCO time charterparty was null, void, and unenforceable, and that the arbitral award subsequently issued by the Singapore Chamber of Maritime Arbitration (SCMA) could not be recognised or enforced in Nigeria. At first glance, the decision appears consistent with a developing line of Nigerian admiralty authorities emphasising the exclusivity of the Federal High Court’s admiralty jurisdiction under Sections 19 and 20 of the AJA. On closer examination, however, the judgment reveals a deeper doctrinal difficulty.

title: From Marks of Origin to Symbols of Power: The Exhaustive Evolution and Expansion of Trademark Law

detail.title: From Marks of Origin to Symbols of Power: The Exhaustive Evolution and Expansion of Trademark Law
detail.abstract: Intellectual property (IP) and intellectual property rights (IPR) are examples of intangible assets that have the ability to influence global economic trends in the future. The knowledge-driven world of today is what drives this essential assistance offered by intellectual property. However, there is scepticism and disagreement surrounding intellectual property rights (IPR), particularly with regard to trademark law, which is inextricably linked to ownership conflicts. But what distinguishes this domain from the rest of IPRs is its development, which has been tainted by innovation and incentives. Trademarks have flourished in popularity and use from the period of the Roman Empire all the way up to the present day. This research would provide light on many aspects of the early IPR, particularly the evolution of trademark law to its present-day preeminence.

title: Who counts as a stakeholder? Evidence from human-wildlife conflict research
affiliations: University of Milan, University of Milan, University of Milan, University of Milan and University of Milan

detail.title: Who counts as a stakeholder? Evidence from human-wildlife conflict research
detail.abstract: Human-wildlife coexistence is shaped not only by ecological dynamics but also by governance processes that determine which actors are recognised as legitimate participants in decision-making. Although the term ”stakeholder(s)” is widely used in human-wildlife conflict research, little is known about its implications for interest groups’ inclusion and representation. We treat the literature as an empirical object and map how the term is deployed in conflict-management studies published between 2000 and 2025. Following a PRISMA-ScR scoping review, 136 articles were analysed using descriptive statistics and simple corresponding analyses. Explicit definitions appear in a minority of studies, indicating limited conceptual grounding. Attention centres on territorially embedded groups experiencing direct, monetisable impacts - especially rural residents, farmers, hunters, and land/wildlife managers - while institutional actors are more often named than systematically engaged in experimental settings. Simple correspondence analyses reveal structured associations between stakeholder profiles, conflict framings, and mitigation strategies: production- and safety-related conflicts cluster with operative measures, whereas regulatory and participatory approaches align with institutional and advocacy-oriented actors. Animals are rarely treated as stakeholders, highlighting the limitations of applying an anthropocentric, economically derived concept to multispecies governance. Overall, the prevailing interpretation of the stakeholder concept in the literature shapes which perspectives are evidenced, and which governance solutions appear legitimate, potentially reinforcing asymmetries in natural resource governance. Future research should examine how alternative definitions of ”stake” as economic interest influence governance outcomes, compare stakeholder configurations across conflict and non-conflict coexistence contexts, and develop proxies for representing wildlife interests within decision-making.

detail.abstract: In recent years Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden have signed or updated bilateral Defence Cooperation Agreements (DCA) with the United States. These agreements were presented as enabling deeper defence cooperation with a strategic ally in a severely deteriorated European security environment. The agreements provided strategic flexibility for increased US presence in Northern Europe. However, rather than signalling unique relations between the Nordic countries and the United States, they should be seen as an extension of America's overall strategic approach to military presence and cooperation with allies and partners in Europe. For the Nordic countries, the implication is that they cannot insulate themselves from political risks in the transatlantic relationship.

title: AI and Copyright Law: Who Lobbies for the Public (Domain)?
affiliations: University College London

detail.title: AI and Copyright Law: Who Lobbies for the Public (Domain)?
detail.abstract: The AI and copyright policy efforts when it comes to licensing large language models have been usually pulled by the AI industry on one side and the rightholders representative bodies on the other. The standard narrative by the rightholders is that in order for generative AI models to function the use they make of the training materials must be licensed, provided it covers copyright protected works. Depending on the jurisdiction, the AI industry has tried to battle this with several points: either that the act of training does not constitute a copyright relevant act or that such activity constitutes an exception, so no licensing is needed. These are complex issues which will entertain courts for years to come. An interesting question emerges in this tug of war – who lobbies for the public domain? On one side, we have trade bodies arguing for more copyright for their rightholders, while on the other side, we have AI companies, which will inevitably impose their own prerogatives through their Terms of Service. Copyright wars have entertained similar wars ever since the digital revolution, but one important interesting side has been slightly overlooked – the public domain. This paper looks at this issue by focusing on the public domain and seeks to unpack the question of inclusivity in AI copyright lawmaking through the lens of the public domain.

title: Freedom of the Arts in Copyright Law
affiliations: University College London

detail.title: Freedom of the Arts in Copyright Law
detail.abstract: Copyright law’s relationship to the freedom of the arts has been notoriously uneasy. This could be somewhat surprising to those not deeply versed with the mechanics of copyright law considering that copyright is the intellectual property (IP) right designated to protect authorial intellectual creation. This situation stems partly from the complicated interplay between IP and human rights regimes to which this edited volume is dedicated. The focus of this chapter is on EU copyright law and the breathing space in its organisation for freedom of the arts. This is not to say that the topic is irrelevant or less thorny in other jurisdictions. On the contrary – ensuring our legal framework encourages artistic freedom is a universal goal for all legal frameworks. That said, as this chapter will demonstrate, the EU’s approach can be characterised as somewhat restrictive, especially in comparison to the US and the flexibility of the fair use doctrine. The main culprit of this setting in the EU is the permitted uses (also called exceptions and limitations) framework, which one finds primarily in the InfoSoc Directive. The analysis traces the organisation and operation of Article 5 of the InfoSoc Directive, which seems to leave little room for considerations on freedom of the arts. Much of this debate entertains discussions of external balancing of copyright and human rights. This is not a mechanism alien to the EU, as it has been demonstrated by the intermediaries’ liability cases. That said, it appears that it is not something the Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU) is willing to engage in when it comes to new creative expressions such as sampling. The potential interference with the legislative limb of the EU has so far put the CJEU off from going beyond the parameters of the InfoSoc Directive. The chapter starts from the mechanics of internal balancing and the organisation of the InfoSoc Directive. Then, it traces the operation of external balancing. It finally zooms on to sampling as the artistic technique which has been on the CJEU agenda testing these questions.

Global Equity & Sustainability Transition Architecture (GEST) is a proprietary capital structuring doctrine developed under the Delkaso Doctrine to address the estimated USD 4 trillion annual financing gap facing developing economies in achieving climate and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) targets. Rather than functioning as a fund, lender, or grant facility, GEST operates as a financial engineering framework designed to mobilize, layer, and de-risk multi-source capital across sovereign, multilateral, and private institutional channels.

The doctrine integrates five coordinated capital layers into a unified stack: (1) sovereign concessional finance, (2) policy-linked reform instruments, (3) private institutional debt and equity, (4) carbon monetization mechanisms under Article 6 and voluntary markets, and (5) structured yield enhancement instruments including green bonds, securitization, and tokenized assets. Through systematic sequencing and risk allocation, GEST reduces weighted average cost of capital, enhances bankability, and enables large-scale climate, infrastructure, and energy-transition projects to reach financial close.

The paper provides legal positioning of GEST as a protected structuring methodology (distinct from ownership of capital), outlines governance and transparency frameworks compatible with MDB safeguards and IMF programs, and details risk mitigation tools including political risk insurance, revenue stabilization mechanisms, MRV systems, and forward carbon contracts.

An illustrative Bamboo Carbon & Bioenergy Platform modeling example demonstrates application of the doctrine, showing how concessional tranches and carbon monetization can produce an IRR of approximately 12% while delivering measurable climate mitigation, renewable energy generation, and socio-economic development impact.

This institutional white paper is intended for:

  • Ministries of Finance and Energy

  • Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs) and Development Finance Institutions (DFIs)

  • Sovereign wealth funds and pension funds

  • Climate funds and carbon market participants

  • Infrastructure sponsors and project developers

GEST advances a systemic approach to climate finance reform by harmonizing sovereign policy frameworks, multilateral instruments, private capital markets, and emerging digital verification technologies into a coherent capital architecture designed for scalability, transparency, and long-term sustainability.

title: Between Geoeconomic Poles: The Changing Business Cycle Synchronization of Russia and Major Developing Countries
affiliations: Bank of Russia and Far Eastern Federal University

detail.title: Between Geoeconomic Poles: The Changing Business Cycle Synchronization of Russia and Major Developing Countries
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the shifting architecture of international business cycles in an era of geoeconomic fragmentation. Classical Dynamic Factor Models typically rely on strict, ex-ante regional classifications, which fail to capture the continuous geoeconomic reorientation of large emerging markets: “swing states”. To address this limitation, we propose a parsimonious hierarchical Bayesian DFM that introduces a continuous latent switching parameter to quantify endogenous drift between the Developed macroeconomic pole and the Developing block anchored by China. To ensure robust identification, we employ bilateral Trade in Value Added data as a covariate-informed hierarchical prior. Treating trade structure as a “soft constraint” allows the Bayesian updating mechanism to identify decoupling episodes where unobservable financial or institutional channels override physical trade gravity. Estimating the model on a panel of 24 major economies from 2001 to 2023, we document a structural shift in international linkages. We quantitatively capture Russia's sharp macroeconomic pivot toward the Developing block following the geopolitical shocks of 2014 and 2022. Conversely, we uncover a distinct decoupling effect in Turkey, where actual macroeconomic dynamics remain synchronized with the Developed block despite shifting trade flows. Finally, variance decompositions confirm that while output and consumption are increasingly linked to regional poles, capital formation remains highly localized across all geoeconomic blocks.

title: Rethinking Bangladesh's Foreign Policy: Test For a More Assertive "Bangladesh First" Doctrine

detail.title: Rethinking Bangladesh's Foreign Policy: Test For a More Assertive "Bangladesh First" Doctrine
detail.abstract: With the final ballots verified on February 12, 2026, the 13th National Election has triggered a profound transformation in Bangladesh's diplomatic trajectory. This milestone does more than just seat a new government; it fundamentally resets the nation's engagement with the global community. Following the landslide victory of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP)-securing 209 seats and a decisive two-thirds majority-the incoming administration inherits a landscape defined by both immense volatility and strategic opportunity. As the nation prepares for the official transition of power, the world is witnessing the birth of a "Bangladesh First" doctrine. This isn't merely a change in leadership, but a shift toward a more assertive, sovereign foreign policy aimed at navigating the complex rivalries of the 21st century.

title: States of Oppression vs. States of Reform: An Analysis of Disability Rights in Iran and Tunisia
affiliations: Winthrop University

detail.title: States of Oppression vs. States of Reform: An Analysis of Disability Rights in Iran and Tunisia
detail.abstract: This paper compares disability rights protections in the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Republic of Tunisia, examining how political structure, constitutional language, and social movements shape legal outcomes. Through constitutional analysis, legislative review, and evaluation of social activism, the study assesses both the scope of formal protections and their practical implementation. While Iran recognizes disability within social welfare provisions and has enacted legislation such as the 2018 Law on Protecting the Rights of Disabled Persons, enforcement remains inconsistent and constrained by authoritarian governance and reliance on Sharia-based legal practices. Tunisia provides more explicit constitutional protections against discrimination and maintains comprehensive legislation under Directive Law No. 83; however, democratic regression and administrative instability have weakened implementation efforts. The findings suggest that although Tunisia’s legal framework appears stronger on paper, both states struggle to translate formal protections into meaningful safeguards. Ultimately, durable disability rights protections depend not only on legislative recognition but on sustained democratic governance and institutional accountability.

title: Predicting Optimal Grid Stability and Welfare in Onshore Power Supply (OPS)
affiliations: Centre for Competition Policy, University of East Anglia, University of Piraeus, University of East Anglia (UEA) - Norwich Business School and Western University

detail.title: Predicting Optimal Grid Stability and Welfare in Onshore Power Supply (OPS)
detail.abstract: Onshore Power Supply (OPS) allows ships at berth to use electricity from the onshore grid instead of relying on auxiliary diesel engines, reducing emissions, noise, and local air pollution in port areas. Despite its growing importance for maritime decarbonisation, OPS deployment remains fragmented and uneven, creating a coordination problem that involves welfare, investment efficiency, and grid stability. We address this problem by developing a multi-objective optimisation model that combines demandelasticity functions with swing-equation dynamics to capture the interaction between market design and electricity network conditions. Our analysis shows that existing market designs face important limitations. Specifically, "Intermediary" market designs pose risks of monopoly pricing and inefficient investment, while "Facilitator" market designs improve welfare but compromise grid stability. To address these problems, we propose a new "Extension-to-Grid" market design, in which the electricity network operator assumes a coordinating role. This achieves a welfare-superior balance between efficiency, stability, and consumer protection. Through illustrative scenarios, real-world pricing data and a case study with two ports in Greece, we demonstrate how the proposed model can identify and help avoid distorted price signals or blackout risks under poorly designed OPS market structures. By integrating infrastructure optimization with institutional planning, our study provides actionable insights for sustainable port electrification and demonstrates how operations research can inform the regulatory decisions for complex socio-technical systems.

title: Dual-Domain Autonomy: Engineering Cognition Across Physical Kinematics and Perceptual Realities

detail.title: Dual-Domain Autonomy: Engineering Cognition Across Physical Kinematics and Perceptual Realities
detail.abstract: In the evolving landscape of strategic competition, the integration of physical and cognitive domains represents the frontier of autonomous systems engineering. This paper introduces Dual-Domain Autonomy as a unified framework that couples high-speed physical kinematics, such as hypersonic propulsion and swarm coordination, with perceptual and cognitive operations, including human decision latency and narrative coherence. By treating cognition as an engineering discipline across both domains, we propose architectures that compress adversarial decision loops in future conflicts. This approach fuses insights from biology, information theory, and psychophysics to create systems that operate at the intersection of matter and mind. We outline key challenges, including latency matching and entropy budgeting, and demonstrate how resolving them will redefine operational superiority in the 2030s and beyond. This framework positions the Michelangelo Project at the frontiers of defense innovation, where autonomy is not merely mechanical but holistically cognitive.

detail.abstract: This study aims to analyze regional economic adaptation strategies in provinces that depend on the extractive sector to face the trend of scarcity of mineral resources and national downstream policies. The high dependence on the extractive sector puts many provinces in Indonesia in a vulnerable position to fluctuations in global commodity prices and the threat of depletion of mineral reserves. This study aims to analyze regional economic adaptation strategies in natural resource-based provinces in dealing with mineral scarcity trends and the implementation of national downstream policies. The main focus of this study is to evaluate the extent to which the regional economic structure is able to transform when the primary sector is no longer the main driver of the regional economy. The research method used is a descriptive quantitative approach through the Shift-Share model to dissect the components of economic growth and Location Quotient (LQ) to identify competitive leading sectors. Through these two analytical tools, structural shifts and economic specializations are identified to map a stronger direction of sectoral diversification. The results of the study show that areas that are overly dependent on mining are at high risk of experiencing symptoms of Dutch Disease if they do not take immediate mitigation. The findings of the study confirm that diversification into the service sector and processing manufacturing (downstreaming) is the main key to maintaining economic resilience. The transformation from raw material exports to high-valueadded products has proven to be able to compensate for the decline in output from the extractive sector. In conclusion, strengthening the non-extractive sector through the integration of the processing industry is very urgent. This study recommends the need for policy synchronization between central and local governments to build a foundation for more stable and sustainable economic growth in the future.

title: Attention-based Vector Autoregressions
affiliations: and

detail.title: Attention-based Vector Autoregressions
detail.abstract: We introduce attention-based vector autoregressions, a new class of nonlinear time series models in which the conditional mean and variance are modeled through the attention mechanism, the core of the Transformer architecture in language modeling. Attention leads to state-dependent, time-varying dynamics, that are deterministic functions of past data. The framework nests constant-parameter linear VARs and approximates Dynamic Factor Models, but provides dimensionality reduction with a natural economic interpretation. We develop Bayesian priors and estimation methods suitable for time series and sample sizes available in macroeconomics and finance, and characterize the model's theoretical properties. An empirical application to forecasting U.S. inflation after the pandemic demonstrates gains in point and density forecast accuracy relative to standard benchmarks.

title: Building a Digital Brain for Research: A Guide to Queryable Knowledge Graphs
affiliations: Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

detail.title: Building a Digital Brain for Research: A Guide to Queryable Knowledge Graphs
detail.abstract:
A digital brain, as coined by Andrej Karpathy, is a personal knowledge infrastructure built from documents you trust. It maps connections between sources, surfaces patterns and inconsistencies. It generates answers on demand with references to the underlying material. The more it is used, the more connections it builds. The output is a private, queryable Wikipedia. On demand, the system generates wiki pages on any theme covered by the corpus, and each new page feeds back into the knowledge base.

This guide documents a pipeline for building such a system from any document corpus, for research purposes. The pipeline adapts Karpathy’s methodology and adds six research-specific contributions. (1) A schema design procedure encodes authority hierarchies and surfaces gaps in the literature. (2) A centrality-weighted wiki generation procedure anchors each article around the most-connected sources. (3) A six-step research protocol produces hypotheses rather than retrieved information. (4) Claim-level extraction moves the unit of analysis from documents to propositions, which makes visible the incompatibilities that document-level graphs hide. (5) A persistent hypothesis register stores every query-generated conjecture and re-tests it as the corpus grows. (6) A complexity-theoretic diagnostic layer measures the graph's network properties and reports how the field is structured. The pipeline is field-neutral. The two implementations documented here, one academic research corpus and one European Commission decisions dataset, are illustrative examples.

title: The Decentralisation of EU Digital Regulation
affiliations: University Villanueva and Universidad San Pablo CEU

detail.title: The Decentralisation of EU Digital Regulation
detail.abstract:
The enforcement of EU digital law stands at a structural crossroads. This chapter interrogates the apparent tension between the centralisation and verticalization impulse of EU institutions and the structural reality of decentralised application at the national level, by arguing that the dichotomy between centralised and decentralised enforcement is, in practice, far more porous than conventional doctrinal analysis concedes. 

Drawing on a bottom-up empirical mapping of the national implementation of four landmark digital instruments, the Digital Markets Act, the Digital Services Act, the Artificial Intelligence Act, and the Platform-to-Business Regulation, across all 27 Member States, the chapter identifies and reinstates three defining trends in the enforcement of the EU’s digital acquis. First, the phenomenon of EU law brutality, whereby the EU legislator’s top-down imposition of new regulatory concepts and institutional mechanisms disrupts existing national frameworks with deliberate disregard for Member State idiosyncrasies. Second, the incidental character of digital enforcement, conditioned by the regulatory density and technical complexity of the rules involved, which generates uneven compliance performance across jurisdictions. Third, the persistence of de facto decentralisation, which is a structural reality that reasserts itself, irrespective of the enforcement model formally chosen by the EU legislator in each digital rule.

The chapter demonstrates that, even where EU institutions purport to centralise enforcement, decentralisation operates as a gravitational force at the implementation stage. Member States selectively allocate competences to authorities structurally detached from the object of regulation and calibrate their enforcement efforts according to domestic political priorities rather than legal obligations. Enforcement data further reveal that enforcement architecture design, centralised or hybrid, directly conditions the depth and breadth of national legislative disruption, with decentralised and hybrid models consistently generating broader and more uneven national adaptation than their centralised counterparts.

In doing so, the chapter exposes a contradiction embedded in the EU’s digital strategy. The EU legislator adopts legislation based on the premise of uniformity. In turn, the regulatory ambition is delivered at the national level through an enforcement architecture that structurally rewards fragmentation. These findings carry significant implications for the coherence and effectiveness of the EU’s digital single market and invite a reassessment of the institutional design choices underpinning the EU’s digital governance framework.

detail.title: Behavioral Preferences of Real Economy
detail.abstract: While macroeconomic variables in the real economy have been extensively studied, their behavioral impacts remain unclear. Behavioral preferences based on perception are significant factors driving real economic outcomes.

title: A Seat at the Table: How Security Council Membership Shapes Public Opinion about the UN *
affiliations: University of Notre Dame,  and University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB)

detail.title: A Seat at the Table: How Security Council Membership Shapes Public Opinion about the UN *
detail.abstract: In an era of rising anti-globalist sentiment, opposition to international organizations (IOs) often centers on concerns over inadequate control. How does countries' influence within IOs shape citizen support for these institutions? We argue that elevated institutional influence improves public opinion about the IO through preferences for policy impact and heightened international status. The static nature of IOs' rules complicates empirical tests; however, we overcome this by analyzing the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), where member states' influence varies over time. Using difference-indifference analyses of repeated cross-sectional survey data (N>900,000), we examine shifts in public opinion about the UN when countries join the UNSC. We complement this with a case study of India, combining a survey experiment with media content analysis. These findings reveal how shifts in institutional influence can sway public opinion, suggesting that struggles for influence within IOs are not just battles among states, but also levers in winning hearts and minds.

title: Stationary Portfolio Goal-Based Optimization
affiliations: Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and Independent

detail.title: Stationary Portfolio Goal-Based Optimization

keywords: Sovereign wealth funds and pension funds

detail.abstract:
Sovereign wealth funds and pension funds require portfolio allocation strategies that maximize the probability of reaching target returns without fixed time horizons. Traditional dynamic allocation approaches face time-dependence issues leading to inconsistent allocation rules. 
We develop a stationary portfolio optimization framework that maximizes target return probabilities, where portfolio weights depend only on market drivers rather than time, ensuring natural backtestability. Our key contributions include: semi-analytical solutions revealing "phase transition" phenomena for short horizons, a stable iterative procedure handling non-convex probability objectives with arbitrary weight constraints, and comprehensive validation through Monte Carlo simulations and historical backtests. 
Performing a backtest for 25 years of GICS sector data, we demonstrate material probability improvements for longer investment horizons, showing that stationary dynamic optimization significantly outperforms natural benchmarks.

title: Generative Agent-Based Modeling for Social Simulations: A Systematic Mapping Study
affiliations: , Northwestern University and

detail.title: Generative Agent-Based Modeling for Social Simulations: A Systematic Mapping Study
detail.abstract: Generative Agent-Based Modeling (GABM) is an emerging simulation paradigm in which autonomous agents leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) to perceive, reason about, and act within complex environments through natural-language processing. Despite rapidly growing interest in simulating social dynamics, opinion formation, and collective behavior, the field lacks a unified characterization of agent architectures, emergent social phenomena, and validation practices. This paper presents a systematic mapping study of 53 primary studies, selected through keyword-based search and forward-backward snowballing, and proposes a three-tiered taxonomy organizing generative agent design along individual-level traits (profile, memory, and action modules), group-level dynamics (information diffusion, relationship formation, and coordination), and community-level features (formation and network properties), enriched with an evaluation dimension. Our analysis reveals five application domains (social dynamics, social media, economics, recommender systems, and healthcare), a predominance of small-scale simulations (66% employing 100 agents or fewer), substantial architectural heterogeneity, and uneven validation practices. We conclude by identifying ten open challenges and outlining research directions toward more robust, interpretable, and scientifically grounded simulation of complex social systems.

detail.abstract: Impulse buying, characterized by unplanned and immediate purchases, represents a significant component of consumer behavior across various sectors, including fashion, electronics, and groceries. Traditional economic models, which assume fully rational decision-making, fail to account for the cognitive and emotional mechanisms driving these spontaneous purchases. Behavioral economics provides a framework to understand how heuristics, such as availability and representativeness, and cognitive biases, including anchoring and scarcity effects, systematically influence consumer choices. Emotional states, situational cues, and individual differences further modulate these effects, creating complex interactions between cognition and context. Empirical evidence from surveys, experiments, and behavioral tracking indicates that these factors substantially increase the likelihood of impulsive decisions, particularly in online environments where time-limited offers and personalized recommendations are prevalent. Understanding these mechanisms offers both theoretical and practical insights, enabling marketers to design ethically informed engagement strategies and policymakers to promote responsible consumption. Future research should investigate longitudinal patterns, cross-cultural variations, and the influence of emerging digital technologies on impulsive behavior.

title: The Multi-Agent World Model: Coordination in the Agentic Economy

detail.title: The Multi-Agent World Model: Coordination in the Agentic Economy

declarations.ethicsApproval: The author declares no conflicts of interest. AI tools (Claude, Anthropic) were used for editing assistance and feedback during the drafting process. All substantive intellectual content, theoretical development, and argumentation are the author's own.

detail.abstract: When agents equipped with world models interact, coordination becomes a problem of reflexive entanglement: each agent's state-transition projections depend on assumptions about other agents' projections, producing recursive anticipation that no individual model can resolve. Existing approaches to the agentic economy assume that coordination will emerge through price mechanisms, Coasean bargaining, or related institutional structures executed at computational speed. However, these mechanisms rely on an implicit precondition-total financializability-that fails in the intangible-dominant domain where agent interactions occur. Under these conditions, coordination substrates do not remain exogenous to the system they organize: prices, rules, contracts, and reputational signals become endogenous to agent behavior, degrading their independent informational content and producing metastable coordination regimes rather than convergence. This paper argues that coordination in such systems requires a substrate that defines a state over its own evolution; without such a substrate, agents must recursively model one another's models, yielding a fixed-point problem with no guarantee of convergence. The multiagent world model is proposed as the minimal class of architectures that satisfies this requirement: it observes agent actions, learns the causal dynamics of the multiagent system, and projects state transitions that agents can condition on, replacing recursive anticipation with a shared, learnable coordination state. Coordination in the agentic economy is therefore not a problem of better agents, but of constructing the environment in which their interaction can be stabilized.

title: A Blended Normal Distribution
affiliations: Concordia University Montreal

detail.title: A Blended Normal Distribution
detail.abstract: We use an example to show that a distribution is asymmetric generally, suggesting that normal distribution is the simplest distribution without momentum (which is fined as the force that drives the asymmetry). We define a distribution with momentum as a blended normal distribution-as if the underlying normal distribution is disfigured by, or blended with, momentum. We suggest that a variable's movement over a period follows a distribution longitudinally, whereas the literature usually examines a variable's population that follows a normal distribution cross-sectionally. Thus, we use the distribution of current observations to predict the likelihood that the variable falls within a specific range at a specific time. This study questions the fundamentals of statistics and econometrics.

detail.abstract: Background: The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria represents one of the most consequential transformations in contemporary sustainable finance. Traditional ESG assessment methodologies suffer from data fragmentation, inter-rater inconsistency, limited real-time responsiveness, and inadequate accommodation of jurisdictional divergence. These limitations are critically amplified in cross-border FinTech contexts, where regulatory heterogeneity, correspondent banking dependencies, and data sovereignty constraints create multi-dimensional ESG risk exposures that existing frameworks are ill-equipped to address. Objectives: This paper provides: (i) a systematic review of AI methodologies applied to ESG scoring in sustainable finance; (ii) a comparative analysis of leading ESG rating frameworks and machine learning model performance benchmarks; (iii) an examination of cross-border FinTech regulatory dynamics across six global regions (EU, UK, US, APAC, MENA, and LatAm); and (iv) the Composite AI-ESG Scoring (CAES) framework — a novel, jurisdiction-aware ESG risk assessment architecture purpose-built for cross-border FinTech operators. Methodology: Following the PRISMA 2020 protocol, this study synthesises 60 peer-reviewed studies and 28 institutional reports (total N=88) retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, JSTOR, and SSRN, covering 2018–2025. Eight AI/ML model categories are benchmarked, and five major ESG rating frameworks are comparatively evaluated. Results: XGBoost-SHAP hybrid models achieve the highest AUC (0.977) and accuracy (91.0%) among structured ESG scoring approaches. Voting ensemble methods attain R²=0.922 on regression tasks. NLP-based BERT+ALBERT ensembles reach 80.8% classification accuracy on unstructured ESG text. Inter-rater divergence across established frameworks reveals governance weighting variance of ±5 percentage points and mean Spearman correlation of ρ≈0.54. Non-compliance fines in global financial services reached USD 1.23 billion in H1 2025 alone — a 417% year-on-year increase. The AI-ESG software market is projected to grow at 62.5% CAGR from USD 1.2 billion (2024) to USD 8.1 billion by 2030. Conclusion: AI-powered ESG scoring substantially outperforms rule-based systems and offers a viable pathway to standardising sustainable finance assessment for cross-border FinTech. The proposed CAES framework provides a technically rigorous, regulatory-aligned, and empirically grounded architecture with open-source Python implementation for peer replication. Future empirical validation across a panel dataset of cross-border FinTech operators is recommended.

detail.abstract: This study introduces an event-driven trading framework that converts unstructured macroeconomic data into low-latency signals in crude oil futures markets We formalize "Latency Alpha" as the economic value derived from minimizing information-processing time The system ingests the U S Energy Information Administration Weekly Petroleum Status Report at release, applies retrieval-augmented large language model analysis, and converts semantic outputs into a numerical signal integrated with a GARCH(1,1) volatility model for risk-adjusted execution A 24-month backtest (2022-2023) on West Texas Intermediate futures yields a Sharpe ratio of 1.82 and a Sortino ratio of 2.89, outperforming a volatility-only baseline Results demonstrate that realtime semantic processing enhances short-horizon forecasting and that latency remains a diminishing but exploitable source of market advantage

title: Car Sales in a Fully Import-Dependent, High-Ownership Country, New Zealand: Evaluating Forecasting with Deep Learning and Econometric Methods

detail.title: Car Sales in a Fully Import-Dependent, High-Ownership Country, New Zealand: Evaluating Forecasting with Deep Learning and Econometric Methods

declarations.ethicsApproval: It does not involve human elements

detail.abstract: This study examined the dynamics of private car sales in New Zealand, a fully import-dependent and tariff-free economy with one of the highest car ownership rates globally. Using monthly data on small vehicle sales (cars, sport utility vehicles, and passenger vans) from 1998 to 2024 (324 observations) obtained from the Motor Industry Association, the study investigated market behavior and external shocks through both a deep learning approach, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and an econometric framework, Exponential Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (EGARCH). The study further examined methodological challenges associated with validating the LSTM model, with particular emphasis on the application of time-series k-fold cross-validation (TSCV) to data characterized by a long-term upward trend. Specifically, it assessed potential distributional inconsistencies between the train and test datasets of individual folds and showed reliability issues in k-fold cross-validation outcomes. Moreover, by construction, the TSCV framework systematically excludes important data segments from model estimation. This exclusion limits the ability of the validation procedure to provide a fully robust assessment of a model ultimately trained on the complete dataset. This study has also explained an underlying cause of negative out-of-sample R-square in k-fold cross-validation tests using a methodological framework and empirical evidence. Forecast performance comparisons between the EGARCH and LSTM models revealed statistically significant differences in their predictions. The study also identified statistically significant differences between models trained on split datasets and those trained on the full dataset. Results suggested that models trained on the full dataset provide more robust predictions and perform comparably to EGARCH, particularly at the beginning of the forecast horizon. The LSTM model effectively captured recent upward drifts and nonlinear patterns, generating point forecasts of expected sales and reflecting long-term trends. In contrast, the EGARCH model captured volatility persistence and mean reversion, offering forecasts that quantify uncertainty and risk. An integrated LSTM-EGARCH framework successfully captures both nonlinear and stochastic dynamics, producing forecasts that are more informative for policy formulation and managerial decision-making. From a policy perspective, the findings indicated that car sales in New Zealand have a long-term upward trend, potentially supported in part by tariff relaxation. However, sales display pronounced volatility clustering, strong mean reversion, and a high likelihood of extreme fluctuations in response to external shocks. Full import dependency is argued to be one contributing factor to this volatility. Sales declined sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic but rebounded rapidly, possibly reflecting strong institutional foundations. Forecasts for 2025-2027 suggest that sales growth is likely to continue, albeit at a marginal pace, approaching a potential peak level. In terms of overall lessons for other tariff-free, import-dependent economies, tariff relaxation, probably supported by favorable measures such as roads and effective institutional backups, can sustain car sales growth and support recovery, even amid market volatility and external shocks.

title: Comparative Analysis of Transfer Pricing Taxation in Former Yugoslavian Countries

detail.title: Comparative Analysis of Transfer Pricing Taxation in Former Yugoslavian Countries
detail.abstract: Transfer pricing, as a potential instrument for avoiding a real tax liability, is one of the growing tax issues of the 21st century. In an effort to illuminate the negative effects of the transfer pricing application on local tax budgets and identify certain mechanisms for efficient tax controls, the paper discusses the basic tax implications of transfer pricing misuses, as well as some instruments of their tax regulation. Also, in order to determine the awareness in former Yugoslavian countries in terms of the seriousness of this issue, the presentation and analysis of the representation of certain instruments of transfer pricing tax regulation in these countries, in the context of supranational regulations, was carried out. The analysis showed that there are large oscillations in shaping the tax approach to the use of transfer pricing controlling when conducting transactions between related legal entities, and that these differences are conditioned by the level of development and construction of the legal regulations.

title: Surge in Manufacturing Employment in India in Recent Years: Patterns of Change and Causes Underlying Job Growth
affiliations: Institute of Economic Growth (IEG) and University of Delhi - Department of Business Economics

detail.title: Surge in Manufacturing Employment in India in Recent Years: Patterns of Change and Causes Underlying Job Growth
detail.abstract: The paper examines trends in manufacturing employment in recent years and notes a surge in growth since 2020-21. The rapid growth in manufacturing employment was accompanied by increases in the share of female workers. Hikes in manufacturing jobs were accompanied by some improvement in their quality, especially in the formal segment of manufacturing. The acceleration in manufacturing employment growth in recent years appears to be driven principally by a significant increase in rural female workforce participation rate and a marked augmentation in the number of women-owned manufacturing enterprises.

title: Designing for Silence: How Healthcare Accountability Was Engineered

detail.title: Designing for Silence: How Healthcare Accountability Was Engineered

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A

detail.abstract: Modern healthcare accountability systems are widely described as underperforming, inconsistent, or culturally biased. This paper advances a more structurally rigorous thesis: contemporary accountability mechanisms were engineered in ways that predictably tolerate certain forms of harm. Drawing from regulatory design theory, compliance governance literature, civil rights enforcement history, and healthcare administrative law, this capstone synthesizes nine prior papers in the Silence & Compliance series to argue that inequity in healthcare accountability is not merely cultural drift or implementation failure, but it is a consequence of design architecture. Through comparative historical analysis linking Black exclusion from care to present-day documentation filtering, professionalism gatekeeping, and enforcement asymmetries, this paper reframes racialized harm tolerance as a systems outcome. It proposes a new compliance paradigm: Design Accountability, which shifts reform efforts from frontline retraining to structural redesign.

title: The Impact Of Conditional Cash Transfers On The Alleviation Of Economic Inequality At The Household Level: Examining The Role Of The Parallel Trend Assumption
affiliations: European University Institute

detail.title: The Impact Of Conditional Cash Transfers On The Alleviation Of Economic Inequality At The Household Level: Examining The Role Of The Parallel Trend Assumption
