detail.abstract: This study adopted a quasi-experimental (Difference-in-Differences) research design to examine the South Sudan Conditional Cash Transfer (CCT). It used survey data to illustrate the parallel trend assumption. The finding indicates a violation of the parallel trend assumption, as the treatment trend falls below the control group trend. This indicates that the CCT intervention programme did not significantly improve the beneficiaries' well-being or reduce their economic inequality. The findings also indicate that the CCT is not particularly effective in alleviating household vulnerability to specific income shocks. Moreover, the regression output clearly shows that households receiving remittances are more exposed to economic shocks. This study provides a concise and precise insight into the effects of economic and political shocks, thereby enhancing robust causal inference. The empirical evidence suggests that CCT programs can be effective in enhancing household welfare and reducing economic disparities when cash transfers are sufficient and, if implemented well, have a long-lasting positive impact on the most vulnerable households.

title: Stablecoin Yield, Governance Rewards, and the Road to the CLARITY Act: Where U.S. Digital Asset Regulation Stands in March 2026
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: Stablecoin Yield, Governance Rewards, and the Road to the CLARITY Act: Where U.S. Digital Asset Regulation Stands in March 2026
detail.abstract: U.S. stablecoin and digital asset regulation has reached an inflection point in March 2026. The Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act (GENIUS Act), enacted in July 2025, established the first federal prudential framework for payment stablecoins and prohibited issuers from paying interest or yield to token holders. Its implementing rulemaking, led by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), was proposed on February 25, 2026, and introduces a rebuttable presumption against indirect yield arrangements routed through affiliates or third parties. In parallel, the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act (CLARITY Act), the broader market structure bill passed by the House in July 2025, has been stalled in the Senate Banking Committee since January 2026, primarily over the stablecoin yield question. On March 20, 2026, Senators Thom Tillis and Angela Alsobrooks announced an agreement in principle, backed by the White House, that would prohibit passive stablecoin yield while permitting activity-based rewards. This article surveys those legislative and regulatory developments, evaluates the substantive distinction at their core, and examines the unresolved governance-reward question that prior scholarship has identified as a potential loophole in the emerging framework.

title: Developing Resilient and Risk-Aware AI-Enabled Supply Chain Systems: Challenges and Opportunities
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Developing Resilient and Risk-Aware AI-Enabled Supply Chain Systems: Challenges and Opportunities
detail.abstract: This study investigates the challenges and opportunities in developing resilient and risk-aware AI-enabled supply chain systems amidst growing global uncertainty and complexity. A qualitative research approach was employed, based on a systematic review and thematic analysis of secondary data from recent academic and industry sources on artificial intelligence, supply chain resilience, and risk management. The analysis identified critical themes spanning technological, organizational, and environmental dimensions of AI adoption. Findings indicate that AI significantly enhances supply chain resilience by enabling predictive analytics, real-time visibility, and adaptive decision-making capabilities. Nonetheless, several challenges persist, including data fragmentation, lack of system interoperability, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, skill shortages, and ethical concerns surrounding AI implementation. Concurrently, opportunities emerge through the integration of advanced technologies, strengthened stakeholder collaboration, and the alignment of sustainability objectives with AI-driven strategies. The study highlights that organizations must adopt a holistic approach to AI implementation, emphasizing robust data infrastructure, organizational readiness, and governance frameworks. It further underscores the importance of combining human expertise with AI capabilities to ensure effective, responsible, and strategic decision-making. These insights provide both theoretical contributions and practical guidance for building resilient, future-ready, and sustainable supply chain systems.

title: Measuring Green Trade Through Carbon Efficiency: A Leontief-Based Approach Using ADB Multi-Regional Input-Output Tables

detail.title: Measuring Green Trade Through Carbon Efficiency: A Leontief-Based Approach Using ADB Multi-Regional Input-Output Tables
detail.abstract: Green trade is commonly tracked through classified goods categorized by HS code and therefore cannot distinguish an environmentally classified good produced with fossil energy from one produced with renewable energy. This paper introduces an alternative, a Carbon Efficiency Index (CEI) defined as the ratio of the Leontief output multiplier to the carbon multiplier. CEI measures economic output per unit of embodied emissions across the full upstream supply chain. Using the ADB Multi-Regional Input-Output Tables in constant 2010 prices, I find that global CEI improved by 27.5% over 2017-2023, but structural decomposition reveals that the scale effect offset 36% of the gains from cleaner production. Carbon source attribution shows that supply chain reorientation redistributes rather than eliminates carbon content: 18.0% of the embodied carbon in Vietnam's 2023 exports to the United States originates from Chinese upstream production, up from 10.9% in 2017. Trade-weighted CEI rankings diverge substantially from production-based measures for GVC-integrated economies such as Korea and Singapore. These findings inform the design of carbon border adjustment mechanisms and the development of process-based green trade metrics.

title: Data as Liability
affiliations: University of Oxford - Department of Economics and University of Cambridge

detail.title: Data as Liability
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence makes data more productive, but it also makes data more costly to govern. This paper asks where that governance cost shows up in firms' own risk disclosures. Using roughly 84000 firm-years of SEC annual filings for US listed firms from 1994 to 2023, the paper builds layered text and LLM measures to separate AI invention from AI adoption and relates both to disclosed attention to data breach risk. AI adoption is associated with roughly 5 per cent higher breach-risk attention relative to the sample mean; AI invention is economically negligible once both margins enter the same specification. The wedge survives an explicit non-AI digitisation placebo built from the same filings. Among adopters, breach-risk attention is highest where deployment is customer-facing. Firms that explicitly connect AI to breach vulnerability describe it as expanding exposure in 101 of 103 directional statements. Supplementary evidence from staggered state Data Breach Notification laws is directionally consistent with the disclosure results.

title:
Managerial Quality as Strategic Capital
Performance, Health, and Societal Consequences of the Manager Effect

detail.title:
Managerial Quality as Strategic Capital
Performance, Health, and Societal Consequences of the Manager Effect

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Eric Knauf is Founder and CEO of BelongHQ, Inc., a belonging infrastructure consulting firm. This paper argues that belonging infrastructure and managerial quality are consequential for organizational performance and health outcomes. Readers should weigh this potential conflict of interest accordingly. No external funding supported this research.

detail.abstract:
Managerial quality is among the largest, least-regulated determinants of adult well-being and organizational performance, yet most firms treat it as an HR hygiene factor rather than strategic capital. This paper synthesizes evidence across three domains to establish the scope of manager impact and identify the operational levers that shift manager quality at scale. 

In workplace performance, within-firm panel studies demonstrate that replacing a manager at the 10th percentile of quality with one at the 90th percentile increases a team's total output by roughly the equivalent of adding a full-time employee to a nine-person team (Lazear, Shaw, and Stanton, 2015). Gallup estimates that manager quality accounts for approximately 70% of the variance in team engagement scores across business units, with high-engagement units showing around 20% higher profitability than low-engagement counterparts.

 In individual health, large prospective longitudinal studies find that employees with supportive, competent managers show 20-39% lower risk of ischaemic heart disease over approximately ten-year follow-up periods, with larger effects among longer-tenured employees, independent of traditional cardiovascular risk factors. Abusive supervision is associated with substantially elevated rates of depression and anxiety across meta-analytic aggregations.

 In family and societal outcomes, chronic job stress attributable to poor management predicts higher marital dissolution risk and elevated behavioral difficulties in employees' children, with observational studies linking stressful working conditions to increased all-cause and cardiovascular mortality risk over time. 

This paper introduces the Seven-Condition Model, comprising clarity and direction, feedback, resources, obstacle elimination, belonging infrastructure, development opportunity, and autonomy, as a unified operational framework for distinguishing effective from harmful managerial behavior. It further identifies systematic failure modes in conventional manager development programs and proposes a selection, incentive, and accountability architecture that treats manager quality as measurable infrastructure with predictable returns within 18-24 months.

title: Toward Regulatory Coherence in Crypto Markets: SEC-CFTC Interpretive Guidance and a Functional Taxonomy of Digital Assets
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: Toward Regulatory Coherence in Crypto Markets: SEC-CFTC Interpretive Guidance and a Functional Taxonomy of Digital Assets
detail.abstract: In March 2026, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission issued joint interpretive guidance clarifying the application of federal securities laws to crypto assets. This article evaluates the significance and limitations of that guidance, focusing on its reliance on the Howey framework and its introduction of a functional taxonomy of digital assets. While the interagency effort represents a meaningful step toward regulatory coherence, the analysis demonstrates that the framework remains incomplete in addressing the increasing financialization of crypto markets, including staking, lending, and yieldgenerating activities. These developments introduce risks analogous to traditional financial intermediation, including liquidity mismatches, leverage, and systemic interconnectedness. To address these gaps, the article proposes a refined, functionally grounded taxonomy that incorporates asset use, governance structure, and risk characteristics. By aligning regulatory treatment with economic substance rather than technological form, the proposed framework enhances both investor protection and market efficiency. The article concludes that continued regulatory coordination, combined with a more granular classification system, is essential to balancing innovation with financial stability in evolving digital asset markets.

title: Digital HR Practices in the Post-Pandemic Era
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Digital HR Practices in the Post-Pandemic Era
detail.abstract: This review examines the way the COVID-19 pandemic propelled the digital HR practices into long-term strategies of managing recruitment, onboarding, learning and development, and employee engagement. The research is based on the qualitative literature review methodology, relying on academic articles and industry reports published in the period between 2020 and 2025. To find recurring trends and insights on the digital transformation of HR processes and employee experience, a thematic analysis was performed. Other issues, recognized in the review, include impaired social integration, algorithmic favoritism, diminished involvement in virtual training, and augmented exposures to isolation, exhaustion, and a loss of touch with organization culture. The results emphasize the importance of digital HR in producing the highest value when it is closely related to the organization leadership and strategy.

title: Legal Aid in England and Wales: A Historical and Budgetary Perspective

detail.title: Legal Aid in England and Wales: A Historical and Budgetary Perspective
detail.abstract: This paper traces the evolution of state intervention in legal aid provision in England and Wales from the 15th century in forma pauperis statute to the present day, revealing a non-linear trajectory from charity to comprehensive welfare provision and back toward restricted access. Employing a process tracing methodology and drawing on legislative histories, government reports, and a manually reconstructed budgetary time-series covering the fiscal years 1949/50 to 2024/25, the analysis documents how legal aid transformed from voluntary provision for paupers into a cornerstone of the postwar welfare state by 1949, before experiencing severe retrenchment. The paper identifies three critical junctures: the 1949 Legal Aid Act which established universal access as a democratic principle; the 1972-1986 golden period of expanded provision into social welfare law; and the 2012 LASPO reforms, which removed entire areas of law from scope, triggering provider closures and creating legal aid deserts. The original budget reconstruction demonstrates that while recent cuts have been justified as austerity measures, they represent a fundamental reconceptualisation of legal aid, from a social right available to 80% of the population at inception to a residual safety net covering less than 25%, a shift that has been obscured by fragmented data and inconsistent measurement methodologies. The paper contributes both a consolidated historical narrative and a novel fiscal dataset to an under-documented area of welfare state scholarship.

title: Momentum Returns and the Role of Liquidity Improvements
affiliations: ATP

detail.title: Momentum Returns and the Role of Liquidity Improvements
detail.abstract: This paper demonstrates that the momentum anomaly arises from cross-sectional liquidity dynamics rather than representing an independent risk premium. I show that past winners systematically improve in liquidity prior to the portfolio formation period, whereas past losers severely deteriorate. By exploiting this asymmetry, I construct a liquidity improvement factor (LIQIM) that captures the reallocation of trading activity across stocks. I provide causal evidence that lagged, pre-formation liquidity changes strongly predict subsequent momentum price drift. Consequently, LIQIM completely absorbs the momentum alpha across standard asset pricing models. These results indicate that momentum profits are structurally generated by the market's gradual price adjustment to changing asset-level liquidity states, fundamentally distinguishing this mechanism from aggregate liquidity risk.

title: Who Owns the Past? Politics and Law in the Restitution of Cultural Property
affiliations: IMT Institute for Advanced Studies

detail.title: Who Owns the Past? Politics and Law in the Restitution of Cultural Property
detail.abstract: The article examines the issue of cultural property restitution as a boundary field between law, politics, and ethics, exploring the legal and symbolic significance of returning works of art to their places, States, or communities of origin. Through a broad survey of historical and contemporary cases—from wartime spoliations to illicit trafficking, from post-colonial restitutions to those linked to Nazi-Fascist persecutions—the Author highlights the different causes, modalities, and rationales of restitution, emphasizing the plurality of actors and instruments involved. The contribution reconstructs the role of both international and domestic law, underscoring their structural limits, in particular non-retroactivity and the inalienability of public cultural property, and shows how restitutions are often grounded in negotiated agreements and forms of soft law rather than in judicial decisions. In conclusion, the article argues that a new ethic of cultural responsibility and an emerging international custom are taking shape, pointing toward the possible affirmation of a “right to restitution,” also understood as a response to a fundamental question in cultural heritage studies: who owns the past?

title: Licensing Enforcement and the Supply of Childcare
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley and University of California, Berkeley - School of Law

detail.title: Licensing Enforcement and the Supply of Childcare
detail.abstract: Licensing authorities enforce regulations through inspections, which can worsen supply restrictions caused by licensing but may improve quality. We study the equilibrium impacts of licensing enforcement in the context of early childhood education. Using the childcare licensing program analysts' stringency as an instrument for violations, we study the causal impact of violations on facility closure. We find that violations lead to an increase of 4 percentage points in the probability of facility closure. Closures are not driven by involuntary administrative penalties like license revocation, but instead result from equilibrium shifts in both supply and demand. Overall, closure is more likely to result from administrative violations, and have greater impact on home daycares and underserved areas. Our results suggest that low quality facilities are more likely to exit after a violation, but that facilities in low supply areas are more likely to exit due to regulatory stringency. This implies licensing authorities facing a tradeoff between quality and adequacy of supply should increase stringency in detecting care-related, rather than administrative, violations.

title: Geography of Power and Development

detail.title: Geography of Power and Development
detail.abstract: This document develops an interdisciplinary reflection on the relationship between essence, space, and human action in shaping economic and social geography, integrating classical and contemporary philosophical perspectives. Drawing on approaches such as those of Aristotle, existentialism, Parmenides, Heraclitus, Hobbes, and Rousseau, it analyzes how individual decisions, institutional structures, and territorial dynamics interact to define economic organization. The role of the social contract in regulating space is examined, demonstrating how its strengthening or weakening affects formality, informality, and illegal economies. Spatial asymmetries, market failures, and inequality are also addressed as factors that condition development. Finally, the need for territorially based public policies that articulate equity, efficiency, and social cohesion to achieve sustainable development is proposed.

title: Geopolitics in the Supply Chain: A Global FVA-Based Exposure Index with Bartik Evidence on Trade Reallocation

detail.title: Geopolitics in the Supply Chain: A Global FVA-Based Exposure Index with Bartik Evidence on Trade Reallocation
detail.abstract: We construct the first global index of supply-chain geopolitical alignment composition using multiregional input-output (MRIO) methods, covering all 80 economies in the OECD Inter-Country Input-Output (ICIO) tables over 2016-2022. Embedding UN-voting-based alignment scores into the Leontief attribution framework, we build Foreign Value-Added Geopolitical Exposure (FVA-GE) indices that measure the mean upstream alignment tilt of each economy's production network-a first-moment measure of supply-chain alignment composition, not a complete vulnerability assessment. The global distribution has mean-0.14 (slightly China-tilted), with substantial crosscountry heterogeneity driven by economic geography: commodity exporters are China-tilted through mining upstream linkages, while manufacturing-integrated OECD economies are US-tilted. A decomposition reveals that short-run variation reflects partners' geopolitical alignment shifts rather than genuine supply-chain restructuring. To validate the index, we implement a Bartik shift-share design using base-year (2016) FVA weights as predetermined shares and annual alignment shocks as shifters (first-stage F = 257). In a horse race, the MRIO-based Bartik dominates a gross-trade alternative, with only the MRIO instrument remaining significant in the joint first stage. Two-stage least squares show that predicted exposure toward US-aligned supply chains increases the US import share by 0.10 percentage points (p < 0.01)-a result immune to the concern that time-varying bloc definitions mechanically correlate with the instrument. The Bartik estimates identify how pre-existing supply-chain structure mediates the transmission of geopolitical alignment shocks to trade composition, providing the first evidence that MRIO-derived upstream weights carry predictive information beyond direct bilateral flows.

title: Justice Under Austerity: The Impacts of Reduced Access to Legal Assistance in England and Wales

detail.title: Justice Under Austerity: The Impacts of Reduced Access to Legal Assistance in England and Wales
detail.abstract: In 2013, England and Wales implemented a legal aid reform that sharply reduced public funding for civil legal assistance, eliminating early-stage support and restricting aid to lastresort, courtroom interventions. This paper examines the broader socioeconomic and public health consequences, focusing on vulnerable households facing housing, debt, and welfare disputes. Using panel data from 2009-2023 on legal aid provider locations, service volumes, court filings, and mortality, we quantify the reform's effects on access to justice and downstream outcomes. Our empirical strategy combines a difference-indifferences design exploiting spatial and temporal variation in access driven by provider closures, with a Bartikstyle instrument based on pre-reform exposure to funding cuts. Exposed areas experienced significant increases in eviction filings and court orders, alongside rises in homelessness and mortality, with effects compounded in areas simultaneously hit by welfare benefit cuts. By defunding early advice and narrowing legal aid to specific practice areas, the reform limited providers' ability to address interconnected problems, rendering the integrated service model-where early intervention, cross-domain casework, and court representation were co-located-financially unviable. Providers delivering this model exited disproportionately, severing the link between upstream problem-solving and court-stage protection. Early advice and court-stage representation appear as complements, not substitutes: preserving one without the other left the most vulnerable households worse off across multiple dimensions. These findings highlight the role of access to justice in social protection and suggest that cutting preventive legal services shifts costs onto local authorities and healthcare systems, revealing unintended long-term consequences of retrenching the social safety net through legal reform.

title: When One Size Doesn't Fit All: U.S. State-Level Inflation Decomposition Throughout the Early 2020s
affiliations: Boston College

detail.title: When One Size Doesn't Fit All: U.S. State-Level Inflation Decomposition Throughout the Early 2020s

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The paper was written by James Coukos, a thesis writer at Boston College. However, there are not personal or financial relationships that impacted this study or its findings.
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: No official funding provided - utilized research tools from Boston College.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the structural drivers of inflation across U.S. states during the early 2020s by extending a supply–demand inflation decomposition framework to the state level. While national inflation surged following the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine, existing research largely obscures geographic heterogeneity within the United States. The results reveal substantial cross-state variation in the composition and dispersion of inflationary shocks. Although national aggregates suggest a coherent narrative of economic shocks throughout the early 2020s, state-level evidence shows that inflation was structurally heterogeneous. State-level decompositions indicate that the relative contribution of supply and demand shocks differed widely across states, while dispersion measures show persistent variation in shock composition throughout 2019–2023. In 2022, negative supply shocks affected over 75 percent of the consumption basket in some states but less than 20 percent in others, while positive demand exposure exceeded 30 percent in some states and remained below 10 percent in others. These findings carry important institutional implications. Since monetary policy operates uniformly across states, its real effects are necessarily asymmetric when inflation reflects geographic heterogeneity. Complementary and geographically targeted fiscal policy may help address these localized economic imbalances. More broadly, this study highlights the need for improved state-level economic reporting to better diagnose inflation dynamics within a heterogeneous national economy.

title: On the Empirical (Ir)Relevance of the Zero Lower Bound Constraint: The Case of Fiscal Multiplier in Japan
affiliations: Nihon University - College of Economics,  and The University of Osaka

detail.title: On the Empirical (Ir)Relevance of the Zero Lower Bound Constraint: The Case of Fiscal Multiplier in Japan
detail.abstract: Japan's prolonged ZLB period alongside substantial debt accumulation makes it a compelling laboratory for testing whether fiscal multipliers differ across normal and ZLB periods. This paper investigates this question using a sign- and zero-restricted TVP-VAR that jointly identifies fiscal rules and structural shocks. We find: (1) government spending and distortionary tax multipliers remain similar across regimes, contradicting standard New Keynesian predictions; (2) fiscal adjustment matters more than the debt-to-GDP ratio in shaping multiplier size; and (3) inflation responses are dampened at the ZLB across various macroeconomic shocks. Our results suggest that the ZLB is irrelevant for output but consequential for inflation.

title: Reshuffling of Human Capital in Financial Intermediation
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University - Smeal College of Business, University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Kenan-Flagler Business School and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title: Reshuffling of Human Capital in Financial Intermediation
detail.abstract: How has private credit reshaped human capital in the financial intermediation sector? We document a large migration of personnel from banks to private credit, accompanied by a substantial reshuffling across functions and hierarchies. Exploiting bank stress tests as a shock that induces outflows, we show that movers to private credit attain higher seniority and experience lower turnover rates. Private credit firms adopt less hierarchical structures with higher senior-to-junior ratios, and allocate more talent towards due diligence roles. Importantly, senior personnel in private credit are more concentrated in due diligence, contrasting with banks where greater focus is placed on deal sourcing and risk control. Private credit loans feature more monitoring and customized covenants, and these differences are largely explained by the observed functional differences. Overall, the growth of private credit has implications for not only a reallocation of financial capital but also a reorganization of human capital into structures that enable more information-intensive lending.

title: Bank to non-bank lending and the reallocation of credit
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Finance, Columbia University - Columbia Business School,  and Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Finance

detail.title: Bank to non-bank lending and the reallocation of credit
detail.abstract: We analyze how bank lending to non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) affects credit supply to the real economy. Using granular supervisory and loan-level data, we document rapid growth in bank lending to NBFIs relative to lending to non-financial firms. This growth is driven primarily by reverse repos to NBFIs that invest in securities, e.g., investment funds, rather than by loans to NBFIs that extend credit to firms, e.g., private credit funds. We show that the expansion in bank–NBFI lending reflects rising NBFI borrowing demand to fund government securities, which stems in part from the tapering of QE and the expansion of government bond supply in the Euro area, US, UK, and Japan. Importantly, loans to NBFIs disproportionately crowd out loans to non-financial firms rather than securities on bank balance sheets, which ultimately contracts credit supply to the real economy. A model rationalizes our empirical findings and quantifies the aggregate crowding-out effect. Taken together, our results imply that the rise of bank lending to NBFIs represents a narrowing of bank business models and a contraction in bank credit intermediation.

title: The Rise of Algorithmic Retail Option Traders
affiliations: Instituto Tecnológico Autónomo de México (ITAM), Wilfrid Laurier University, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign - Department of Finance and Instituto Tecnológico Autónomo de México (ITAM) - Department of Business Administration

detail.title: The Rise of Algorithmic Retail Option Traders
detail.abstract: We show that retail participation is increasingly rule-based rather than discretionary, leaving sharp and recurring intraday footprints in trading activity. Using transaction-level data from SPX zero-days-to-expiration (0DTE) options, we document pronounced volume spikes exactly at the hour and half-hour marks that emerge almost instantaneously and dissipate within seconds. These spikes intensify over time, are concentrated in complex multi-leg trades, and are largely absent in longer-dated contracts. Spike-time trading is dominated by small, standardized, shortpremium strategies consistent with template-driven execution and mechanical risk budgeting, and we do not find evidence that these trades are systematically wealth-depleting. Around these deterministic windows, quoted spreads tighten while effective spreads widen, indicating intensified liquidity provision alongside higher execution costs. Overall, fintech-enabled retail automation generates synchronized order flow that reshapes intraday liquidity and market quality.

title: Common Regulatory Exposure and Firm Misconduct
affiliations: Cornell University, Pennsylvania State University and Pennsylvania State University - Department of Finance

detail.title: Common Regulatory Exposure and Firm Misconduct
detail.abstract: Firms face common regulatory exposures when subject to similar regulations or under the purview of the same regulatory agencies. We examine the role of two types of common regulatory exposures for firm misconduct: unconditional common exposures arising from similar rules and regulations and conditional common exposures arising from enforcement criterion affected by previous actions on similar firms. We find that while unconditional common regulatory exposures discourage misconduct, conditional common exposures incentivize misconduct. Moreover, the two forces interact in that the misconduct-provoking side-effect from regulatory spillover is more pacified when the ex-ante regulations are more similar. Our study points to policy discussions about industry-specific rule-making and regulation by enforcement, along with testable predictions.

detail.title: What Drives Crypto Prices?
detail.abstract: Westudyintraday price discovery in cryptocurrency markets using high-frequency session-level data across global trading zones over March 2024–March 2026. We identify two primary and distinct drivers of crypto price variation. First, the Amihud (2002) illiquidity ratio explains up to 70% of the magnitude of intraday price movements during the New York morning session (9 AM–12 PM ET), with higher illiquidity systematically associated with larger absolute price changes. This result is robust across most global sessions. However, the illiquidity channel predicts the size of price moves, not their direction. Second, changes in stablecoin prices during the European lunch session (7 AM–9 AM ET) explain up to 90% of crypto price variation in the subsequent New York morning (9 AM- 12 PM ET) and lunch (12 PM–1 PMET) sessions. This stablecoin channel is concentrated in price deviations from the dollar peg: using two-stage least squares (2SLS), we show that stablecoin volume carries no predictive power once instrumented, while price deviations retain strong and statistically significant predictive content. Stablecoin driven predictability dissipates sharply during New York afternoon trading hours, consistent with the influx of informed institutional investors actively rebalancing their portfolios and ETFs. Our findings carry direct implications for financial stability: regulators should focus surveillance on intraday stablecoin price deviations as an early-warning indicator, rather than on volume-based metrics alone. The time-zone asymmetry in predictability further calls for internationally coordinated, session-aware oversight of stablecoin markets.

title: From Efficiency to Sustainability Governance: A Bibliometric and Critical Review of Precision Agriculture's Economic and Policy Impacts

detail.title: From Efficiency to Sustainability Governance: A Bibliometric and Critical Review of Precision Agriculture's Economic and Policy Impacts
detail.abstract: Precision agriculture (PA) is increasingly promoted as a "more-with-less" pathway that can raise farm efficiency while supporting sustainability goals. This paper provides a bibliometric and critical review of PA's economic and policy impacts, with emphasis on diffusion patterns, evidence quality, and the data foundations needed for sustainability governance. Using approximately 3,600 Web of Science recordsabout 2,000 in general PA research and 1,600 in PA-and-economics-this study maps keyword cooccurrence networks in VOSviewer and compares how themes emerge across the two literatures. Three dominant clusters structure the PA-and-economics field: input optimization, information/externalities, and predictive analytics. Across clusters, economic evaluation consistently lags technological and agronomic innovation by roughly 2.25 years, creating an "economic verification gap" in which adoption and policy interest can advance before credible estimates of profitability, risk, and public environmental benefits are available. Evidence synthesis further indicates that PA returns are heterogeneous and often modest on average, shaped by fixed costs, managerial capacity, complementarities, and infrastructure (e.g., connectivity and data systems). Closing the verification gap will require improved measurement and government documentation capacity, data standards, and adaptive incentives that target binding constraints while supporting equitable diffusion.

detail.abstract:
The global gaming industry generated approximately $298 billion in revenue in 2024 and is projected to exceed $505 billion by 2030, yet its potential in politically constrained emerging markets remains understudied. This paper presents the first comprehensive analysis of Iran's gaming industry potential under post-sanctions, liberalised governance - the Iranian Gaming Renaissance. Drawing on Nye (2004), Porter (1990), Scott (2000), Flew (2012), and Florida (2002), the study combines comparative case study methodology with scenario-based financial projections benchmarked against studio data from Poland, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia.

Iran has 34 million active gamers, a median gamer age of 23, and the 50,000-verse Shahnameh as unexploited cultural IP. Base Case projections indicate $40 million in annual revenue and 2,360 total economy-wide jobs by Year 10, contributing $33 million annually to GDP; the Optimistic scenario reaches $95 million and 5,605 total jobs. A four-phase roadmap is proposed, beginning with a mobile adaptation of the Eranshahr board game and scaling to international AAA co-production. Risk-adjusted analysis reduces the Base Case to $28 million and 1,400 jobs. This paper contributes the first systematic framework for analysing creative industry potential in sanctioned emerging markets.

detail.abstract: We propose a signal-to-noise framework (η) that formalizes the conditions under which market capitalization weighting produces suboptimal index returns. Extending Hsu (2006)'s noisy market hypothesis, we show that cap weighting's performance drag is decreasing in η-the ratio of fundamental-driven to noise-driven variation in market capitalization-and amplified by asset-class volatility. We derive three formal propositions: (i) cap-weight drag scales as σ 2 P /(1 + η), (ii) risk-adjusted weighting dominates cap weighting on a risk-adjusted basis when η falls below a critical threshold η * , and (iii) asset classes characterized by boom-bust dynamics exhibit structurally low η, making cap weighting a systematic drag rather than a passive benchmark. We validate the framework empirically across three regimes-equities, commodities, and cryptocurrencies-and propose a practitioner decision rule for selecting index methodology based on estimated η.

title: Land Appreciation as a Theory of Ordinary Inflation: Evidence from 65 Years of U.S. Data
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Land Appreciation as a Theory of Ordinary Inflation: Evidence from 65 Years of U.S. Data
detail.abstract:
Land appreciation appears to function as the primary upstream driver of ordinary inflation in a market economy. The conclusion follows from two key empirical findings.

First, cumulative existing real estate capital gains track approximately 93% of cumulative labor productivity growth over 63 years of U.S. data (1960–2023), indicating that land captures the vast majority of the economy's productivity gains.

Second, the cumulative ratio of annual U.S. real-estate capital gains divided by GDP — a measure defined in this paper as landflation — tracks approximately one-half of cumulative consumer price inflation over the same period. This is consistent with a propagation structure in which land appreciation costs enter the price system directly (through a mortgage or lease increase) and then propagate indirectly through wages, energy, and goods in an approximately 1:1 direct pass-through to future prices.

Both findings assume a real estate share parameter of 0.555, meaning that real estate makes up approximately 56 percent of total US capital gains on a long-run basis.  This ratio includes owner-occupied residential property, commercial real estate, farmland, and land value embedded in corporate assets.

The paper does not attempt to isolate a single causal channel in a traditional econometric sense, but rather to identify a coherent accounting-consistent mechanism that can jointly explain several persistent empirical patterns.

detail.abstract: Despite the strong commitment of European countries to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, the extent to which key policies and drivers jointly shape emissions dynamics remains insufficiently investigated. To fill this gap, the study investigates the combined effects of the circular economy, energy transition, emissions trading systems, carbon tax, and digitalization on carbon reduction in the EU member states. Using annual data from 2000 to 2023, the analysis integrates causal discovery, time-varying dependence modeling, and machine learning methods to unravel system-level causal structure, dynamic connectedness, and future emission trajectories. The Directed Acyclic Graph method, especially the Fast Adjacency Skewness algorithm, identifies both contemporaneous and lagged causal relationships, in which resource productivity acts as a transmission channel within the system. Lagged disequilibrium shocks propagate from upstream circular economy factor (material footprint) and digitalization to midstream efficiency (resource productivity), and ultimately are transmitted to emissions. Time-varying copula models confirm significant heterogeneity and evolving dependence among key factors, highlighting the nature of the dynamic relationships. Forecasting results, based on a Support Vector Regression model under the European Union's 2030 climate policy target, indicate a persistently declining emission trajectory, however at an insufficient speed to meet the EU's 2030 target. Sensitivity analysis indicates that this gap does not reflect a policy failure but the need for accelerated policy adjustments.

title: Banks as Stewards
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York, University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business and Columbia Business School

detail.title: Banks as Stewards
detail.abstract: Banks may play a more active role in corporate finance than previously documented. We document that banks hire industry experts and then steward firms to undertake investments in expansion (new to the firm) sectors.  In supervisory data including detailed regulatory risk measures and granular loan-level industry attribution, expansion loans are double as likely to emerge in bank-firm potential pairs when the bank has precise industry specialization or higher degree experts. Results are robust to specifications that build off dynamic comparables strategies (Sun and Abraham, 2021), `within-firm' (Khwaja and Mian, 2008}) and `within-bank'  (Blickle et al., 2024) analyses, and fully saturated bank-firm-time models (Paravisini et al., 2023). Conceptualizing our setting, we frame that bank stewarding will be more prevalent where firms neglect expansion investment because of high discount rates. Empirically, the effect of bank expertise and specialization unlocking expansion loans is increasing in firms' short-termist discount rates.  Finally, we document the mechanism through loan pricing:  banks provide loans at 7-to-72 bps lower interest rates to induce loan volume, and thereby overcoming Kodak moments. Such expansion stewarding is likely most valuable in moments of transition for an industry.  We corroborate our general expansion evidence in the context of firm expansion investments from the energy transition.  Active bank stewarding moves the literature beyond the classic view of banks as mere credit providers.

title: Program Design and the Distributional Incidence of Housing Transfers. Evidence from a Universal Housing Allowance
affiliations: University of Auckland Business School

detail.title: Program Design and the Distributional Incidence of Housing Transfers. Evidence from a Universal Housing Allowance
detail.abstract: This paper provides the first population-level distributional analysis of housing allowance incidence. Exploiting population-level data across 1,489 housing sub-markets, I estimate the effect of a universal housing allowance structured as a negative income tax on rents across the conditional distribution. Identification draws on a government communications campaign that increased claiming by 28 percent without altering the benefit formula. Quantile regressions reveal two distributional gradients. Within the recipient segment, allowance expenditure has no effect on lower quartile rents at any quantile from the 10th to the 90th percentile, while the poverty-concentration effect of take-up steepens monotonically, strongest where landlords have room to moderate rent growth. Across the full market, the take-up effect peaks at the 25th percentile where the recipient cohort is most concentrated, attenuating as higher-income renters dilute the signal. These gradients are the distributional signature of poverty, not demand. Comparative institutional analysis reveals that where allowances operate under the negative income tax formula without dollar-for-dollar rent coverage, indexation to rents, transparent subsidy communication, or dwelling quality conditionality, the result is a null incidence - consistent across the EHAP experiments, the Finnish allowance, and the present study. Where these features are present, positive effects emerge as the capture channel operates. Program design determines incidence.

title: Portfolio Exposure as Rainbow Options: Fast and Noise-Free CVA and PFE Computation for Linear FX Portfolios

detail.title: Portfolio Exposure as Rainbow Options: Fast and Noise-Free CVA and PFE Computation for Linear FX Portfolios
detail.abstract: Fast and stable computation of counterparty credit risk metrics such as Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) and Potential Future Exposure (PFE) remains a central challenge in the pricing and risk management of derivative portfolios, particularly in real-time and incremental settings. Monte Carlo simulation, while flexible, is often computationally expensive and introduces noise that complicates sensitivity analysis and day-on-day P&L attribution. In this paper, we propose a semi-analytic framework for the efficient computation of exposure profiles for portfolios of linear foreign exchange (FX) instruments, including FX forwards and swaps. The key idea is to express the portfolio value as a linear combination of underlying FX rates and to approximate the resulting exposure distribution using tractable basket option representations. Expected Positive Exposure (EPE) is obtained via a spread option approximation, while PFE is computed through inversion of a corresponding digital spread formulation. The proposed approach delivers fast, stable, and noise-free estimates of both EPE and PFE, making it well suited to real-time applications and incremental risk calculations. The framework naturally extends to portfolios with linear exposure to equities and commodities, and is applicable to both real-time and end-of-day CVA and PFE calculations. In the latter setting, the methodology enables stable and noise-free day-on-day P&L attribution. Numerical results demonstrate strong agreement with benchmark Monte Carlo simulations while achieving significant gains in computational efficiency and numerical stability.

title: Video Games and user Rights in Copyright Law

detail.title: Video Games and user Rights in Copyright Law
detail.abstract: This chapter explores the evolving concept of users in the video game industry and its intersection with copyright law, particularly within the EU. Traditionally centred around individual players, the notion of users has expanded to include eSports athletes, streamers, influencers, cloners, modders, and fan fiction authors. These user categories have shifted from passive consumers to active contributors in the creative landscape of video games. This transformation brings forward legal implications, especially concerning "user rights" – a term rooted in EU copyright law. The chapter focuses on the challenges and opportunities of incorporating these evolving user practices into the EU legal framework, with occasional reference to U.S. copyright law. It outlines the historical development of video game users, discusses the scope and recognition of user rights, and highlights the complexity of aligning emerging user behaviours with existing legal structures.

title: Classification Cascades: Evidence from ICD Code Transitions in Healthcare Delivery and Spending

detail.abstract: Classification systems—standardized taxonomies such as the International Classification of Diseases (ICD), the Harmonized System (HS) for trade, and the Classification of Functions of Government (COFOG)—constitute foundational infrastructures of modern governance and economic measurement. This paper introduces the concept of classification cascades: the hypothesis that revisions to classification systems generate predictable, multi-stage disruptions that propagate from administrative coding through institutional processing to measurable behavioral and economic outcomes. I test this hypothesis using two complementary empirical strategies. First, I estimate event-study models exploiting staggered ICD adoption across 15 OECD countries (2005–2020), documenting discontinuities in pharmaceutical consumption consistent with cascade-induced shifts in recording and utilization at the point of classification revision. Second, I implement a difference-in-differences (DiD) design using U.S. Medicare claims data surrounding the ICD-9 to ICD-10 transition (October 1, 2015), comparing psychotherapy codes (treatment group) against evaluation and management codes (control group). The DiD estimates reveal a statistically significant increase in claim denial rates of +3.36 percentage points in the transition year (p = 0.004) and +2.99 percentage points in the post-transition year (p = 0.014). Descriptive evidence further documents a 6.9% decline in service volume and a 7.6% decline in Medicare payments by 2016 relative to the 2014 baseline. These findings are externally validated by Stewart et al. (2019), who document parallel disruptions in diagnosis recording across ten U.S. health systems. I argue that classification cascades represent a general class of administrative policy shock with implications extending beyond healthcare to international trade, public finance, and regulatory governance.

title: Rethinking Excise Incidence on Tobacco Products -Toward a Harm-Based Specific Tax

detail.title: Rethinking Excise Incidence on Tobacco Products -Toward a Harm-Based Specific Tax
detail.abstract: The European Commission's July 2025 proposal to revise the Tobacco Taxation Directive represents a welcome step forward, raising the EU minimum excise duty, and extending taxation to new products. However, the benefits and cost of the excise incidence requirement needs more careful analysis. Our empirical analysis of EU27 countries over 2016-2025 reveals that the excise incidence requirement itself-mandating that excise duties represent at least 60% of the Weighted Average Price (WAP) has not achieved its stated objectives of price harmonization and consumption reduction. Despite the 60% WAP rule remaining unchanged since 2011, crosscountry gaps in excise burdens and retail prices have widened rather than converged. In addition, panel regressions controlling for country and year fixed e!ects reveal that excise incidence is not a reliable predictor of retail prices, tax revenues, or consumption outcomes. Moreover, countries with restrictive regulations on alternative nicotine products experienced increases in smoking prevalence (as share of population), while countries with less restrictive approaches showed steady reductions. We propose an alternative framework based on harm-based specific taxation, indexed to inflation, which di!erentiates tax rates according to product-specific health risks. We theoretically demonstrate that for every uniform tax regime, there exists a harm-based tax that reduces public health costs while maintaining or increasing budget revenues.

detail.abstract: Psilocybin simultaneously holds six contradictory legal classifications across jurisdictions: Schedule I (US federal), Breakthrough Therapy (FDA), legal therapeutic use (Oregon, Colorado), Schedule 8 medical use (Australia), and pending rescheduling review (DEA/HHS). This regulatory fragmentation constitutes a classification cascade-a multi-stage disruption propagated through administrative, clinical, and economic channels when a single substance is reclassified unevenly across overlapping governance systems. Using four complementary empirical strategies, I document the cascade's progression: (i) a 21-country policy panel tracking 44 psychedelic regulatory events across 6 substance categories (1992-2025), revealing a sharp inflection at the 2018 FDA Breakthrough Therapy Designation; (ii) PubMed publication data extracted via NCBI E-utilities API showing psilocybin-depression research growing at 58.6% compound annual growth rate (2015-2025)-the fastest in psychedelic medicine, with total psilocybin publications increasing 54-fold from 12 (2000) to 656 (2025); (iii) trade flow analysis using difference-indifferences designs showing that botanical pharmaceutical imports (HS 1211) diverge sharply from control commodities following cannabis/psychedelic policy reforms, with estimates ranging from +67% to +97% in liberalizing countries; and (iv) FDA pipeline analysis documenting COMP360's consecutive Phase 3 successes (MADRS-3.6 and-3.8 versus placebo, both p < 0.001) alongside simultaneous political vetoes. The findings demonstrate that classification cascades-previously documented in healthcare billing (Tamba 2026)-extend to substance regulation, where they generate measurable distortions in research output, trade flows, clinical access, and enforcement patterns. I introduce the concept of the classification split-a state in which a single entity simultaneously occupies contradictory 2 categories across overlapping governance systems-as a distinct and increasingly prevalent form of regulatory failure. As psilocybin approaches FDA approval (NDA expected Q4 2026), the cascade documented here is accelerating rather than resolving.

title: Pay For Performance - CEOs vs Baseball Players

detail.abstract: Corporate boards and baseball team owners face some common challenges in managing pay. Both try to create strong incentives for outstanding performance and both have to balance their desire for strong incentives with the need to retain key talent and control cost. In this paper, I present an analysis of relative pay vs relative performance that allows us to compare CEO and baseball player pay on four dimensions: pay leverage, pay alignment, the pay premium at average performance and relative pay risk. We can measure these pay dimensions at the individual level, the team or company level and the industry level. When we do so, we come to four surprising conclusions. First, the median baseball team has much more consistent pay leverage than the median S&P 1500 public company. Second, pay leverage is far more consistent across teams than across S&P 1500 companies. Third, baseball, as an industry, has higher pay leverage than 50 of the 58 GICS industries studied and higher pay alignment than every GICS industry. Fourth, baseball teams and boards both sacrifice incentive strength for retention, leading them to overpay for performance, but baseball teams are more discriminating about where they overpay and have smaller overpayments.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the fiscal effects of Mexican migrants on the U.S. social security and welfare systems from 2007 to 2017. Using a dual-methodology approach-micro-level data from the Current Population Survey (CPS) and macro-level budgetary data from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO)-the analysis estimates the net fiscal balance of Mexican migrants compared to U.S. natives and other migrant groups. The findings reveal a persistent fiscal deficit among migrant groups, regardless of citizenship status, driven by structural disparities in legal status that limit tax contributions and benefit access. However, the results also show that time since arrival negatively correlates with welfare utilization, suggesting economic assimilation over time. The study underscores the need for policy frameworks that facilitate formal labor market integration to enhance migrant contributions and mitigate fiscal pressures.

title: Policy Capacity and Institutional Reform for Social Work in Southeast Asia

detail.title: Policy Capacity and Institutional Reform for Social Work in Southeast Asia
detail.abstract: In Southeast Asia, social work has emerged as a critical profession for addressing complex social issues including poverty, rapid urbanization, labor migration, population aging, child protection, and mental health. Even with increasing demand, social work policy frameworks remain uneven, under-institutionalized, and under-professionalized in the region. As a representative and strategically critical paper, the authors have attempted to examine how social work policy can be strengthened in Southeast Asia. Through comparative regional analysis, policy documents, and academic literature, the paper analyzes how social work evolved. It also examines existing governance and regulatory gaps, non-governmental organizations, international cooperation, and emerging best practices. Despite achievements in formal recognition, workforce development, and service expansion, Southeast Asian social work policy trajectory remains challenging due to fragmented governance, limited professional autonomy, and uneven service quality. Reforms across legislation, education, workforce regulation, financing, and intersectoral collaboration are needed to strengthen social work policy. In conclusion, a multilevel policy framework is proposed to advance professionalization, institutional capacity, and social protection outcomes.

title: Category Theory as a Unifying Language for Artificial Intelligence: Functors, Monads, Parametric Maps, String Diagrams, and Toposes
affiliations: Artificial Intelligence in Finance Institute

detail.title: Category Theory as a Unifying Language for Artificial Intelligence: Functors, Monads, Parametric Maps, String Diagrams, and Toposes
detail.abstract: Two recent programmes independently converge on category theory as the right language for artificial intelligence. Noguer i Alonso [2026] organises the feedback loop between ideal mathematics and computational practice into ten pillars-computability, complexity, approximation, optimisation, statistical learning, numerical analysis, differential equations, path signatures, geometry, and mathematical physics-and proposes adjoint functor pairs F ⊣ G as the unifying structure, with the transformer as a central case study. Gavranović et al. [2024] establishes that equivariant layers are monad algebra homomorphisms, that recurrent and recursive networks arise as lax algebras for free parametric monads in the 2-category Para, and that weight tying is a comonoid structure (their Theorem G.10). The present paper aligns and extends both frameworks. Its main contributions are three modest observations. First, the group action monad and the Giry probability monad share structural features through Dirac-supported embeddings, clarifying an analogy between equivariance and probabilistic semantics. Second, every parametric map f : P × A → B in Para is a coKleisli morphism for the product comonad W P = P ×-, which gives a clean categorical reading of weight tying as the cartesian diagonal ∆ P : P → P × P. Third, in-context learning admits a presheaf-topos interpretation: forcing at stage k captures stable posterior concentration on a hypothesis, monotonicity is the sheaf condition, and emergence corresponds to a Heyting-algebra phase transition. A synthesis table maps each pillar to its categorical structure, and four open problems are identified.

title: FlowPulse: A Flow-Based Liquidity Factor Framework for Corporate Bond Markets

detail.title: FlowPulse: A Flow-Based Liquidity Factor Framework for Corporate Bond Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is employed as an E-Trading Division Manager at SEQ Technology LLC. detail.abstract:
Corporate bond markets are characterized by fragmented liquidity, dealer-intermediated trading, and limited real-time transparency into supply and demand dynamics. Traditional valuation frameworks rely primarily on historical spread relationships, macroeconomic variables, and issuer fundamentals, while largely ignoring the informational content embedded in trading flows themselves. This paper introduces FlowPulse, a flow-based analytical framework designed to quantify directional liquidity pressure in corporate bond markets using aggregated institutional trading activity. The framework transforms transaction-level flow information into structured indicators of sector-level and security-level demand imbalances across issuers, sectors, and maturity buckets, constructing a systematic measure of market-wide liquidity pressure interpretable as a flow-based liquidity factor.

FlowPulse integrates three analytical layers: (1) a flow aggregation engine consolidating institutional trading activity—including both pre-trade dealer interest data and TRACE-reported executed trades—to identify directional buying and selling pressure; (2) a valuation layer comparing observed bond spreads with Ridge-regression-estimated fair-value spreads to identify relative-value dislocations; and (3) a predictive modeling layer incorporating Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks, Ridge regression, and mean-reversion signals trained on 12 features across a 70/30 rolling train-test framework with weekly retraining.

The framework has been implemented as a research prototype analytics platform designed for institutional fixed-income trading workflows. This paper presents the framework architecture, mathematical factor definitions, feature construction methodology, and proposed empirical specifications for evaluating the FlowPulse factors against credit spread dynamics. Prototype extensions to cryptocurrency and options markets are also presented, demonstrating the cross-asset applicability of the dual-stream flow aggregation approach.

detail.abstract: Pharmaceutical waste represents a significant and structurally underaddressed cost burden across healthcare systems globally, with upstream causes — over-prescribing, inappropriate dispensing quantities, and supply chain inefficiencies — receiving far less policy attention than downstream disposal and remediation. This paper draws on MBA research conducted at De Montfort University examining the feasibility of an AI-driven pharmaceutical waste reduction framework in the UAE healthcare context, and explores its implications for the US healthcare system. The UAE's centralised regulatory architecture, encompassing the Dubai Health Authority, the Department of Health Abu Dhabi, and the federal Ministry of Health and Prevention, combined with a maturing national health data infrastructure including the Riayati unified medical records platform, NABIDH, and Malaffi, provides an unusually tractable environment for developing and testing upstream intervention models. The framework integrates three data streams — prescribing pattern analysis, patient adherence modelling, and inventory management optimisation — into a unified clinical decision support interface. While the UAE and US health systems differ significantly in structure, the analytical logic underpinning the framework is transferable. The US regulatory environment, including NIH SBIR funding programmes and EPA pharmaceutical contamination priorities, provides complementary policy infrastructure to advance what the UAE context has helped establish conceptually.

title: What Gets Funded Depends on How Intent Is Translated: Translation Dynamics in Funding Systems (ERC, Novo Nordisk Foundation, Gates Foundation)

detail.abstract: This paper examines how institutional intent becomes the basis on which funding decisions are made. It shows that allocation does not operate directly on abstract institutional concepts such as excellence, impact, or innovation, but on the decision-relevant representations into which these concepts are translated within governance artefacts. Using three funding systems—the European Research Council (ERC), the Novo Nordisk Foundation (NNF), and the Gates Foundation—the paper traces how concepts articulated in founding mandates and programme frameworks are transformed into criteria, programme structures, and decision signals that enable evaluation, comparison, and selection. The analysis applies a minimal, rule-based, and replicable method that follows a small set of semantic anchors across publicly available artefacts, selecting the first formulation in each artefact where the concept defines a decision condition. Across the three cases, a consistent pattern is observed: concepts are progressively specified, structured, and operationalised into forms that make proposals comparable and selectable. However, the location and form of this translation differ across funding architectures—occurring through standardised evaluation criteria (ERC), programme-specific criteria (NNF), or the prior definition of problem domains and acceptable solution models (Gates Foundation). The contribution is methodological and empirical. The paper demonstrates that translation dynamics can be made directly observable in ordinary governance artefacts and provides a replicable approach for tracing how institutional intent becomes decision-relevant. By shifting the object of analysis from outcomes to the formation of allocation criteria and signals, the paper makes visible the representations on which funding decisions actually operate. This paper is part of the Coherence Programme on institutional decision systems.

title: Incentive Design in the Nonprofit Sector: Determinants, Discretion, and Organizational Outcomes
affiliations: University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business, University of California, Riverside (UCR) - School of Business Administration and Arizona State University (ASU) - School of Accountancy

detail.title: Incentive Design in the Nonprofit Sector: Determinants, Discretion, and Organizational Outcomes
detail.abstract: We examine how agency problems and performance measurement shape nonprofit executive compensation structure, and how this structure affects organizational outcomes. Analyzing 136,764 organization-year observations of Section 501(c)(3) nonprofits from 2018 to 2023, we distinguish between fixed, discretionary, and formula-based nonfixed bonus compensation, dimensions largely absent from prior research. We find that the likelihood of nonfixed and discretionary bonus compensation increases with external monitoring, compensation design oversight, labor market competition, and performance measurability. Discretionary bonus compensation specifically, not bonus compensation in general, drives future direct donations and program service expenses. Charity Navigator star ratings, however, improve with all forms of bonus compensation. Discretionary and nonfixed bonuses also increase pay-performance sensitivity based on both financial and mission-related performance. Our findings demonstrate that carefully designed bonus compensation, especially discretionary bonuses, can mitigate agency conflicts and enhance organizational performance in mission-driven organizations.

title: From Risk Registers to Control Systems: The Inverse Risk Register and Objective-First ERM

detail.title: From Risk Registers to Control Systems: The Inverse Risk Register and Objective-First ERM
detail.abstract: Risk registers remain the dominant operational instrument of enterprise risk management (ERM), yet persistent evidence suggests they fail to influence strategic decision-making or real-time organizational response. This paper argues that the limitation is structural rather than procedural: traditional risk registers organize information around risk events rather than organizational objectives, creating an open-loop system in environments that require continuous, signal-driven adaptation. Drawing on ERM frameworks (COSO, ISO 31000), objective-centric management literature (OKRs), and closed-loop control systems theory, this paper introduces the Inverse Risk Register (IRR)-a novel objective-first framework that redefines risk as a derivative of performance variance relative to strategic intent. The IRR repositions the objective as the primary index of risk information and structures risk management as a continuous feedback loop consisting of performance metrics, variance signals, causal drivers, and conditional response levers. The framework is operationalized through a five-step methodology and a formal mapping to closed-loop control system architecture, demonstrating how existing monitoring infrastructure can be repurposed for real-time risk detection and response. The IRR is proposed not as a replacement for existing frameworks, but as an operational mechanism to realize their longstanding objective-integration mandate.

detail.abstract: The Brown Theory of Experiential Intelligence™ (Brown, 2026) established that intelligence can be developed through lived experience as a structured, interpretable, and measurable process-producing not only knowledge but architectural thinking, leadership systems, and generational impact. This paper advances that foundational contribution into the domain of institutional application. Co-authored by the theory's originator, Donna M. Brown, and institutional development specialist Jonique P. Williams, this study examines how experiential intelligence can be operationalized within nonprofit organizations, higher education systems, and community-based environments. Drawing on the four proprietary models introduced in Brown (2026)-the KE Learning Model™, the Brown Experiential Architecture Model of Learning™, the Brown Experiential Intelligence Pyramid™, and the Experiential Framework Builder Model™-this paper introduces an applied implementation framework that translates theory into curriculum development, leadership pipelines, organizational infrastructure, and institutional policy. Case application is drawn from the Brown School of Experiential Leadership™. The paper further identifies funding mechanisms, partnership strategies, and a multi-phase institutional engagement model designed to support adoption at scale. Findings suggest that when experiential intelligence is formally recognized and systematically developed within institutional contexts, the result is more inclusive leadership, stronger community responsiveness, and sustainable systems change.

title: A Regime Switching Approach for Mortality Modeling in Presence of Climate Change and Pandemic Effects
affiliations: Western University, Canada, Oregon State University and Western University

detail.title: A Regime Switching Approach for Mortality Modeling in Presence of Climate Change and Pandemic Effects
detail.abstract: Understanding and forecasting mortality trends is critical, especially in the face of extreme events such as pandemics and the growing influence of climate change. While the former introduces abrupt and transitory shocks to mortality, the latter imposes gradual but potentially persistent effects, particularly at older ages. In this study, we extend the classical Lee-Carter model by incorporating a climate-sensitive component that modulates the period effect, allowing the model to better capture temperature-related mortality fluctuations. To enhance the forecasting feature, we depart from the standard multivariate random walk with drift commonly used for forecasting the Lee-Carter time index. Instead, we adopt a regime-switching framework that accounts for structural changes in mortality trends, including recovery dynamics after periods of higher mortality. We apply our proposed model to U.S. mortality data and compare its in-sample and out-of-sample performance against several competing models from the literature. Our results show that the extended model not only offers a more realistic representation of age-specific mortality during climate extremes and mortality shocks, but also delivers improved forecasting accuracy in terms of multiple evaluation metrics. The framework thus provides a valuable tool for policy planning in the context of ongoing demographic and environmental change.

title: The Pied Piper of Crypto: Influencer Finance, Regulatory Failure, and the Risks of Youth-Oriented Digital Assets
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: The Pied Piper of Crypto: Influencer Finance, Regulatory Failure, and the Risks of Youth-Oriented Digital Assets
detail.abstract: The integration of cryptocurrency into youth-oriented financial platforms presents a significant and underexamined risk within modern financial systems. This paper analyzes the convergence of influencer culture, financial technology innovation, and regulatory fragmentation through the case of Beast Industries' acquisition of Step, a mobile banking application designed for minors. Drawing on regulatory enforcement actions, agency reports, and evidence from the 2024 collapse of Synapse Financial Technologies, the paper argues that existing oversight mechanisms are structurally inadequate to protect minors from speculative financial exposure. Specifically, the combination of parasocial influence, gamified financial interfaces, and fragmented jurisdiction across regulatory bodies creates a pathway through which high-risk financial products can be normalized and distributed to underage users with limited scrutiny. The analysis demonstrates that current frameworks, which rely heavily on disclosure and post hoc enforcement, fail to address the unique risks posed by influencer-mediated financial promotion. The paper concludes by proposing targeted regulatory reforms, including restrictions on the marketing of high-risk assets to minors and enhanced accountability within fintech-bank partnership models.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Monetary Policy: A Framework and Perspective on Cyclical Transmission, Structural Transition, and Financial Stability

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Monetary Policy: A Framework and Perspective on Cyclical Transmission, Structural Transition, and Financial Stability
