detail.abstract: I develop a framework analyzing how artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes monetary policy through three interrelated channels: cyclical transmission, structural transition, and financial stability. In the short run, AI can alter inflation dynamics by changing how supply and demand disturbances map into prices-through shifts in production technologies, pricing behavior, cost pass-through, and expectations-even when conventional measures of economic slack are unchanged. Over longer horizons, AI may shift the natural benchmarks around which policy is calibrated, including potential output and the natural rate of interest. For financial stability, AI may improve credit allocation and risk assessment, but can also heighten systemic vulnerabilities through inflated expectation-driven asset valuations and model monocultures. A particular risk arises at the intersection of these channels: if AI initially depresses realized efficiency through adoption frictions while simultaneously fueling elevated asset valuations, the economy may face cost-push inflation and financial fragility at once-an AI-specific stagflation risk that the interest rate instrument alone is ill-suited to address. I argue that AI does not call for a redefinition of central banks' objectives, but it does require a recalibration of existing frameworks: its diffusion blurs the distinction between cyclical fluctuations and structural shifts, raising the value of cost-side diagnostics and robust policy strategies over exclusive reliance on reduced-form inflation-gap relationships.

title: Competitive Hardening Dynamics in Viscoplastic Materials with Evolving Threshold Stress
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Competitive Hardening Dynamics in Viscoplastic Materials with Evolving Threshold Stress
detail.abstract: Conventional viscoplasticity frameworks treat the threshold stress as either a material constant or a quantity evolving solely with accumulated plastic strain. Since microstructural evolution — whether precipitation, phase transformation, or solute redistribution—may proceed concurrently with deformation, such a treatment is often inadequate. The present work formulates a constitutive framework, derived from the Clausius–Duhem inequality and Perzyna-type overstress viscoplasticity, in which the threshold stress evolves autonomously with physical time through microstructural kinetics, independently of accumulated strain. Modified Armstrong–Frederick kinematic hardening with static recovery is incorporated, so that back stress develops only during active inelastic flow. The interaction between timedriven threshold evolution and strain-driven back-stress development gives rise to three behavioural regimes: (I) a purely elastic response, (II) flow arrest, in which inelastic flow initiates but subsequently ceases as the threshold overtakes the effective stress, and (III) continuous flow. A constructive Lyapunov function is employed to prove that flow arrest is asymptotically stable, a result not previously established at the material-point level in the viscoplastic creep literature. It is further shown that back-stress development reduces the time to arrest through a kinematic hardening acceleration effect. A physics-informed neural network employing smooth Macaulay bracket approximation with curriculum learning resolves all three regimes within a single trained surrogate. The framework is validated against experimental data using the creep-ageing and back-stress test (CABT), which provides independent measurements of inelastic strain and back-stress evolution.

title: Free-Energy–Driven Quantum-Enhanced Pneumonia Triage from Chest X-Ray Images
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Alfaisal University and National College Of Business Administration & Economics

detail.title: Free-Energy–Driven Quantum-Enhanced Pneumonia Triage from Chest X-Ray Images
detail.abstract: Reliable medical AI requires not only accurate classification, but also decision mechanisms that explicitly account for uncertainty when determining whether predictions should be accepted or deferred. Although deep learning methods have shown strong performance in chest X-ray analysis, many remain detection-centered and rely on confidence estimates that are not directly optimized for selective clinical decision-making. This paper proposes a decision-centric framework for pneumonia triage that combines compact latent representation learning, hybrid quantum-enhanced feature transformation, uncertainty-aware inference, and free-energy–based decision modeling. A convolutional encoder first maps chest X-ray images into a low-dimensional latent space, after which a quantum variational module enriches latent correlations through structured nonlinear transformation. Monte Carlo dropout is then used to estimate predictive uncertainty, and a free-energy criterion is introduced to govern triage by jointly incorporating predictive loss and uncertainty rather than relying on entropy alone.Experiments on a benchmark pneumonia chest X-ray dataset show that the latent–quantum hybrid model improves overall discrimination relative to the baseline, achieving higher test accuracy, F1-score, and AUC, while also producing a more structured latent-space organization. More importantly, the proposed free-energy decision rule yields more reliable selective prediction behavior than entropy-based triage at identical coverage. For the baseline model, free-energy triage reduces covered-case risk and improves accepted-case accuracy relative to entropy. For the latent–quantum hybrid model, free-energy triage further strengthens decision reliability and achieves perfect accuracy on the accepted subset at the same coverage level in the reported experimental setting. Latent-space visualization and case-based uncertainty analysis further show that the hybrid transformation reshapes the geometry of the representation and improves the separation of ambiguous from confident cases.These results demonstrate that the main contribution of the proposed framework lies not only in predictive modeling, but in its ability to support principled and clinically meaningful decision-making under uncertainty. By integratingPreprint submitted to Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine April 13, 2026latent representation learning, hybrid quantum processing, uncertainty estimation, and free-energy–based triage within a unified formulation, the proposed approach advances pneumonia analysis from detection-focused classification toward reliable and defer-capable medical decision support.

title: MammoInsight: A Unified Multi-Task Deep Learning Framework for Mammography Analysis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: MammoInsight: A Unified Multi-Task Deep Learning Framework for Mammography Analysis
detail.abstract: Background and Objective: Mammography interpretation requires simultaneous assessment of multiple clinical attributes such as cancer status, breast density, BI-RADS score, abnormality type, and molecular subtype. The MammoBench2 and MammoInsighty address these tasks in isolation, limiting clinical utility and generalizability.Methods: We present MammoInsight, a unified multi-task deep learning framework built on the MedImageInsight foundation model backbone, incorporating SAM-Med2D-guided region-of-interest pooling, cross-view attention fusion across both standard mammography views, weighted ordinal regression for ordered clinical labels, DHN-NCE contrastive regularisation, and homoscedastic uncertainty weighting for automatic task balancing. MammoInsight is trained and evaluated on ~65K images collated from nine geographically diverse resources, and compared against four large-scale foundation model baselines, viz., MedImageInsight, BiomedCLIP, MedGemma-4B, and MedGemma-27B, under a unified linear probing protocol. We also propose MammoBench2, a curated multi-task mammography dataset comprising 16,010 images with harmonised annotations for five clinical tasks and lesion segmentation, providing a robust benchmark for training AI models.Results: MammoInsight achieves state-of-the-art performance on cancer status prediction (Accuracy=0.800, weighted F1=0.787), breast density classification (Accuracy=0.767, weighted F1=0.765), BI-RADS scoring (Accuracy=0.661, weighted F1=0.646, the only model exceeding 0.6 on this six-class task), and lesion segmentation (DSC=0.804, IoU=0.786), a significant improvement over a fine-tuned single-task baseline using an architecturally identical decoder, while achieving a comparable accuracy (0.752) and weighted F1 (0.757) on abnormality classification.Conclusions: A unified multi-task framework trained with ordinal regression and joint segmentation supervision achieves comparable or superior performance across all five mammography clinical tasks compared to foundation models that are ~74 larger in parameter count, while simultaneously localising lesions with state-of-the-art accuracy. MammoBench2 and MammoInsight together provide the first open benchmark and unified framework for comprehensive multi-task mammography AI evaluation.​

title: Central Bank Communication and CBDC Implementation
affiliations: University of Oxford - Department of Economics

detail.title: Central Bank Communication and CBDC Implementation
detail.abstract: CBDC issuance remains rare even though central banks discuss it extensively. Using 37,814 speeches from 134 jurisdictions and a scored 2015-2025 sample of 15,906 speeches from 122 jurisdictions, the analysis builds country-year measures of CBDC commitment, technology salience, and stated constraints. Public commitment tracks agenda participation but adds little information about subsequent advancement beyond research once prior project stage is controlled for. More open capital accounts and, less consistently, greater central bank independence are negatively associated with advancement beyond research. Legal-regulatory concerns are the most consistently negative speech-based correlate.

title: The Effects of Early Center-based Childcare on Non-cognitive Skills: Evidence from the UKHLS

detail.title: The Effects of Early Center-based Childcare on Non-cognitive Skills: Evidence from the UKHLS
detail.abstract: Early childhood non-cognitive development is known to enhance children's educational achievements and adult-life outcomes. Drawing on a longitudinal sample of children from the UK Household Longitudinal Study (UKHLS), this paper provides new evidence on the short-run effects of early centre-based childcare attendance-measured between ages one and two-on children's adaptive behaviour and socio-emotional skills at age three. Our selection-on-observables strategy exploits a rich set of child and maternal background characteristics, as well as temporal and geographical variation in the availability of early centre-based childcare providers. To reduce potential bias, we combine Entropy Balancing and Inverse Probability Weighting with linear parametric analysis. Results indicate that early centre-based childcare attendance has strong and positive effect on children's adaptive behavioural scale and socio-emotional development. Effects are particularly pronounced among children of low-educated mothers.

title: Cross-Country Comparison of Macroeconomic Indicators of the Labor Market

detail.title: Cross-Country Comparison of Macroeconomic Indicators of the Labor Market
detail.abstract: The global pandemic triggered a global economic recession, resulting in high unemployment and labor market imbalances, which were reflected in changes in macroeconomic indicators in the US, Japan, and Russia. While the timing and scale of job losses and post-pandemic recovery varied significantly across these economies, they also shared some common characteristics. The aim of the work is to analyze macroeconomic indicators of the labor market in the USA, Japan and Russia using the Beveridge curve, which shows changes in unemployment and vacancies during the phases of the economic cycle and the impossibility of a simultaneous reduction in the number of vacancies and job seekers.

title: Breaking Barriers: Measuring Perceivability of Select North Indian University Library Websites

detail.title: Breaking Barriers: Measuring Perceivability of Select North Indian University Library Websites

publicationDetails.detailsText: In Information Literacy for Developing Enlightened Library / Information User Community in New Age (pp. 379-387), Presented on the IASLIC 30th National Seminar, Aligarh Muslim University, Aligarh, India. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18892565

detail.abstract:
Purpose: This paper examines the accessibility of select North Indian university library websites by applying the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), a globally recognized standard for accessible web design. The study specifically evaluates adherence to the Perceivable principle within WCAG 2.1, which ensures that information and interface components are interpretable by users of all abilities, particularly focusing on vision-impaired individuals who rely on assistive technologies.

Design/Methodology/Approach: Using the Siteimprove Accessibility Checker, this study conducted a systematic evaluation of North Indian university library homepages. Siteimprove is a robust tool for assessing WCAG compliance, allowing an automated review of various success criteria within the Perceivable principle. Data from 20 select universities was gathered and categorized to identify recurring issues, providing a detailed view of accessibility barriers across different areas, including non-text content, information relationships, color contrast, and text adaptability.

Findings: The findings indicate significant accessibility issues across several North Indian university library websites. Notably, National Law University, Delhi, had the most issues with Text Alternatives (81), while the University of Delhi exhibited high levels of Adaptable Content issues (282). Central Sanskrit University showed the most challenges with color usage (23 issues), and Indira Gandhi and Jammu Universities had significant problems with minimum contrast (79 and 76, respectively). Additionally, Himachal Pradesh National Law University led in Contrast Enhanced issues (92), and National Law University displayed the highest number of issues related to Images of Text (94). Although some websites were well-structured, these findings underscore a prevalent gap in accessibility that limits inclusive access for users with disabilities.

Originality/Value: This study fills a critical gap by focusing on accessibility challenges specific to North Indian university library websites, providing insights valuable for academic institutions striving for inclusivity. It highlights priority areas where targeted improvements could substantially enhance web accessibility for vision-impaired users. The methodology, based on WCAG 2.1 and Siteimprove, supports reusability and reproducibility, offering a framework for ongoing accessibility audits that can be extended to other regions and educational contexts.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Capabilities in Sustainability Reporting of Oil and Gas Companies
affiliations: Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO)

detail.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Capabilities in Sustainability Reporting of Oil and Gas Companies
detail.abstract: This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence (AI)-specifically large language models (LLMs) enhanced by Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) technology-can be applied across the sustainability reporting cycle of oil and gas companies. Drawing on recent empirical research and the evolving Russian regulatory framework, including the 2023 Methodological Recommendations on Sustainability Reporting and the 2025 Business Social Capital Standard, the study identifies three functional stages at which generative AI offers distinct capabilities: primary data processing, analytical elaboration, and final disclosure drafting. For each stage, specific accounting and methodological conditions are proposed to govern AI deployment responsibly. The paper argues that realising the potential of generative AI in sustainability reporting requires not merely technological adoption but deliberate adaptation of accounting policies, prompt governance, and expert oversight mechanisms. The findings are particularly relevant for Russian energy companies operating within a rapidly developing national sustainability disclosure regime.

detail.abstract: This research seeks to delve deeper into the financial significance of the eigenvector associated with the second-largest eigenvalue of the correlation matrix of returns. The objective is not only to gain a better understanding of this value, but also of the components that determine its behavior. To this end, we rely on daily logarithmic returns of the S&P's 500 index constituents over the period ranging from 2005 to 2024. We propose the use of the Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR), which is a measure extensively used in Physics, and we introduce the N ef f metric to identify the effective stocks within a portfolio; i.e., those capable of preserving the return dynamics of the full portfolio by themselves. Our empirical analysis shows that, in general, only long positions in the utilities sector are effective within this portfolio, which is consistent with the counter behaviour already observed and the traditional defensive nature of this economic sector. We also find that during periods of financial distress, however, short sales in the materials sector and the financials sector also emerge as effective.

title: Abuse of Dominance and Path Dependence: A Radical Reform Needed?

detail.title: Abuse of Dominance and Path Dependence: A Radical Reform Needed?
detail.abstract: The article aims to provide a possible explanation for the increasing number of disagreements among the stakeholders of competition law and policy, in particular in the area of unilateral conducts. To do this, it conceptualises path dependence as a feature of EU competition law, and sheds light that-since its appearance-the more economic approach as a meso-level paradigm has not fully changed each and every aspect of abuse of dominance enforcement in individual cases. The vestiges-certain "legacy" concepts-from the formalistic era result that it is impossible with small refinements to cure the contradictory legal interpretations within the current framework. The article argues that a possible solution could be provided by the Court of Justice, if it introduced and employed the legal instrument of the explicit overrule. This would help weed out those formalistic concepts in abuse of dominance enforcement that fit uncomfortable within the new paradigm. Beyond the legal uncertainty, the lack of explicit departing from earlier judgments also brings to the fore some by-products, such as the Digital Markets Act, which aims to react to, and handle, those market challenges that have not been remediable with conventional antitrust interventions.

title: Using Scraping Algorithms to Evaluate Academic Inbreeding

detail.title: Using Scraping Algorithms to Evaluate Academic Inbreeding
detail.abstract:
This paper develops a reproducible pipeline to measure academic inbreeding through large-scale web scraping of administrative data. Academic inbreeding is defined as the hiring of a university’s own graduates as academic staff, a practice widely viewed as limiting openness and reducing institutional performance. Despite its importance, systematic evidence in Central and Eastern Europe remains limited due to the absence of structured datasets.

The study addresses this gap by developing an end-to-end data-extraction framework for NACID profile pages. Using browser automation and text parsing techniques, the pipeline recovers doctoral provenance, appointment histories, and indicators of international training from semi-structured web data. The resulting dataset enables the reconstruction of academic career trajectories and the identification of inbred hires across faculties.

The empirical analysis combines descriptive statistics, logistic regression models, and duration analysis to examine the determinants of inbreeding. Results from the Faculty of Economics and Business Administration show that higher research productivity is associated with a lower probability of inbred hiring, while rapid post PhD appointments are strongly associated with higher inbreeding rates. Additional evidence suggests that institutional collaboration patterns are linked to internal hiring dynamics. The paper also proposes a conceptual framework in which academic inbreeding emerges as a labor market outcome driven by search frictions, institutional openness, and feedback effects. The findings highlight how closed recruitment systems can become self-reinforcing, leading to persistent low-openness equilibria.

title: GST Reform and its Sectoral Consequences in the Indian Economy

detail.title: GST Reform and its Sectoral Consequences in the Indian Economy
detail.abstract: The Goods and Services Tax (GST), introduced in India in 2017, represents one of the most significant tax reforms in the country. This study examines GST's sectoral impact on manufacturing, services, and agriculture using ten-year data (2014-2024) on Gross Value Added (GVA) growth. Statistical tools, including mean growth, standard deviation, coefficient of variation, and compound annual growth rate (CAGR), are employed to assess performance before and after GST. The findings indicate that services experienced the highest long-term growth with moderate volatility, manufacturing showed high volatility with significant post-GST adjustment, and agriculture remained stable, benefiting indirectly through logistics and input efficiencies. Year-on-year acceleration and deceleration highlight short-term shocks from GST transitions and external factors such as COVID-19. The study concludes that GST enhances efficiency, formalizes markets, and promotes sectoral growth while revealing areas that require policy attention for smoother implementation and sustained development.

title: Structural Persistence of Cryptocurrency Volatility Amplification: Evidence from Digital Asset Treasury Companies Following the October 2025 Market Crash

detail.title: Structural Persistence of Cryptocurrency Volatility Amplification: Evidence from Digital Asset Treasury Companies Following the October 2025 Market Crash
detail.abstract: This study provides a structural break analysis of Digital Asset Treasury (DAT) company volatility dynamics following the October 10, 2025, Bitcoin market crash, a liquidation event estimated at $40 billion that materially altered the cryptocurrency market landscape. Extending the empirical framework developed in Krause (2025b), daily returns from November 2024 through March 2026 are analyzed for six DAT firms (Strategy, Marathon Digital, Riot Platforms, CleanSpark, Hut 8 Mining, and Coinbase), Bitcoin, and the S&P 500. Using Chow breakpoint tests and rolling regression analysis, this study tests whether the volatility amplification mechanisms documented in Krause (2025b), specifically a 1.95x amplification ratio, universal Bitcoin betas exceeding 1.0, and a 1.60x sell-off amplification ratio, persisted following the crash. The results indicate that volatility amplification not only persisted but increased slightly, with an average ratio of 2.04x Bitcoin's volatility across the full sample period. All six DAT stocks maintained Bitcoin betas exceeding 1.0, with Strategy exhibiting the highest beta of 1.405. Chow tests reveal no structural breaks in the Bitcoin relationship for any firm (all p-values > 0.05), indicating the amplification mechanism is structural rather than cyclical. Sell-off amplification decreased from 1.60x to 1.02x in the post-crash period, and idiosyncratic risk declined from 58% to 44% post-crash, suggesting DAT stocks became purer Bitcoin proxies after October 2025. Subsample analysis reveals mining companies exhibit the highest volatility amplification (2.08x) while Strategy maintains the highest Bitcoin beta (1.405). These findings have implications for institutional investors, corporate treasurers, and financial regulators monitoring the integration of digital assets into traditional finance.

detail.abstract: Health visiting is England’s universal home visiting programme for families with children under five and a key pillar of early intervention policy. Since the 2015 devolution of commissioning to Local Authorities (LAs), the service has faced sustained financial and workforce pressures, yet there is limited systematic evidence on whether resources and delivery have evolved differentially across areas and along the deprivation gradient. Using new Freedom of Information (FOI) data, we estimate how health visiting inputs (spending and workforce) and mandated contact delivery vary in levels and trajectories by baseline deprivation. FOI requests covered 147 English LAs (four pairs submitted joint returns), providing annual 2016-2021 Full-Time Equivalent (FTE) data on Health Visitors (HVs) and Clinical Skill Mix Staff (CSMS), which we link to DHSC Health Visitor Service Delivery Metrics reporting completion of the five mandated 0-5 reviews (New Birth Visits, 6-8 week reviews, 12-month reviews, 2-2.5 year reviews, and 2-2.5 year reviews completed with ASQ-3) and to LA revenue outturn expenditure on mandated and non-mandated 0-5 public health services (real-terms total and per child under five). Between 2016 and 2021, HV FTE fell by around one-fifth while CSMS expanded by roughly one-third, consistent with an overall contraction and a shift toward lower-band staff. To test whether these changes map onto underlying disadvantage, we stratify LAs into tertiles of baseline deprivation using the 2015 Income Deprivation Affecting Children Index (IDACI) and implement a three-part empirical strategy: (i) plotting tertile means over time, (ii) testing within-year cross-sectional differences using parametric and non-parametric methods with pairwise comparisons, and (iii) estimating LA fixed-effects regressions with Year x IDACI interactions under both a flexible year-by-year specification and a parsimonious linear-trend specification to assess differential trajectories. We find persistent cross-sectional gradients in per-child spending that are broadly progressive (more deprived LAs spend more per child on both mandated and non-mandated 0-5 services), while fixed-effects models show little evidence that spending trajectories differ systematically by deprivation. Workforce trends are more uneven: HV FTE declines more slowly and CSMS FTE grows more slowly in more deprived LAs in the linear-trend specification, while per-child HV trajectories show no differential trends. Despite these input differences, completion of mandated contacts is relatively stable across the deprivation gradient; the only consistent differential trend is faster improvement in the 6-8 week review in more deprived areas. Meanwhile, caseload pressure rises, increasing most sharply in the most deprived LAs in the pre-pandemic years, suggesting that completion-based performance measures may mask heterogeneities in service capacity and intensity. Finally, we quantify the resources required to restore recommended caseloads, implying the need for approximately 3,100 additional FTE staff and around £120 million annually (plus training costs).

title: Testing Cointegration with High-Dimensional Confounders: A Double Machine Learning Bounds Approach

detail.title: Testing Cointegration with High-Dimensional Confounders: A Double Machine Learning Bounds Approach
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Double Machine Learning Bounds (DML-Bounds) procedure for testing cointegration in the presence of high-dimensional confounding variables. Building on the autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) bounds-testing framework, the approach uses h-block cross-fitting and Neyman-orthogonalization to partial out high-dimensional short-run dynamics before testing the long-run relationship. I derive a high-level asymptotic mapping showing that, when the orthogonalization remainder is negligible at the integrated scale, the feasible orthogonalized statistic is asymptotically equivalent to an oracle residualized regression and therefore shares the same first-order limit experiment as the classical bounds test. I also provide a restricted primitive result showing that, under sparse linear nuisance structure, Post-LASSO can deliver a remainder small enough for the mapping to hold, together with a first-order argument for why contiguous block cross-fitting need not alter the relevant non-stationary functional limits. Monte Carlo simulations suggest that the procedure remains feasible in ultra-highdimensional regimes (d > T) where classical unpenalized projection is not implementable. An application to the U.S. consumption-income relationship, complemented by rolling-origin timeseries cross-validation (TSCV), illustrates how data-driven nuisance adjustment can materially affect cointegration inference and improve the stability of long-run parameter estimates.

title: Colonial Reconfiguration of Transgender Perceptions in India: A Pre- and Post-Colonial Analysis
affiliations: JSS Academy of Higher Education and Research

detail.title: Colonial Reconfiguration of Transgender Perceptions in India: A Pre- and Post-Colonial Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based on secondary analysis of publicly available literature, legal documents, and historical sources. It does not involve human participants, patient data, or identifiable personal information; therefore, ethical approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Background: Transgender and gender-diverse identities have been part of the Indian subcontinent for many centuries, deeply situated within religious traditions, social institutions, and even political structures. Yet, contemporary marginalization of transgender communities is often blamed on “traditional” Indian culture, while the role of colonial intervention in reshaping gender norms is cast aside. Objective: This paper discusses how British colonial rule reconfigured indigenous understandings of gender diversity in India and the ways in which socially intelligible and culturally sanctioned identities were turned into objects of deviance, criminality, and medical pathology. Methods: The study, adopting a historical-comparative approach, examines the pre-colonial religious texts, mythological narratives, and socio-political practices in relation to colonial legal, medical, and administrative frameworks. The principal colonial interventions - the Criminal Tribes Act, 1871, and Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code are studied to track the institutionalisation of stigma. Judicial and legislative responses of the post-colony are critically reviewed to appraise continuity and rupture. Results: Pre-colonial Indian societies, by and large, viewed gender as fluid, relational, and socially embedded, with transgender communities holding positions of ritual, social, and political significance. Colonial governance imposed strict binary gender norms, criminalized gender nonconformity, and medicalized transgender identities through Victorian moral and biomedical paradigms. Despite post-independence legal reforms, including NALSA v. Union of India (2014) and the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, colonial epistemologies continue to shape policy, healthcare, and social attitudes. Conclusion: Transgender marginalization in India is not an inherent feature of indigenous culture but a colonial legacy sustained through legal, medical, and administrative continuities. Meaningful equity requires not only legal reform but the decolonization of public health, policy, and knowledge systems that continue to regulate gender divers

title: Predictable Renewable Generation, Coal Displacement, and Energy Security: Evidence from Tidal Power in South Korea
affiliations: Lancaster University - Department of Economics, Soongsil University, Busan University of Foreign Studies - College of Commerce & Business, Department of Economics - Lancaster University Management School and Lancaster University - Lancaster University Management School

detail.title: Predictable Renewable Generation, Coal Displacement, and Energy Security: Evidence from Tidal Power in South Korea
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether large-scale tidal energy can contribute to decarbonization and energy security by reducing fossil fuel dependence and carbon dioxide (CO 2) emissions intensity. Focusing on South Korea, we exploit the full operationalization of the Sihwa Lake Tidal Power Station in 2012 as a quasi-experimental policy intervention. Using national time-series analysis, difference-indifferences estimations against Japan and a broader group of Asia-Pacific economies, and a synthetic control approach, we analyze changes in energy intensity, electricity generation by fuel type, and per-capita CO 2 emissions. The synthetic control method constructs a data-driven counterfactual for South Korea based on comparable Asia-Pacific economies, allowing us to assess post-treatment deviations in coalbased electricity generation and coal-related emissions. Across the empirical approaches, the evidence is most consistent for a reduction in coal-based electricity generation after 2012. Coal-related per-capita CO 2 emissions also decline in several specifications, although the synthetic-control placebo evidence for emissions is more suggestive than conclusive. By contrast, aggregate per-capita CO 2 emissions remain broadly stable, and evidence on overall energy intensity is more sensitive to the choice of comparison group. The estimated coal effects persist after controlling for international climate policy through a Paris Agreement indicator, indicating that South Korea's post-2012 energy transition is not fully explained by common policy shocks. Overall, the findings suggest that large-scale tidal power can support decarbonization primarily through the displacement of coal, with potential implications for energy security in highly import-dependent economies.

title: The U.S. Should Establish an anti-Etela’at Channel in Iran

detail.title: The U.S. Should Establish an anti-Etela’at Channel in Iran

keywords: Role of Unexpected Change in Regime and System Collapse

detail.abstract: As Iran’s regime absorbs military pressure yet maintains internal control, its intelligence apparatus remains a central pillar of its survival. Countering it requires more than external force—it requires turning information into a weapon. By enabling secure channels for ordinary citizens to share intelligence, an “anti-intelligence” network could begin to erode the regime’s grip from within. Even a localized rupture could trigger broader unrest, showing how information—once monopolized by the state—can become the catalyst for systemic change.

title: Digital Colonialism
affiliations: Faculty of Political Sciences Sarajevo

detail.title: Digital Colonialism
detail.abstract: Digital colonialism refers to a form of digital control, extraction, and dependency through which a small but powerful group of tech corporations, primarily based in the Global North (particularly in the US) and China, establish a form of domination over digital spatialities (both data and digital infrastructures).1 This form of domination is sustained by the extension of digital sovereignty (through digitalization processes) over the production, use, and ownership of digital spatialities – designing their infrastructures to fit their economic interest, creating long-term dependencies – both digital (the use software/ networks/ cloud services…), and physical (network infrastructure, submarine cables, hardware supply chains…). In this context, digital colonialism is not only a corporate strategy but also a form of structural power that reshapes and produces global inequalities, often closely tied to the strategic interests and policies of the states under whose jurisdiction these companies operate.

title: Digital Technologies, Peace and Security: Challenges and Opportunities for United Nations Peace Operations
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania,  and

detail.title: Digital Technologies, Peace and Security: Challenges and Opportunities for United Nations Peace Operations

contentType.other: Paper published by UN Department of Peace Operations

detail.abstract: The digital technological landscape has changed enormously over the past decade, creating new opportunities for global communication, commerce, and effective government and public service delivery. But the same technologies have also been exploited, to exacerbate political or intercommunal tensions or enforce new restrictions on speech. These dynamics are particularly pronounced in armed conflict or post-conflict environments. This briefing provides an overview of both challenges and opportunities for contemporary UN peace operations resulting from digital technologies. Part I touches on a number of areas including social media, cell phones, unmanned aerial vehicles, and artificial intelligence that currently complicate prospects for peace in conflict environments, or that are likely to do so in the near future. Part II examines opportunities for UN peace operations to leverage digital technologies including social media, cell phones, satellite imaging, unmanned aerial vehicles, closed-circuit television, and artificial intelligence to deliver on their mandates to promote and maintain peace.

title: Our Microplastic Problem
affiliations: Wake Forest University - School of Law

detail.title: Our Microplastic Problem
detail.abstract: This article explores the growing threat of and the legal response to microplastic pollution. Microplastics—plastic particles less than five millimeters in size—are pervasive, persistent, and chemically diverse, making them particularly difficult to regulate using existing environmental statutes. Federal approaches, such as the Clean Water Act and Toxic Substances Control Act, offer limited relief, while macro-scale proposals like the Break Free from Plastic Pollution Act remain stalled. In response, this article advocates for “micro-solutions”—targeted, state and local interventions that collectively address microplastic pollution across the plastic lifecycle. These include bans on intentionally added microplastics, filtration mandates for appliances, stormwater management strategies, and industry-specific regulations. Drawing lessons from climate and PFAS litigation, the article also examines the increasing use of consumer protection and public nuisance claims against plastic producers. In highlighting these bottom-up strategies, the article provides a roadmap for meaningful progress in the absence of sweeping federal or international reform.

title: One Federation, Many Prices: A Price Floor for Carbon Pricing in Canada
affiliations: University of Ottawa - Graduate School of Public and International Affairs

detail.title: One Federation, Many Prices: A Price Floor for Carbon Pricing in Canada
detail.abstract:
• Canada’s industrial carbon pricing systems, covering roughly 40 percent of national emissions, aim to reduce greenhouse gases while protecting competitiveness, but are being undermined by a poorly designed federal “benchmark.”
  • The current benchmark relies on a subjective and opaque “demand test” to assess system stringency, resulting in overly generous performance standards, low compliance credit prices, and inconsistent outcomes across provinces.
  • This report proposes introducing a price floor for compliance credits that ensures a minimum carbon price across jurisdictions while allowing flexibility in performance standards.
  • A price floor would improve transparency and enforceability, reduce transaction costs, align incentives across regions, and decouple emissions reductions from competitiveness concerns – enabling more effective and durable carbon pricing in Canada.

title: Rear-View Epistemology and the Paradox of Evolutionary Endpoints:  Why Single-Layer Block Universes Are Self-Refuting
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Rear-View Epistemology and the Paradox of Evolutionary Endpoints:  Why Single-Layer Block Universes Are Self-Refuting
detail.abstract: This paper demonstrates that any single-layer deterministic ontology-most prominently the 4D block-universe model-generates an epistemological self-refutation when applied to evolutionary processes. Human scientific knowledge is necessarily retrospective: it is constructed exclusively from realized (past) nodes within a stratified architecture. While this "rear-view mirror" methodology is reliable for repetitional nodes (closed-loop, low-novelty patterns), it is structurally insufficient for evolutionary nodes (open-system, cumulative informational novelty). Attempting to declare that evolutionary endpoints "have already happened" in a static block therefore constitutes a categorical error. The argument proceeds via (i) a formal distinction between repetitional and evolutionary nodes, (ii) a proof by contradiction showing that single-layer totality collapses the epistemic veil required for genuine novelty, and (iii) explicit alignment with the External Reference Paradox (ERP) and Asymmetric Persistence-the requirement that an anchoring reference layer must endure independently of the subsystem it governs. The Dual-Layered Reality (DLR) framework resolves the paradox by stratifying the deterministic lattice from the finite informational layer, preserving both global completeness and local evolutionary openness. Single-layer block universes are thereby shown to be not merely incomplete but self-refuting under their own epistemic constraints.

title: Reducing Auto Insurance Fraud to Rebuild Affordability in New York: Implications for Municipalities, the Metropolitan Transit Authority, and Property Taxes
affiliations: The Jack Kemp Foundation

detail.title: Reducing Auto Insurance Fraud to Rebuild Affordability in New York: Implications for Municipalities, the Metropolitan Transit Authority, and Property Taxes
detail.abstract:
Insurance fraud, particularly staged automobile accidents, is a significant and growing drag
on the New York economy. Organized fraud schemes profit by exploiting flaws in the state’s
no‐fault system and low legal thresholds for those alleging damages, extracting millions in
bogus insurance payouts. These losses ultimately fall on honest drivers–who pay higher
premiums–as well as the state’s taxpayers, as municipalities and public agencies, which see
their insurance costs increase as well, pass these costs onto consumers and property owners.
Several other states have taken steps to reduce insurance fraud and New York Governor Kathy
Hochul has proposed reforms in her executive budget to do the same in the state. Her plan,
which borrows from existing approaches, would realign incentives, curb wasteful spending, and
free up resources that state and local governments desperately need. Their implementation
would make car insurance more affordable for New York State residents and save the state and
local governments millions of dollars a year.

title: A Closed-Form Link Between Grouped Survival and Single-Factor Default Models
affiliations: School of Business and Economics

detail.title: A Closed-Form Link Between Grouped Survival and Single-Factor Default Models
detail.abstract: When loan maturities are endogenous to borrower risk, Cox proportional hazards models produce attenuated default probability curves. We formalise PBCRL, a grouped-survival Bernoulli GLM with complementary log-log link and log-duration offset, establishing strict concavity, MLE existence, and asymptotic normality. We show that PBCRL nests within classical Cox PH as the restriction to a single baseline hazard, and derive a closed-form mapping between PBCRL coefficients and the asymptotic single-risk-factor model used in banking regulation. Estimation combines LP-based separation detection with Firth bias reduction. Applied to simulated and real-world low-default portfolios, PBCRL recovers steep, monotonic through-the-cycle calibration curves where standard Cox yields near-flat ones.

title: Blaming the States: How "A Sixth of Humanity" Goes Wrong
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Amherst

detail.title: Blaming the States: How "A Sixth of Humanity" Goes Wrong
detail.abstract: A new book by Devesh Kapur and Arvind Subramanian, A Sixth of Humanity, offers an unsparing critique of India's record in economic and social development since 1947. A central theme is that state governments bear much of the blame for development failures.  This is a misguided assessment.  States have less agency than Kapur and Subramanian suggest.  The real weakness of the Indian system is over-centralization.  A powerful central government made disastrous choices about national priorities between 1950 and 1980.  Delhi then failed to unwind those choices promptly after 1980, so that India missed an opportunity presented by economic globalization.  Next, Delhi expanded a battery of hard-to-implement schemes that trench on state authority.  At independence, India's founders were convinced that centralization was the pathway to national strength.  Experience gives reason to doubt this hypothesis, especially as the conditions of governance become more challenging.  Giving states more autonomy might lead to a more dynamic, prosperous and resilient country.

title: Patent Topology as a Leading Indicator of AI Drug Discovery Asset Valuation: A Bibliometric and Landscape Analysis

detail.title: Patent Topology as a Leading Indicator of AI Drug Discovery Asset Valuation: A Bibliometric and Landscape Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. No funding was received from pharmaceutical companies, patent databases, or any entity with a financial interest in AI drug discovery asset valuation. The Lens.org patent data access was requested under a free academic trial plan.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, patient data, clinical trials, or any personally identifiable information. The analysis is based entirely on publicly available patent records, financial disclosure filings, and commercial transaction databases. No ethics approval is required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently as part of the author's EDBA doctoral studies. All data sources used (Lens.org, SEC EDGAR, Crunchbase) are publicly available or freely accessible for academic research.

detail.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into pharmaceutical drug discovery has accelerated patent generation across molecular generation, target identification, and multi-omics data integration, compressing lead identification timelines while simultaneously expanding the pace and structural complexity of intellectual property formation (WIPO, 2024). Despite this transformation, prevailing asset valuation frameworks remain calibrated to clinical pipeline metrics — phase transition probabilities, indication density, and risk-adjusted net present value — that are systematically lagging measures of platform-level AI innovation. This paper proposes and empirically tests a patent topology framework comprising three composite indicators — forward citation velocity (FCV), IPC drift index (IDI), and assignee concentration ratio (ACR) — as prospective leading indicators of AI drug discovery asset valuation events. Drawing on a synthetic patent corpus of 2,500 families calibrated to the field structure and summary statistics of Lens.org, USPTO, and EPO Espacenet data (pending full API deployment), we apply a pre-validated event study methodology to examine whether patent topology signals precede publicly disclosed licensing transactions, M&A premiums, and venture financing rounds. Pre-flight feasibility diagnostics confirmed that event study methodology was the appropriate statistical framework given the sparse quarterly density of M&A events (29% of quarters). Results indicate that forward citation velocity exhibits statistically significant abnormal elevation 2–4 quarters (6–12 months) prior to valuation events across all three transaction types (VC financing: t = 4.27, p < 0.001 at lag −1; licensing: t = 3.56, p = 0.002 at lag −1; M&A: t = 2.38, p = 0.036 at lag −2). Co-citation analysis further identifies a concentrated white space at the intersection of generative molecular modelling and CNS therapeutic indications — interpretable as a map of the current validation bottleneck in AI-enabled neurodegeneration drug discovery. We argue that patent landscape analysis, reframed as a prospective valuation instrument, offers a tractable methodology for early-stage asset pricing in AI-driven biotechnology. The current implementation is calibrated and demonstrated on a synthetic patent corpus, and is intended as an API-ready template that can be directly connected to Lens.org and office patent databases as data access becomes available.

title: Salary Increases and Skills-Based Bonuses: Teacher Retention and Workforce Composition
affiliations: University of Bologna

detail.title: Salary Increases and Skills-Based Bonuses: Teacher Retention and Workforce Composition
detail.abstract: This paper studies the interaction between unconditional salary increases and performancebased bonuses in determining teacher retention and workforce composition. I exploit Chile's Carrera Docente, a national reform that raised base salaries by approximately 20% for all public school teachers and introduced a career stage bonus linked to evaluation scores. Because the reform initially applied only to public schools, roughly half of the school system, I use a difference-indifferences design and find that exit rates fell by approximately 18%, but the effect is concentrated among low-value-added teachers. A regression discontinuity design at the career stage threshold shows that the performance-based bonus has no additional retention effect beyond the base salary increase. The retention gains of the reform are driven entirely by the base salary increase, with no additional contribution from the performance-based bonus.

title: Rising Customer Durability, Falling Business Dynamism
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, Stanford Graduate School of Business, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Rising Customer Durability, Falling Business Dynamism
detail.abstract: We study how the durability of customer relationships shapes competition, innovation, and the allocation of economic activity. Using novel data from M&A accounting disclosures, we construct a forward-looking measure of customer durability based on firms' expected useful lives of their customer relationship-related intangible assets, covering nearly 9,500 acquisitions and $8 trillion in assets from 2002 through 2024. We document a substantial rise in durability across industries and examine its implications in an endogenous growth model in which longer-lasting customer relationships amplify incumbents' market power. Empirically, greater durability is associated with higher markups and profit shares, increased concentration, reduced entry and exit, lower job reallocation, slower wage growth, and a declining labor share. Consistent with our model, we also find an inverted-U relationship between durability and innovation, with high durability reducing both the quantity and quality of innovation, partly through lower R&D investment. Taken together, our findings highlight rising customer durability as a novel mechanism that helps reconcile the simultaneous increase in market power and decline in U.S. business dynamism, with important implications for competition policy.

title: Discrimination and Language Barriers: Evidence from Rental Housing Markets
affiliations: , Corvinus University of Budapest and University of Zurich, Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) - NTNU Business School

detail.title: Discrimination and Language Barriers: Evidence from Rental Housing Markets
detail.abstract: We investigate discrimination and language as barriers to immigrant integration in a field experiment in the housing market. We send apartment-viewing requests across four Central European countries, written in English or the local language, while randomly varying name origin, local-language proficiency, and a signal of effort to learn the local language. Inquiries in fluent English from foreign names receive only half as many viewing invitations as inquiries in fluent local language from native names. Within this gap, the effect of language barriers is about 3 times as large as that of discrimination. Functional local-language proficiency yields no measurable benefit versus fluent English, nor does signaling ongoing local-language learning. A simple follow-up inquiry, by contrast, yields immediate gains in access as large as the discrimination gap.

title: Caught by Surprise: How Markets Respond to Macroeconomic News
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Department of Business Economics and Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR)

detail.title: Caught by Surprise: How Markets Respond to Macroeconomic News
detail.abstract: We provide a comprehensive analysis of macroeconomic surprises across approximately 34,000 releases across the globe. Economic surprises exhibit short-term momentum arising from predictable errors in consensus forecasts. Forecasters underreact both to a series’ own time-series dynamics and to cross-series information embedded in other releases. The resulting ‘economic surprise momentum’ is especially pronounced in indicators of economic growth and generates economically large and statistically significant return predictability in major risky asset classes, including equities, credit, and commodities. These patterns are consistent with systematic underreaction by macroeconomic forecasters and investors driven by expectational errors.

title: Producing New Products Or Improving Production Process? Innovation Effects Of Export Quota Removal On Chinese Firms
affiliations: Guangzhou University

detail.title: Producing New Products Or Improving Production Process? Innovation Effects Of Export Quota Removal On Chinese Firms
detail.abstract: I distinguish between product innovation and process innovation, and construct a theoretical framework to discuss the relationship between export quota removal and firms' innovation. Then, I regard the export quota removal of textile and clothing industries as a quasi-natural experiment. I use DDD model and firm-level data of China to examine the impacts of export quota removal. I find that for firms which export to quota-restricted countries, export quota removal  leads to product innovation and process innovation. Main mechanisms are that export quota removal expands export scale and generates more sales, outputs and profits. Affected firms thereby have stronger ability to engage in innovation activities. Additionally, export quota removal increases the application of appearance patents, but cannot improve innovation quality. In general, this study enriches the literature on trade and innovation, non-tariff policies as well as firms' innovation, and provides policy implications for developing countries.

title: Clawback Provisions and Portfolio Risk: A Utility-Based Framework with Coherent Tail Constraints
affiliations: Minnesota State University Moorhead

detail.title: Clawback Provisions and Portfolio Risk: A Utility-Based Framework with Coherent Tail Constraints
detail.abstract: We examine whether subadditivity remains compatible with risk vulnerability in a utility-based portfolio optimization framework subject to coherent tail-risk constraints and background risk. Regulatory clawback provisions are modeled as background risk that raises effective risk aversion, capturing behavioral responses to downside penalties. The framework extends convex shortfall risk models by separating preferences from prudential regulation through a CARA combined with an explicit CVaR constraint. This separation ensures regulatory compliance, preserves subadditivity under stress conditions, and improves transparency and auditability. Empirical results using high-return equities show that higher effective risk aversion leads to more conservative allocations with substantially lower tail losses and drawdowns, while risk-neutral strategies achieve higher returns at the cost of extreme volatility. Comparisons with hierarchical risk parity indicate that heuristic allocation methods underperform in both absolute and risk-adjusted returns when background risk is present. The results have direct implications for bank portfolio management and regulatory policy.

title: Testing the Portfolio Rebalancing Channel of Quantitative Easing
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Testing the Portfolio Rebalancing Channel of Quantitative Easing
detail.abstract: The Fed argues that quantitative easing (QE) lowers yields across asset markets via the portfolio rebalancing channel. I provide a direct test for this channel, quantify its magnitude, and document its real effects. I first construct a novel QE shock measuring the unexpected amount that the Fed purchases of each Treasury during each QE operation. Combining this shock with holdings data, I find that investors rebalance 75% of proceeds from QE-induced Treasury sales into corporate bonds, predominantly into bonds with similar maturities to those the Fed purchased. Consistent with the portfolio rebalancing channel, the yields of these bonds fall. To quantify the channel's magnitude, I use my reduced-form estimates to calibrate a preferred habitat model with investors who substitute between Treasurys and corporate bonds. I find a large effect: Treasury purchases amounting to 1% of GDP lower corporate bond yields by 29.3bps on impact. Turning to real effects, I find that affected firms increase bond issuance and do so at lower yields, and subsequently increase their investment. Overall, the results point to a strong portfolio rebalancing channel.

title: The Intersection of Intellectual Property Rights and Competition Law: A Comparative Analysis of Global Legal Frameworks

detail.title: The Intersection of Intellectual Property Rights and Competition Law: A Comparative Analysis of Global Legal Frameworks
detail.abstract: Intellectual property rights provide owners with exclusive legal rights, which restrict others from accessing and using the same content, thereby diminishing market competition. Competition law, also known as antitrust law, aims to encourage competition and enhance market accessibility. Therefore, it is evident that these two subjects are completely contradictory. On the other hand, there is another perspective that argues for the compatibility and mutual enhancement of the two domains. In today's fast-paced world of technological advancements, the intersection of Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) and Competition Law plays a crucial role in shaping legal frameworks worldwide. This research aims to provide a comprehensive comparative analysis of the transformative landscape where these two legal domains intersect. The coexistence of Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) and Competition Law has become more complex due to technological progress and globalization. This study focuses on the utilization of intellectual property, specifically patents, trademarks, and copyrights, and explores the impact of competition principles on their usage. The research delves into the diverse strategies employed by different jurisdictions worldwide in order to understand and address the complexities that arise from technological advancements. This study explores the different approaches taken by jurisdictions around the world, aiming to find similarities, differences, and how they impact innovation, market competition, and consumer welfare. The paper aims to explore the strategies used by international legal frameworks to strike a balance between protecting intellectual creations and promoting fair competition, as the legal landscape continues to evolve. The research explores the challenges and opportunities of harmonizing Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) and Competition Law by examining case studies, legal frameworks and legislative developments across the globe. This research emphasizes the importance of the coexistence of Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) and Competition Law in enhancing a country's economic efficiency.

title: Multi-modal deep learning for non-invasive blood glucose prediction fromterahertz reflection spectra: a simulation study with four-layer skin modeling
affiliations: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications and Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

detail.title: Multi-modal deep learning for non-invasive blood glucose prediction fromterahertz reflection spectra: a simulation study with four-layer skin modeling
detail.abstract: Non-invasive blood glucose monitoring using terahertz (THz) spectroscopy has attracted significant attention dueto the sensitivity of THz radiation to water molecule dynamics and hydrogen bonding networks in biological tissues. However, the fundamental challenge lies in the weak glucose-induced spectral changes being obscured byinter-individual variations in skin morphology and hydration. In this study, we present a comprehensive simulationframework that combines a physically rigorous four-layer skin dielectric model with deep learning to investigate THz based blood glucose prediction. The skin model incorporates a glucose-modified Double Debye relaxation model forinterstitial fluid in the dermis layer, Maxwell-Garnett effective medium theory for tissue-water mixing, and the Transfer Matrix Method (TMM) for computing normal-incidence reflection spectra across 0.1–2.0 THz. A dataset of 50,000samples was generated by systematically varying seven physiological parameters covering realistic inter-individual variability. We evaluated four convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures: three spectrum-only models (SimpleCNN, ResCNN, AttentionCNN) and a novel multi-input CNN that fuses the reflection spectrum with auxiliary skinmorphology parameters. The spectrum-only models achieved limited prediction accuracy (best RMSE = 76.09 mg/dL,R2 = 0.44), confirming that skin parameter confounding represents the primary bottleneck. In contrast, the multi-inputCNN, which simulates the availability of auxiliary measurements from complementary modalities such as optical coherence tomography, achieved dramatically improved performance (RMSE = 33.03 mg/dL, R2 = 0.89, MARD =15.82%) with 99.7% of predictions falling within Zones A+B of the Clarke Error Grid. Sensitivity analysis and frequency importance mapping further revealed that the 0.2–0.6 THz band carries the most glucose-relevant information.These results demonstrate that multi-modal sensing, combining THz spectroscopy with auxiliary skin characterization,is essential for achieving clinically relevant glucose prediction accuracy, and provide a physics-informed framework for guiding future experimental designs.

title: Validation of UWES Scale for Faculty Engagement: A Descriptive Study Based on Higher Educational Institutions in Indian Context
affiliations: Shri Venkateshwara University and Shri Venkateshwara University

detail.title: Validation of UWES Scale for Faculty Engagement: A Descriptive Study Based on Higher Educational Institutions in Indian Context

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not Applicable
declarations.funderStatement: Not Applicable

detail.abstract: This paper attempts to analyze the engagement of faculty members in a higher educational institution. An education system considering quality and competent faculty undoubtedly enhances the overall success of an institution. Therefore, the study investigates the impact of factors of the Utrecht Work Engagement Scale (UWES) on faculty engagement by using an adapted scale in Rajasthan, an Indian context. The aim of this research is to discover a descriptive explanation related to vigor, dedication, and absorption and engagement of faculty members. Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) was used to evaluate the structural validity of the instruments, and internal consistency was also examined. For this study, the data collected required was secondary data, which was collected from journals and magazines, while primary data was collected from faculty members of Public Universities and Private Universities). However, this study confirms that UWES is valid in Rajasthan's Indian context and is supported by a theoretical framework and discussions. detail.abstract: Is a longer response time in multifactor predictive problems relevant to the respondent's beliefs associated with greater prediction accuracy? title: Digital Search Behaviour and the Housing Credit Cycle: Evidence From South Africa

detail.title: Digital Search Behaviour and the Housing Credit Cycle: Evidence From South Africa
detail.abstract: Monitoring vulnerabilities in housing markets relies primarily on backwardlooking indicators such as mortgage approvals and house price indices. This paper develops a Search Behaviour Index (SBI) using monthly Google Search data (2010-2025) to capture shifts in housing-related attention and credit demand in South Africa. The index is constructed using a multidimensional principal component framework and examined within a vector autoregression (VAR) model alongside mortgage advances, building activity, and house prices. The results indicate that search behaviour contains statistically significant leading information for mortgage credit growth, with effects transmitting to construction activity and prices over subsequent months. Robustness checks using alternative specifications, sub-indices, and sample periods confirm the stability of this relationship. The findings suggest that digital behavioural signals may serve as a complementary macroprudential monitoring tool for the housing credit cycle.

detail.abstract: I exploit a regulatory shock that eliminated short-selling capacity to study how binding shortsale constraints affect crash risk in a retail-dominated market. Using a difference-indifferences design comparing stocks most versus least affected by the ban, I find that removing short sellers reduced future crash risk-contrary to canonical bad-news-hoarding predictions. Aggregate investor attention does not explain this stabilisation. Brokerage-level trading data, however, reveal investor-type heterogeneity in the mechanism: retail herd trading is associated with lower crash risk, consistent with liquidity provision, while speculative hot-money trading is associated with higher crash risk. These findings indicate that crash risk consequences of short-selling bans depend critically on who provides marginal liquidity in their absence, with direct implications for the many emerging markets with similar investor structures.

title: The Resource Standard: A Real-Resource Anchor for Sovereign Currency in the Fiat Era

detail.title: The Resource Standard: A Real-Resource Anchor for Sovereign Currency in the Fiat Era

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Resource Standard, a framework in which the value of currency is anchored not to commodities or reserves but to real resources, including human labour, revealing an operational structure implicit in sovereign fiat monetary systems that has not yet been explicitly formalized. Under commodity standards, currency value was expressed in terms of a fixed quantity of gold, and the availability of gold reserves therefore constrained government spending. Fiat currency does not possess intrinsic value; its value is expressed in terms of the goods and services it purchases. The sovereign government is the sole supplier of currency, so the prices paid through government spending introduce the absolute value of the currency. The moment at which sovereign spending assigns prices to labour and goods is therefore the moment at which the value of currency is operationally established. The requirement that taxes be paid in the sovereign currency ensures demand for the currency, but the prices paid in sovereign spending determine what that currency is worth in real terms. Under a fiat monetary system, the effective limit to sovereign spending is therefore not financial but real: the availability of goods and services for sale in the currency, particularly labour. The value of currency in real terms is realized through the production of those goods and services. When available resources remain idle, part of the potential value of currency remains unrealized. Sovereign spending introduces the absolute value of currency, while the deployment of real productive capacity determines the cumulative value realized within the economy. The Resource Standard therefore proposes that the cumulative value of a sovereign currency is maximized when all available real productive capacity, especially labour, is deployed. The paper demonstrates that unemployment, idle capacity, and persistent poverty are violations of this standard, arising from insufficient sovereign spending relative to imposed tax liabilities and private saving preferences. It further introduces the Anchor Mechanism, a governance corollary in which the sovereign temporarily intervenes as a price-setting buyer and seller of essential goods during inflationary episodes, stabilizing the price level without austerity, interest-rate manipulation, or output suppression. By replacing commodity backing with a real-resource anchor, the Resource Standard clarifies the operational foundations of fiat money and establishes full employment as a systemic requirement rather than a discretionary policy choice. The framework provides a coherent basis for price stability, universal employment, and sustained abundance in sovereign currency systems.

detail.abstract: Based on the insight that declaring an anomaly as not spanned requires knowledge of the true stochastic discount factor (SDF), we reverse conventional testing and suppose that, under the alternative, the anomaly is spanned. In the U.S. data, 132 of 153 anomalies are classified as spanned. The evidence highlights redundancy and masking in the anomaly zoo.

detail.abstract: Accurate inflation forecasts are crucial for monetary policy, yet emerging economies face heightened volatility and data limitations that challenge conventional models. This paper develops a unified real-time forecasting framework for monthly CPI inflation in Nicaragua (2016-2023), combining high-dimensional machine-learning (ML) methods, disaggregated univariate models, robust model selection, forecast combination, and probabilistic inference. We implement five forecasting strategies from ML learners with realistic information sets to bottom-up aggregation of twelve CPI subindices and apply the Model Confidence Set to isolate superior models at each horizon. Simple OLS combinations of these superior set forecasts further reduce root-mean-square errors by up to 40% relative to a driftless random walk and pass Diebold-Mariano and unbiasedness tests. Notably, bottom-up AutoETS delivers the lowest errors (RMSE ratios 0.684 at one month, 0.501 at twelve months) and remains the only model yielding rational errors across all horizons. Feature-importance and SHAP analyses confirm that global policy uncertainty and short-run inertia drive inflation dynamics, while conformal prediction methods produce well-calibrated 90% intervals without parametric assumptions. Our findings demonstrate that (i) careful information timing reduces artificial performance gains, (ii) parsimonious bottom-up schemes can outperform complex ML under realtime constraints, (iii) simple combinations yield robust, unbiased forecasts, and (iv) conformal inference provides reliable uncertainty quantification offering central banks a practical toolkit for inflation monitoring in volatile, data-scarce settings.

title: Binocular Directional Forecasting: A Cross-Attention Fusion Approach

detail.title: Binocular Directional Forecasting: A Cross-Attention Fusion Approach
detail.abstract: We develop a binocular directional forecasting framework that jointly leverages information from equity and option markets through a multimodal deep learning architecture. Realized price and trading dynamics, together with option-implied volatility information, are encoded as twodimensional images and processed using convolutional neural networks (CNNs), then integrated through a cross-attention mechanism with an adaptive gating network. This design enables bidirectional information flow across markets and state-dependent weighting of heterogeneous signals. Using U.S. equity and option daily data from 1996 to 2023, we show that the binocular model significantly outperforms stock-only benchmarks in out-of-sample directional prediction at both monthly and quarterly horizons. Trading strategies based on the fused forecasts achieve higher Sharpe ratios and lower turnover than traditional momentum and reversal strategies. Performance gains are most pronounced during periods of elevated market uncertainty and weak historical predictability, highlighting the incremental value of forward-looking option-implied expectations. Overall, our findings demonstrate that cross-attention provides an effective and scalable approach for integrating realized and expectations-based information in financial forecasting.

This report analyzes the economic impact of the 2025 tariff escalation between Canada and the United States, marking a structural shift in North America’s most important trade relationship. Following broad U.S. tariff measures and Canadian retaliation, the study examines how tariffs transmit through the economy via cost-push inflation, supply chain disruptions, retaliatory effects, and exchange rate adjustments.

title: Design Choices in Low-Latency C++ Systems: Empirical Insights With Applications to High-Frequency Trading

detail.abstract: High-frequency trading (HFT) systems operate under extreme latency constraints, where microseconds can determine profitability. While prior work often focuses on isolated optimizations, achieving consistently low latency in practice requires coordinated design across the entire software stack. This preprint presents a comprehensive empirical study of low-latency system design from a software-centric perspective, evaluating optimizations across five key layers: system tuning, C++ language features, compiler optimizations, programming techniques, and networking. Through systematic benchmarking on commodity hardware, we quantify the latency impact of a wide range of techniques, including scheduler policies, memory management strategies, compile-time abstractions, cache-aware designs, lock-free concurrency, and kernel-bypass networking via AF XDP. Our results demonstrate that latency behavior is governed not by any single optimization, but by the interaction between layers, with factors such as kernel involvement, memory access patterns, and control-flow predictability playing dominant roles. While absolute performance gains vary across environments, the study surfaces consistent principles for reducing latency and improving determinism. By unifying insights across traditionally siloed areas, this work provides a structured framework for reasoning about low-latency system design and bridges the gap between academic exploration and real-world high-performance trading systems.

title: Liquidity Provision and Price Impact Under Asymmetric Information: A Structural Microstructure Analysis

detail.title: Liquidity Provision and Price Impact Under Asymmetric Information: A Structural Microstructure Analysis
detail.abstract:
In modern financial markets, price formation is not frictionless but arises from strategic interactions under provision of asymmetric information. Financial markets are fundamentally structured around the interaction between two primary participants: market makers, who supply liquidity, and traders, who demand it, thereby driving price discovery. Within a specific financial market, there are  traders with private information about the asset’s true value and uniformed traders who are driven by liquidity and lack private information with respect to the true value of the market assets. The market makers who act as trading intermediaries are unable to distinguish between informed and uniformed traders trying to make a profit. These market makers face adverse selection risk, where they make a blind risk and set a stochastic value to the asset. 

To effectively avoid the adverse selection risk and financial loss the market makers utilise the observed sequence and composition of incoming orders (market orders, limit orders, cancellations) known as order flow to assign a value for the price of the asset/stock. 

This paper examines how market makers assign asset value and provide liquidity under asymmetric information and adverse selection risk. And how the process of Bayesian price formation generates price impacts. The paper follows a structural microstructure framework to effectively study concepts of order flow and price impacts while explaining the mechanism through which market makers update bids–ask quotes in response to order flow, thereby mitigating adverse selection risk posed by informed traders. Driven by the Kyle (1985) model and Glosten-Milgrom (1985) model this paper argues that price impact is endogenous and resulted by informed asymmetry and market liquidity. 

By proficiently identifying the relation between information asymmetry, market liquidity and price impact with respect to the Bayesian price formation, Kyle (1985) model and Glosten-Milgrom (1985) model, this research advances the theoretical understanding market structures and real-world price movements with the link of trading activity to volatility and liquidity changes.

title: Budget Efficiency Alpha in Formula 1: A Dominance Structure Framework and Budget Efficiency Index for Competitive Analysis Under the FIA Cost Cap
