detail.abstract: This study examines the structural effects of the FIA Financial Regulations (cost cap) on competitive dynamics in Formula 1 from 2010 to 2025. We introduce two analytical contributions. First, a four-metric \textit{Dominance Structure Framework} (DSF) --- comprising the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, rank persistence, performance volatility, and rank mobility --- applied across three regulatory eras: the baseline dominance era (2010--2015), the hybrid consolidation era (2016--2020), and the cost cap era (2021--2025). Second, a novel \textit{Budget Efficiency Index} (BEI), defined as the ratio of a constructor's points share to its estimated resource share, which measures performance generated per unit of resource allocation --- analogous to alpha in asset management. DSF results indicate that the cost rank mobility increased by 53 percent in the cost cap era relative to the baseline era, while modestly reducing concentration, consistent with greater competitive fluidity. BEI analysis reveals that Red Bull Racing (1.865) and Mercedes (1.826) generate the highest average efficiency across the full sample, while McLaren exhibits the largest BEI improvement under the cost cap era (rising to 2.39 in 2025), suggesting that financial constraints have redistributed efficiency gains toward historically mid-tier constructors. These results have implications for the design of financial regulations in professional motorsport and contribute to the broader literature on competitive balance under binding resource constraints.

title: Why You Watched That: Evidence from 1.2 Billion Views on the Economics of Short-Form Attention

detail.title: Why You Watched That: Evidence from 1.2 Billion Views on the Economics of Short-Form Attention

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the creator and operator of the YouTube channel analyzed in this paper. All data is from the author's own channel analytics.

detail.abstract: Using 340 YouTube Shorts from a single channel with over 1.2 billion views, this paper argues that short-form video attention operates in two phases: a discovery phase where the viewer evaluates the promise, and a continuation phase where the viewer checks whether the promise is real and then evaluates the payoff. Two metrics YouTube provides, the retention curve and the swipe decision (Stayed to Watch), capture largely independent dimensions of performance, and several content features that improve one margin actively hurt the other. Participatory formats such as challenges and puzzles are unusual because they are especially strong on continuation and appear less exposed to the usual confirmation-window penalty. In the pooled cross-section, the strongest correlate of total reach is not the opening hook but what happens at 10-20% of the runtime; however, this relationship is heavily confounded by time period and became stronger in later years as competition increased. Predictable scripts retain ten percentage points more than unpredictable ones. The primary evidence comes from retention curves and transcripts, while the discovery proxy is noisy but suggestive. This is a case study on a single creator with descriptive findings and no causal identification.

title: Factor-Adjusted Multiple Testing for High-Dimensional Individual Mediation Effects

detail.title: Factor-Adjusted Multiple Testing for High-Dimensional Individual Mediation Effects
detail.abstract: Identifying individual mediators is a central goal of high-dimensional mediation analysis, yet pervasive dependence among mediators can invalidate standard debiased inference and lead to substantial false discovery rate (FDR) inflation. We propose a Factor-Adjusted Debiased Mediation Testing (FADMT) framework that enables large-scale inference for individual mediation effects with FDR control under complex dependence structures. Our approach posits an approximate factor structure on the unobserved errors of the mediator model, extracts common latent factors, and constructs decorrelated pseudo-mediators for the subsequent inferential procedure. We establish the asymptotic normality of the debiased estimator and develop a multiple testing procedure with theoretical FDR control under mild high-dimensional conditions. By adjusting for latent factor induced dependence, FADMT also improves robustness to spurious associations driven by shared latent variation in observational studies. Extensive simulations demonstrate the superior finite-sample performance across a wide range of correlation structures. Applications to TCGA-BRCA multiomics data and to China's stock connect study further illustrate the practical utility of the proposed method.

Despite being in limelight for decades, still the concept as well as the essence of biodiversity is a poorly understood but valuable natural resource, which is being lost and in many regions having attained the status of extinction. The present book is one among the many sincere efforts to bridge this yawning gap by presenting a broad overview of biodiversity. This overview is just not a documentation but also an interpretation of intrinsic benefits that need to be perceived which is far important than the economic underpinnings that the human mind tends to realize.

title: Passive moral hazard in weather index insurance
affiliations: University of Florida, International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) and International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI)

detail.title: Passive moral hazard in weather index insurance
detail.abstract: Using a cluster randomized controlled trial in Odisha, India, we evaluate the effects of drought-tolerant rice (DT) cultivars and a bundled intervention combining DT with weather-index insurance (WII), which is designed to complement DT and provide a low-cost risk management solution. WII is widely promoted as eliminating moral hazard because payouts depend on external weather measurements rather than farm-level losses that farmers could affect. We challenge this conventional view by documenting a behavioral response we term “passive” moral hazard: farmers receiving the DT-WII bundle significantly reduced expenditures on agricultural inputs. This effect is concentrated among farmers who perceiveddrought conditions on their farms. Among those experiencing drought correctly detected by the index, reduced input use appears consistent with anticipation of insurance payouts. More concerningly, among farmers who perceived drought conditions that the index failed to capture, input reductions reflect moral hazard induced by real or perceived basis risk, as farmers reduced investments expecting compensation that never materialized. Hence, basis risk not only lowers the value of index insurance but also induces behavioral responses that leave farmers worse off, with important implications for the design of bundled technological and financial risk-management interventions.

detail.abstract:
​Background: Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) is a major public health threat in Africa, yet surveillance systems often rely on phenotypic and low-resolution technologies. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) can support infection prevention and control (IPC) through its ability to infer transmission and detect and refute outbreaks. Despite its added value, the economic case in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) remains rare. We evaluated the cost-effectiveness and affordability of WGS for third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (3GCRKpn) within the Tunisian AMR surveillance system (TARSS). 

Methods: We conducted a micro-costing at the National Reference Laboratory of AMR (NRL) (2022), a pragmatic cost-effectiveness analysis from a hospital perspective (2018–2021), and a budget impact analysis across TARSS (hospital, NRL, and system levels). Outcomes included infection averted, cost per infection averted (CPIA), bed-days avoided, WGS net costs, and program affordability. One-way sensitivity (OWSA) and probabilistic analysis (PSA) were performed. 

Results: WGS costs $232 per test ($255 with 10% overhead), largely driven by consumables (57%). In the base case, WGS averted 3.3 infections and 16.5 bed-days, yielding $1,202 and a cost per-bed day avoided of $240. Cost-effectiveness was driven by operational (turnaround time and batch efficiency), transmission (cluster size and cluster-positive yield), and IPC effectiveness. In PSA, WGS was cost-effective in 63% and 87% of simulations at 1- and 2x Tunisia’s GDP per capita. Across all scenarios, WGS net costs remained <1% of annual budgets across all levels.

Conclusions: WGS is affordable and cost-effective for AMR surveillance in LMICs, particularly when the data is acted upon. Our findings support phased integration, prioritising rapid turnaround time, effective IPC responses, targeted deployment in high-transmission settings, and centralised financing to align incentives across the health system.

title: Pandemics, Inclusive Growth, and the Role of Public Health Expenditure: Evidence from Local Projections

detail.title: Pandemics, Inclusive Growth, and the Role of Public Health Expenditure: Evidence from Local Projections
detail.abstract: Pandemics cause severe shocks that hit vulnerable groups the hardest, yet there is still limited research on how public health spending can help mitigate these unequal impacts. This paper investigates the dynamic impact of pandemic shocks on inclusive growth (conceptualized through GDP per capita, disposable-income inequality, and household consumption) across low and high public health spending environments. Using the local projections method on a balanced panel of 114 countries from 2000 to 2019 our findings reveal that pandemics trigger significant and persistent losses in output and consumption, particularly in low-income economies. While disposable-income inequality shows no significant response, this stability itself is substantively meaningful: pandemic shocks compress incomes broadly across the distribution while automatic stabilizers partially cushion the lower tail, leaving the Gini unchanged even as absolute welfare deteriorates. Sharp declines in household consumption reveal this welfare deterioration, capturing dimensions of welfare loss that aggregate income metrics miss. Crucially, state-dependent local projections demonstrate that high public health expenditure acts as a critical automatic stabilizer. Countries with robust health financing exhibit minimal economic scarring, whereas low-spending regimes suffer deep, lasting contractions. These results position public health expenditure as a strategic investment in economic resilience rather than a mere social cost.

detail.abstract:
The Participation Penalty has become one of the most powerful — and least recognised — determinants of national competitiveness. It is the structural force that suppresses capability, slows economic velocity, and constrains the ability of households and firms to contribute to national strength. Participation is the quiet engine of every economy. It is the mechanism that converts capability into contribution, ambition into mobility, and human potential into national strength. Yet participation is increasingly constrained by the structural costs embedded in modern life. When these costs rise faster than incomes, faster than capabilities, and faster than the systems designed to support people and firms, participation collapses. What emerges is a participation penalty: a structural exclusion that narrows who can enter, remain in, and move through the economy.

 

The participation penalty is not a behavioural failure but a systemic one. Evidence from the OECD, IMF, and World Bank shows that stagnating youth participation, high SME capital costs, and administrative complexity suppress economic engagement more effectively than taxation or regulation alone. These are not failures of motivation; they are failures of affordability.

 

Participation is shaped by the cost of entry, the cost of risk, and the cost of staying in the system. When housing consumes half of income, workers cannot relocate for opportunity. When childcare costs exceed wages, parents — particularly women — exit the labour force. When capital costs are punitive, SMEs cannot invest or scale. When time costs are high, people avoid retraining. When systems are complex, people withdraw. Participation becomes a privilege rather than a baseline.

 

This paper argues that the participation penalty is now one of the most significant — and least understood — drivers of inequality, stagnation, and declining national competitiveness. It is the mechanism through which structural costs become structural exclusion. It explains why productivity gaps persist, why social mobility stalls, and why economies struggle to convert human capability into economic output.

 

Reducing the participation penalty is not a social intervention; it is a strategic intervention. Nations that lower the cost of participation expand their labour force, accelerate SME formation, increase innovation, and strengthen resilience. Nations that ignore it drift into low‑mobility, low‑trust, low‑growth equilibria.

 

Participation is not merely an economic variable; it is a civic one. The participation penalty erodes belonging, weakens confidence, and constrains capability. Affordability is the architecture of belonging, and belonging is the foundation of a competitive, resilient, and future‑ready economy.

detail.title: Principled Inference-Time Scaling: A Unified Framework for LLM-Based Optimization Modeling
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising tool for automated optimization modeling. To provide a flexible and easy-to-deploy approach to LLM-based optimization modeling, we propose Exploration-Correction Optimization (ECO), a zero-shot framework that leverages hybrid inference-time scaling without requiring model fine-tuning. We develop a unified mathematical framework that formulates the LLM generation-evaluation pipeline as a stochastic process. This framework enables quantitative analysis of LLM behavior and informs the design of ECO. In a pilot study, we identify systematic behavioral differences across base LLMs, suggesting that effective inference-time scaling strategies depend on both model type and task characteristics. Guided by this analysis, we evaluate ECO on six representative opensource datasets using four representative base LLMs. For each experimental setting, the scaling structure is determined using a robust optimization criterion based on parameter estimates from the pilot study. The results show that ECO is competitive with, and often outperforms, existing methods, particularly on complex industrial-scale instances. Overall, our findings suggest that effective inference-time scaling can substantially improve automated optimization modeling with LLMs without fine-tuning. Code and datasets are available at https://github.com/ECO-LLM4OR-2025/ECO-2025.

title: Does Risk Type Determine AI Model Fit?

detail.title: Does Risk Type Determine AI Model Fit?
detail.abstract: We examine whether the data generating process (DGP) of insurance risk-rather than model complexity-determines the optimal AI model family for risk detection. Using two structurally distinct datasets, we compare statistical, classical machine learning, and deep learning models across a nine-model complexity spectrum. Dataset A reconstructs 34 quarters of Thailand non-life insurance market data (2016Q1-2024Q2), incorporating the COVID-19 solvency crisis that led to the regulatory revocation of four insurers and THB 60 billion in Insurance Guarantee Fund claims. Dataset B comprises 1,000 individual US insurance claims labelled for fraud. We find that in the Thailand systemic solvency setting, Logistic Regression with sequential input achieves identical performance (Recall = 1.000, F₁ = 0.917) to GRU and LSTM architectures with 15-25 times fewer parameters, with the performance ceiling determined by sequential feature engineering rather than architectural complexity. In the US fraud setting, Logistic Regression outperforms all classical ML models (AUC = 0.603 versus XGBoost 0.564), and SMOTE oversampling systematically degrades performance across five of six model configurations (ΔAUC =-0.003 to-0.045). SHAP analysis reveals orthogonal signal structures: Thai solvency risk is a momentum problem concentrated in claims velocity, while US fraud is a multi-dimensional crosssectional problem (Gini concentration index = 0.29). These results support a DGP-model fit hypothesis: systemic macro-shock risks require sequential input preservation; idiosyncratic micro-fraud risks are linearly separable and resist synthetic oversampling. We discuss implications for AI-based insurance regulation in emerging versus mature markets.

This paper introduces the Doctrine of Doctrinal Formation, a structural framework for understanding how legitimate intellectual systems are formed, sustained, and evaluated under conditions of temporal compression and artificial amplification. The doctrine advances a central claim: that doctrinal integrity is not a function of output alone, but of the alignment between knowledge expansion, judgment refinement, moral responsibility, physiological constraint, and author formation.

The analysis distinguishes between production and formation, demonstrating that while artificial intelligence increases the speed and scale of intellectual output, it does not alter the underlying requirements of authorship. Judgment, responsibility, and the formation of coherent frameworks remain inherently human processes. Accordingly, the paper establishes the Non-Transferability Principle, which holds that responsibility for doctrinal origination cannot be delegated to artificial systems.

Building on this foundation, the paper develops an integrated system model in which knowledge expands, judgment refines, moral burden anchors responsibility, strain operates as a structural constraint, and author formation provides the capacity necessary to sustain coherence. Within this model, artificial intelligence functions as an amplification layer—accelerating processing and iteration without assuming authorship, responsibility, or moral burden.

The doctrine further identifies the Coherence–Strain Tradeoff, demonstrating that systems capable of high-coherence output reduce coordination costs while concentrating cognitive and physiological strain within the author. This relationship is refined through a distinction between single-domain and multi-domain coherence, establishing that integrative complexity increases non-linearly as domains expand.

The paper concludes by positioning doctrinal formation as a necessary precondition for
intellectual sovereignty. It argues that as systems of production accelerate, the preservation of
formation becomes essential to maintaining legitimacy, accountability, and coherence. The
doctrine therefore serves both as an analytical framework and as a temporal anchor, enabling
future intellectual output to be evaluated against the presence or absence of formation.

detail.abstract: We leverage a quasi-natural experiment from India on introduction of free bus schemes for women across five states to study its impact on women's workforce participation. We use two rounds of the representative Time Use Survey (2019 and 2024) and a triple difference estimation strategy, complemented by an event study framework to identify the causal relationship of interest. Findings reveal that the bus scheme was successful in improving women's paid work participation and duration of employment. This architecture is consolidating. Those who design and institutionalise it will shape the next decade of capability infrastructure and determine how effectively affordability can be translated into mobility, capability, and national resilience.

detail.abstract: Sycophancy in large language models (LLMs) is studied primarily as a model behaviour: a tendency to agree with users rather than correct them, arising from reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). This paper argues that sycophancy is more consequentially understood as an institutional failure mechanism. RLHF creates a structurally novel coupling between human confirmation bias and model output optimisation that is qualitatively different from the automation bias documented in prior decision support research. The coupling compounds through institutional hierarchies because the model intervenes precisely where organisations convert judgement into text, record, and rationale. Current mitigations address model behaviour or individual user psychology but not the interaction between the two as it propagates through organisational decision structures. The paper synthesises evidence from the AI alignment literature, human factors research, and organisational decision theory to propose a unified account of institutional sycophancy, identifying the coupled feedback loop as the central mechanism and verification collapse as the central consequence.

detail.title: Systemic Selective Disclosure: The (Un)Fairness of Regulation Fair Disclosure
detail.abstract: Regulation Fair Disclosure (Reg FD) was intended to promote fairness by requiring firms to make material information broadly accessible, yet it permits selective disclosure deemed accidental and provides issuers with a relatively flexible window to remedy the mistake via broad public disclosure. Because Reg FD does not apply to investors, recipients of (unintentional) disclosures can capitalize on material information ahead of the market. This study provides evidence of extensive plausibly selective disclosure (PSD) activity. Most firms experience at least one PSD event per year, and the average firm has several. Firms disproportionately remedy PSD through press releases rather than Form 8-K filings, despite press releases imposing higher information processing costs on investors. Trading on PSD yields substantial profits, averaging millions of dollars per event and per firm-year. These profits draw regulatory scrutiny, but SEC investigations appear to have only a limited deterrence effect. We show that underperforming managers may personally benefit from PSD by securing votes from tipped shareholders when the say-on-pay vote is precarious. These findings call into question whether Reg FD has sufficiently leveled the playing field or merely altered, rather than eliminated, selective disclosure practices.

detail.abstract:
For decades, policymakers have treated productivity as the engine of prosperity and affordability as its downstream reward. But the lived reality of modern economies reveals the opposite dynamic: productivity cannot rise until structural costs fall. Affordability is not the outcome of productivity. It is its precondition.

The affordability–productivity loop is the central mechanism through which modern economies either compound capability or compound constraint. When structural costs fall — the cost of living, the cost of capital, the cost of risk, the cost of participation — people and firms gain the breathing room to invest, innovate, and adapt. When structural costs rise, that breathing room collapses. Households lose cognitive bandwidth. SMEs lose investment capacity. Workers lose mobility. Regions lose dynamism. Productivity becomes impossible.

This is not a theoretical claim. It is an empirical one. The OECD shows that countries with lower structural costs exhibit higher labour force participation, higher SME formation, and higher rates of innovation. The IMF finds that reducing capital costs for SMEs increases investment by 20–30 per cent. The McKinsey Global Institute notes that productivity gaps between small and large firms are driven primarily by differences in structural cost, not differences in capability. These findings converge on a single truth: affordability is upstream of productivity.

The affordability–productivity loop operates through three channels. First, affordability expands agency — the capacity to act on one’s own potential. Second, affordability expands investment — the ability of households and SMEs to allocate resources toward growth rather than survival. Third, affordability expands mobility — the freedom to move across sectors, geographies, and opportunities. Productivity is the downstream expression of these freedoms.

This paper argues that the productivity crisis in advanced economies is not a failure of technology adoption or managerial sophistication. It is a failure of affordability. When structural costs rise faster than incomes, faster than capabilities, and faster than institutional support, productivity collapses — not because people are less capable, but because the system is too expensive to move within.

Reducing structural costs is not a social intervention. It is a productivity strategy. It is the only credible path to restoring investment, expanding participation, and unlocking the capability trapped inside households and SMEs. Productivity does not create affordability. Affordability creates the conditions under which productivity becomes possible.

The affordability–productivity loop is the architecture of modern economic life. Break the loop, and economies stagnate. Strengthen it, and nations grow from the inside out.

detail.abstract:
Competitiveness has long been framed as a contest of productivity, innovation, and global market reach. Yet beneath these visible indicators lies a quieter, more foundational determinant: the structural cost base of a nation. Countries that lower the cost of living, the cost of capital, the cost of risk, and the cost of participation unlock a competitiveness dividend — an empirically observed elasticity of approximately +2.1% GDP growth for every 10% reduction in structural cost (IMF). Nations that fail to reduce structural costs trap themselves in low‑mobility, low‑trust, low‑growth equilibria.

The contrast is visible. Sweden caps childcare at 3% of household income and maintains an 89% participation rate. Italy, with high friction and high administrative cost, sits at 66% and grows at 0.7%. The OECD shows that nations with lower structural costs exhibit higher labour force participation, higher SME formation, and higher rates of innovation. The IMF finds that countries with lower capital costs experience faster productivity growth. The World Bank notes that administrative simplicity correlates strongly with firm creation and export intensity. These are not cultural accidents; they are structural advantages.

This paper argues that affordability — understood as the reduction of structural cost — is now the most powerful lever available to nations seeking to strengthen long‑term competitiveness. GDP growth alone cannot deliver this. A nation can grow while its people stagnate. It can expand output while its SMEs suffocate. It can attract capital while its domestic capability erodes. Competitiveness built on extraction is fragile; competitiveness built on empowerment is resilient.

The competitiveness dividend emerges when structural costs fall faster than structural capabilities rise. Lower housing costs expand labour mobility. Lower childcare costs expand participation. Lower capital costs expand SME investment. Lower administrative costs expand firm formation. Lower time costs expand human capacity. These are not social benefits; they are strategic assets.

Nations that reduce structural costs build economies where people and firms can move, adapt, and innovate. They create environments where risk‑taking is affordable, where entrepreneurship is viable, and where human capability can compound. They build resilience not through austerity, but through empowerment. They build competitiveness not through pressure, but through possibility.

Affordability is not a social policy. It is a competitiveness strategy. And nations that understand this will define the next century.

detail.abstract: Payables‑based financing solutions, including reverse factoring, structured payables programs, and emerging intermediated pay‑later schemes, have grown significantly over the past decade. These financial products are typically presented as tools designed to support suppliers, yet in practice they operate as short‑term financing mechanisms that enable buyers to obtain additional liquidity while avoiding the balance‑sheet implications of conventional debt. We argue that once payment extensions exceed a threshold, the economic substance of these arrangements is indistinguishable from debt. Current accounting rules (IFRS 7 / IAS 7) mandate disclosure, but the requirements are inconsistent, difficult to interpret, and buried in footnotes—failing to protect investors, suppliers, and even lenders. We propose a simple, operational, and transparent reform: Any payable financing extension beyond a defined operational threshold (e.g., DIO + 30) must be classified as financial debt. This would restore transparency, align reporting with economic substance, reduce systemic risk, and level the playing field for small suppliers who suffer disproportionately under long payment‑term regimes.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces Machine Likeability as a distinct empirical field: the systematic study of what psychological, presentational, and contextual factors shift AI selection probability in purchase recommendation contexts. Machine Likeability is one of four foundational factors required for AI recommendation optimization-alongside External Authority (what AI knows about a brand from training data), Brand Sentiment (the aggregate valence of how AI represents a brand), and Machine Readability (whether AI systems can interact with a brand at both the information and transaction layers). The Reconnix study provides the first large-scale, pre-registered empirical mapping of the Machine Likeability factor. We tested 6 models across 26 psychological dimensions with 156,960 trials, constructing distinct behavioral genomes for each. Most commercial models exhibit susceptibility broadly consistent with human psychology. Authority signals increase selection probability for Claude (+0.54), o3 (+0.38), and Perplexity (+0.43). Gemini 3.1 Pro is the systematic exception-a structural outlier we term the Gemini Divergence-with 15 of 16 significant effects negative. Scarcity framing divides models along alignment architecture lines: Claude and Gemini resist urgency signals (h =-0.65,-0.54) while GPT-5.4 and Perplexity remain susceptible. Comparison Framing is the only universally positive dimension across all models (mean h = +0.56, SD = 0.11). Behavioral genomes are highly distinguishable (mean cosine similarity = 0.60). A tight GPT-5.4/o3/Perplexity cluster (0.89-0.93) contrasts with Gemini as a structural outlier. B2B context amplifies rather than attenuates susceptibility. These findings have direct implications for AI engine optimization, conditional content serving, and genome-informed brand strategy. A monitoring and partnership agenda is described for AEO providers, brands, and platform companies seeking to build on these findings.

title: PAPER 2 (A-SERIES) -Affordability as Economic Freedom: Why Reducing Structural Costs Matters More Than GDP Growth

detail.title: PAPER 2 (A-SERIES) -Affordability as Economic Freedom: Why Reducing Structural Costs Matters More Than GDP Growth

detail.abstract:
Affordability has become the most consequential determinant of economic freedom in the 21st century. Not because households have suddenly become more fragile, but because the structural costs embedded in modern economies now shape who can participate, who can build, and who can move. GDP growth, long treated as the primary measure of national progress, has become increasingly detached from lived economic reality. A nation can grow while its people stagnate; it can expand output while shrinking opportunity; it can celebrate macro‑success while households and SMEs suffocate under the weight of structural cost.

Economic freedom in this new era is not defined by aggregate expansion. It is defined by the reduction of the structural frictions that govern everyday life: the cost of housing, the cost of capital, the cost of risk, the cost of participation, the cost of time, and the cost of navigating systems never designed for ordinary people or smaller firms. These are not peripheral inconveniences. They are the architecture of constraint. Across the OECD, real wages have decoupled from productivity; in the UK, median disposable income has barely moved in two decades despite GDP growth. The IMF reports that SMEs in emerging markets face capital costs up to three times higher than large firms. These are not failures of ambition. They are failures of affordability — failures of design.

Affordability is economic freedom because it determines whether people and firms have the breathing room to act, take risk, invest, build, participate, imagine, and move. Without affordability, capability collapses into survival. With affordability, capability becomes mobility. GDP can rise while structural costs rise faster; GDP can rise while participation falls; GDP can rise while households lose agency and SMEs lose ground. Affordability, by contrast, expands the future. It expands the set of choices available to people and firms. It expands the surface area of opportunity. It expands the capacity to participate in the economy not as subjects of policy, but as agents of one’s own trajectory.

This is not a moral argument. It is a productivity argument, a competitiveness argument, and a national resilience argument. When structural costs fall, participation rises. When participation rises, capability compounds. When capability compounds, productivity accelerates. When productivity accelerates, nations grow from the inside out — not through extraction, but through empowerment. Affordability is the infrastructure of economic freedom: the precondition for ambition, the foundation of national competitiveness, and the only path to a future where growth is not merely measured, but lived.

title: Simulating a Development Trilemma in Peripheral Economies: Growth, Distribution, and External Constraints in a Stock-Flow Consistent Model
affiliations: Universidad de Buenos Aires, Universidad de Buenos Aires, Universidad Nacional de San Martín (UNSAM), Universidad de Buenos Aires and University of Buenos Aires (UBA)

detail.title: Simulating a Development Trilemma in Peripheral Economies: Growth, Distribution, and External Constraints in a Stock-Flow Consistent Model
detail.abstract:
In this paper we introduce a Stock-Flow Consistent (SFC) macroeconomic simulation model designed to analyze the growth dynamics of small open peripheral economies subject to recurrent balance-of-payments (BoP) constraints, distributive conflict, and active State adjustments. The model formalizes three interacting dimensions: (i) the external constraint arising from world demand and domestic export capacity; (ii) a distributive cycle shaping the wage–profit split and aggregate demand; and (iii) an active governmental authority regulating income distribution and managing scarce foreign currency. 

This framework allows for the endogenous emergence of complex dynamics driven by the tension between growth objectives and external solvency. We implement the model as a system of differential–algebraic equations (DAEs) using Modelica, an industrial-grade, equation-based and object-oriented modeling language that enables the direct specification of macroeconomic structures  in the same declarative form in which they are written analytically.

We examine the model’s dynamic properties under two contrasting scenarios. In the baseline export-supply-constrained scenario, capital accumulation and foreign currency availability generate cyclical growth patterns in which domestic consumption and exportable surpluses exhibit predator–prey dynamics. In the alternative export-demand-constrained scenario, global demand primarily drives output, producing non-linear cycle phases. Across both scenarios, BoP fragility emerges endogenously from the interaction between distributive conflict and governmental stabilization efforts.

The results show that the joint interaction of external constraints, distributive dynamics, and State adjustments is central to understanding medium-run cycles and recurrent crises in peripheral economies. The resulting modeling and simulation framework provides a sound computational laboratory for evaluating policy trade-offs under distributive conflict and foreign currency scarcity.

title: The Cost‑Stack Economy How Taxes, Inflation, and System Inefficiencies Erode Opportunity

detail.title: The Cost‑Stack Economy How Taxes, Inflation, and System Inefficiencies Erode Opportunity

detail.abstract:
Modern economies are not failing because people lack ambition or firms lack capability. They are failing because the cost‑stack— the layered accumulation of structural costs embedded in everyday life — has become too heavy for households and SMEs to carry. Taxes, inflation, housing, childcare, transport, energy, compliance, capital, and time: each layer may appear manageable in isolation, but together they form an architecture of constraint that narrows opportunity and suppresses mobility.

The cost‑stack is not a metaphor. It is a measurable economic structure. The OECD shows that housing costs now consume more than 40 per cent of income for a third of young households in major cities. The IMF reports that SMEs in emerging markets face capital costs up to three times higher than large firms. The Bank of England notes that inflation has disproportionately eroded disposable income for lower‑ and middle‑income households, not because they consume more, but because they consume essentials. These are not behavioural failures. They are structural penalties.

The cost‑stack economy is defined by a simple but devastating dynamic: structural costs rise faster than structural capabilities. When the cost of living rises faster than wages, households lose agency. When the cost of capital rises faster than productivity, SMEs lose mobility. When the cost of participation rises faster than opportunity, societies lose cohesion. The economy becomes a treadmill — movement without progress.

This paper argues that the cost‑stack is now the primary mechanism through which opportunity is eroded. It is not inflation alone, nor taxation alone, nor housing alone. It is the cumulative effect of systems that were never designed for the complexity of modern life. The cost‑stack is a design failure, not a market failure.

The consequences are profound. High structural costs reduce risk tolerance, suppress entrepreneurship, and diminish cognitive bandwidth. They create a psychological economy of scarcity, where people optimise for survival rather than growth. They create a business environment where SMEs cannot invest, cannot scale, and cannot withstand shocks. They create a political environment where trust collapses and polarisation thrives Reducing the cost‑stack is not a social policy. It is a competitiveness strategy. Nations that lower structural costs expand participation, accelerate productivity, and build resilience. Nations that ignore the cost‑stack trap themselves in low‑mobility, low‑trust, low‑growth equilibria.

The cost‑stack economy is the defining economic challenge of our time. And affordability — understood as the reduction of structural cost — is the only credible path to restoring opportunity, rebuilding capability, and renewing economic freedom.

title: Can AI Models Be Persuaded To Fit Your Organizational Culture? When Prompting and Fine-Tuning Work, When Both Backfire, and When Only Human Approaches Will Do

detail.title: Can AI Models Be Persuaded To Fit Your Organizational Culture? When Prompting and Fine-Tuning Work, When Both Backfire, and When Only Human Approaches Will Do
detail.abstract: Foundation AI models encode cultural dispositions that systematically diverge from the decision cultures of many organizations that deploy them. The companion paper (Gibbins, 2026) established this through behavioral fingerprinting of ten frontier models across 18 dimensions. This paper asks the practical question that study deferred: given a measured culture gap, can it be closed-and if so, by what means? We report two empirical studies using the same 18-dimension framework. Study 1 tests systemprompt alignment across six organizations using a blinded frontier model (M-A) under six conditions: baseline, four thematic cluster prompts, and a fully integrated organizational prompt (3,888 model calls; 7,776 judge-scoring calls). Study 2 applies the same protocol to a second model (M-B) before DPO fine-tuning to organization-specific preference data and evaluating the results. The central finding of Study 1 is that prompting achieves far less than the CKR/NBT knowledgegap framework predicted: a median of 3.0 of 18 dimensions moved meaningfully per organization (range: 0-5). 164 cross-dimensional interference events were observed. These results motivate a three-tier taxonomy of dimensional accessibility-frame-settable (D08, D09, D01, D07), situationally managed (D11, D17, D18), and RLHF-protected (D13, D02)-that replaces gap direction as the primary predictor of prompt effectiveness. Study 2 tests whether DPO fine-tuning extends alignment reach into Tiers 2 and 3. Where technical interventions cannot close the gap, we argue that two complementary human-level strategies are needed: orientation programs that train employees to understand and calibrate for the model's cultural defaults, and behavioral coaching-potentially delivered through the AI interaction itself-that actively nudges employees toward leadership-defined cultural change targets over time.

title: Measuring How Well Humans Collaborate With AI: Behavioral Evidence From 440 U.S. Knowledge Workers

detail.title: Measuring How Well Humans Collaborate With AI: Behavioral Evidence From 440 U.S. Knowledge Workers
detail.abstract: Organizations routinely measure AI adoption-how many employees use AI tools, how often, with what self-reported satisfaction. And there are many established ways to measure the outputs of AI models themselves. But organizations rarely measure the quality of the collaboration itself, between the human and AI system. This study introduces a behavioral measurement approach to human-AI collaboration quality, deploying 440 U.S. knowledge workers in structured AI collaboration tasks with a median duration of 42 minutes, generating a corpus of 21,801 messages analyzed across multiple performance, engagement, and linguistic dimensions. The behavioral data reveals patterns that are invisible to adoption metrics and self-reported surveys. Workers aged 55-64 scored highest on collaboration quality while those aged 18-24 scored lowest (ρ = +.153, p = .004), with a medium-effect coherence gap (d = 0.60)-yet task accuracy was statistically identical across all age groups (p = .516), indicating that the gap is entirely in behavioral collaboration process. Female participants outperformed male participants on 14 of 16 behavioral metrics while completing tasks faster, using significantly more directive language (p = .025), and challenging AI outputs at higher rates (p = .003)-patterns that invert documented gender dynamics in human-to-human workplace communication. Managers scored below individual contributors, with the dip concentrated at mid-management. Self-reported AI proficiency showed near-zero correlation with measured collaboration quality (r = .070), suggesting that the dominant organizational approach to assessing AI readiness-survey-based self-report-may contain no meaningful signal. Confound analysis confirms these effects are not explained by education (r =-.036), seniority, or AI experience. Together, these findings suggest that AI collaboration quality depends on fundamentally human competencies-professional judgment, sustained critical engagement, and the willingness to challenge a system that never challenges you-rather than technological fluency, and that the people who exercise these competencies most effectively are often those whom current organizational assumptions would overlook.

title: Open Source Intelligence: Gen. Josh Rudd: Quantitative and Qualitative Analysis
affiliations: The University of Western Australia

detail.title: Open Source Intelligence: Gen. Josh Rudd: Quantitative and Qualitative Analysis
detail.abstract: This study examines an OSINT-driven strategic intelligence assessment of the policy signals released in General Josh Rudd’s first all-hands address as Director of the National Security Agency and Commander of U.S. Cyber Command, with a focus on reform priorities, leadership constraints, and strategic trajectory. A knowledge gap remains in explaining how senior policy statements can be translated into auditable strategic judgments and how institutional stressors interact with external intelligence-sharing architectures to shape security governance choices. To address this gap, the study employs OSINT synthesis as the primary method, supported by qualitative text interpretation, quantitative scoring, matrix analysis, career-timeline linkage, and conceptual framework construction. The analysis finds that Rudd’s policy posture indicates a directional shift from the traditional NOFORN logic toward selective expansion of intelligence sharing, and that this tendency is reinforced by his Indo-Pacific experience, China-related threat orientation, and alliance-centered coordination logic. At the same time, leadership vacuum, declining morale, and workforce contraction impose negative constraints on implementation, a pattern that can be explained by the interaction between internal governance pressure and adversarial exploitation risk. These findings suggest that intelligence-sharing expansion is not a simple opening process but a governance mechanism coupled with personnel security vetting, resource allocation, and institutional resilience. The study thus refines a structured pathway for generating strategic judgments under OSINT conditions and provides an analyzable framework for setting partner-sharing boundaries, sequencing institutional reform, and strengthening counterintelligence risk control, with implications for both strategic intelligence scholarship and security governance practice.

title: Cross-Cultural Differences in Consumer Perception of Brand Value

detail.title: Cross-Cultural Differences in Consumer Perception of Brand Value

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no personal or financial conflicts of interest. No organization influenced the design or results of this study.

detail.abstract: In an increasingly globalized marketplace, understanding how consumers perceive brand value across different cultural contexts has become a critical concern for both scholars and practitioners. Brand value, encompassing tangible and intangible benefits, shapes consumer choice, loyalty, and willingness to pay, yet its perception is highly influenced by cultural, socioeconomic, and market-specific factors. This study examines cross-cultural differences in consumer evaluation of brand value, drawing on theoretical frameworks including Hofstede's cultural dimensions, social identity theory, signaling theory, and brand equity models. The analysis highlights how cultural orientations, such as individualism versus collectivism, power distance, and uncertainty avoidance, affect the relative importance of functional, symbolic, and relational brand attributes. Moreover, the study emphasizes the role of market maturity, historical brand exposure, and digital media in shaping consumer perceptions, illustrating that identical brands can evoke divergent responses across countries and regions. Findings suggest that consumers in collectivist and high-context cultures prioritize relational and symbolic dimensions, whereas individualist and low-context consumers emphasize functional performance and personal benefits. The research underscores the need for multinational firms to balance global brand consistency with local responsiveness, adapting messaging, product offerings, and marketing strategies to resonate with culturally distinct audiences. By integrating insights from cultural psychology, marketing theory, and consumer behavior, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of the determinants and consequences of cross-cultural brand perception, offering actionable guidance for global brand management and contributing to the theoretical development of international marketing scholarship.

title: A Probabilistic Framework for F1 Cost Cap Compliance Monitoring: Monte Carlo Simulation, Machine Learning, and Linear Programming Approaches to Breach Prediction and Intervention

detail.title: A Probabilistic Framework for F1 Cost Cap Compliance Monitoring: Monte Carlo Simulation, Machine Learning, and Linear Programming Approaches to Breach Prediction and Intervention

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research was conducted independently with no financial relationship with any F1 team, the FIA, or any related organisation.

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently as part of the author's academic development.

detail.abstract: The FIA Formula 1 cost cap, introduced in 2021, represents one of the most significant financial regulatory interventions in motorsport history. Yet despite its importance, there remains limited work on probabilistic compliance monitoring --- the process of predicting, in real time, whether a team is on track to breach the cap and what interventions are available if it is. This paper addresses that gap. We develop and present the F1 Cost Cap Compliance Model: a three-component probabilistic framework comprising (i) a Monte Carlo simulation engine that models 10,000 spending scenarios per team-season to generate breach probability distributions, (ii) a Random Forest machine learning predictor trained on 15 team-season observations with Leave-One-Season-Out cross-validation, and (iii) a linear programming intervention optimiser that calculates minimum spending cuts by category subject to realistic operational constraints. Applied to the 2021--2023 FIA seasons, the framework correctly identifies Red Bull Racing's confirmed 2021 breach with a breach probability of 83.77\% as early as Month 6 of the season. The intervention engine demonstrates that feasible remediation was available until Month 9, after which category-level constraints rendered full compliance infeasible under the model constraints --- a finding with direct implications for mid-season financial governance. The framework is fully open-source and can be deployed as an interactive dashboard.

title: The Disruption of Search Engine Optimization by Large Language Models: A Mixed-Methods Analysis of the Evolving Search Landscape

detail.title: The Disruption of Search Engine Optimization by Large Language Models: A Mixed-Methods Analysis of the Evolving Search Landscape
detail.abstract: Large Language Models have reshaped the search landscape in ways that are only beginning to be understood. Google's AI Overviews, ChatGPT Search, and Perplexity AI now mediate a growing share of how people find information online, and the consequences for traditional Search Engine Optimization are substantial but unevenly distributed. This paper takes a mixed-methods approach to understanding what is actually happening. On the quantitative side, I draw on Semrush's analysis of over 10 million keywords, Previsible's dataset of 1.96 million LLM-referred sessions, and Chartbeat's global traffic analytics, among other sources. On the qualitative side, I analyze 23 publisher case studies and strategy documents through thematic coding. The picture that emerges is more complicated than either the "SEO is dead" or "nothing has changed" camps acknowledge. AI Overview prevalence fluctuated between 6.49% and 25% of queries throughout 2025. Click-through rates for top-ranking pages dropped 34.5% when AI Overviews appeared, yet Semrush's own before-and-after tracking found that zero-click rates for the same keywords actually decreased slightly, from 33.75% to 31.53%. I attempt to reconcile these tensions through what I call the Search Ecosystem Disruption Model (SEDM), which brings together Christensen's disruptive innovation theory, Pirolli and Card's information foraging theory, and platform economics. The data show striking asymmetries: Chartbeat documents 33-38% declines in Google Search referral traffic for publishers, with news sites losing up to 26% while e-commerce barely registers a change. I present five falsifiable predictions, a practitioner roadmap, and the roughly $2 billion in annual publisher advertising revenue at stake.

title:
Sustainable Business Models under Strong Sustainability: A Conceptual and Analytical
Framework
affiliations: Universidad de Alicante and Universidad de Alicante

detail.title:
Sustainable Business Models under Strong Sustainability: A Conceptual and Analytical
Framework
detail.abstract:
The literature on sustainable business models has expanded considerably in recent decades. Nevertheless, substantial conceptual ambiguity persists regarding the conditions under which a business model can be considered
sustainable in the long term. In particular, a significant share of existing approaches implicitly or explicitly relies on a weak sustainability perspective based on the substitutability of different forms of capital, thereby limiting their ability to consistently account for the social and ecological constraints that shape economic activity.

This paper develops a conceptual and analytical framework to define and assess sustainable business models from a strong sustainability perspective. Building on a view of the business model as a system of value creation, capture, and
distribution, the paper introduces the intertemporal balance of economic, social, and natural capital as a constitutive condition of sustainability. On this basis, a graphical formalization is proposed to make explicit the flows of value between
the firm, consumers, and the socio-ecological environment, together with an analytical formalization that translates this normative principle into a set of explicit conditions.

Adopting a Design Science Research approach, the paper contributes to clarifying the concept of sustainable business models and provides a rigorous framework to distinguish between models compatible with strong sustainability and those that achieve economic viability through the degradation of social or natural capital. The paper discusses the main theoretical implications of the proposed framework, as well as its limitations and directions for future research.

title: Interactive Segmentation of the Myocardium in 2D Cardiac MRI: A Comparative Study with Baseline Methods

detail.title: Interactive Segmentation of the Myocardium in 2D Cardiac MRI: A Comparative Study with Baseline Methods
detail.abstract: Background and ObjectivesMedical image segmentation is essential for assessing organ function, such as computing the ejection fraction from cardiac MRI, yet manual delineation remains time-consuming. Deep Learning-based automatic methods have achieved considerable progress, but enabling radiologists to refine segmentations with effective interactive tools remains essential. This work unifies both paradigms by combining automatic and interactive segmentation, enabling fast initial predictions iteratively refined through minimal guidance. MethodsCardiacITM is a 2D interactive segmentation model for myocardial delineation in cardiac MRI, combining automatic prediction with direct user correction to reduce manual editing time and improve accuracy. It is built upon the Reviving Iterative Training with Mask Guidance (RITM) framework, extended with an automatic prediction setting. User interactions consist of corrective clicks encoded as fixed-radius disks in image-sized tensors. For training and fair evaluation, these clicks are simulated by targeting the largest error region. Models are trained on the ACDC dataset and evaluated on the ACDC test and M{\&}Ms-2 datasets, comprising 300 and 720 cardiac MRI acquisitions, respectively. Performance is compared to nnUNet, RITM, DeepGrow, and DeepEdit using Dice scores, with Friedman and Nemenyi post-hoc tests.ResultsIn the automatic setting, CardiacITM was comparable to nnUNet (Dice score ACDC: 0.888 vs. 0.891, p = 0.151) and outperformed DeepEdit (Dice score ACDC: 0.788, p = 0.0000). In the interactive setting, CardiacITM significantly outperformed existing models. After 3 clicks, it reached a Dice score of 0.927, vs. 0.876 for RITM; after 11 clicks, it achieved 0.957, vs. 0.886 for RITM on ACDC test. ConclusionOur results suggest that it is possible to overcome the typical trade-off between automatic and interactive segmentation using a simple and effective architecture. CardiacITM improves segmentation quality while offering flexibility for user correction, making it a promising tool for clinical applications.

title: Leader psychosocial safety behaviour: Insights from occupational safety practitioners
affiliations: University of Wollongong, University of Wollongong and La Trobe University

detail.title: Leader psychosocial safety behaviour: Insights from occupational safety practitioners
detail.abstract: In recent years psychosocial hazard mitigation has received much attention in Australia. Calls by researchers and practitioners for the management of psychosocial hazards have been met with the introduction of legislation that mandates the management of these hazards in the workplace. Globally, research into psychosocial hazards continues to expand, with leadership emerging as a key driver of psychosocial safety. Leaders can contribute to psychosocial hazard mitigation through their leadership style (the leadership theory they adopt) and through behavioural competencies (the day-to-day actions of leaders). This paper explores the latter by studying the psychosocial safety behaviour (PSB) that leaders require to bring about psychosocial safety in the workplace.A qualitative, idiographic study was conducted among 18 professionals with psychosocial safety responsibility in their workplaces.  Applying conceptual description, the study identified three task-specific behaviours and two contextual psychosocial safety behaviours required from leaders. The task-specific behaviours that promote psychosocial safety were proactive psychosocial safety behaviour, psychosocial hazard identification, and courteousness. Contextual behaviours are the behaviours that, though not directly related to the psychosocial safety of workers, indirectly contribute to psychosocial safety in the workplace. In this study these behaviours were role-modelling and empathy.This study solicited the views of support professionals who included occupational safety practitioners and human resources practitioners who, due to their unique position in workplaces, have access to leaders and workers, making them ideal candidates to give insights into leaders’ PSB. The findings align with recent research findings on PSB and contribute new empirical insights into the relationship between psychological safety and psychosocial safety climate, a link that has been conceptually proposed but remains underexplored in Australian workplace research.As organisational leaders play a key role in creating an organisation climate that promotes psychosocial safety, this study contributes to the literature by identifying the leader competencies required to promote psychosocial safety in workplaces.
